ProximalLangevin/Proximal.lean.title: Proximal minimizers and subgradient optimality
ProximalLangevin/Proximal.lean.summary: On a real inner-product space, define \(Q_{\lambda,x}(p)=f(p)+\|p-x\|^2/(2\lambda)\). A proximal point minimizes this objective globally. In finite dimension, convexity, a lower bound for the function, and \(\lambda>0\) give existence by compact attainment. The scaled residual is a subgradient at the minimizer; subgradient monotonicity then proves uniqueness and firm nonexpansiveness. The variational statements also apply to any point already known to minimize the objective.

steps.title: The objective and global subgradient supports
steps.body:
The condition \(p\in\arg\min Q_{\lambda,x}\) means global minimization of the quadratic-penalized objective. The support condition \(s\in\partial f(p)\) means that \(f(p)+\langle s,y-p\rangle\le f(y)\) for every competitor \(y\). Apply these global support inequalities at \((p,s)\) and \((q,t)\), taking each support point as the competitor for the other. Addition cancels the function values and gives \(\langle s-t,p-q\rangle\ge0\).

The resulting inequality \(0\le\langle s-t,p-q\rangle\) is monotonicity of the subdifferential. Its proof uses only the support inequalities and inner-product algebra, and remains valid at nondifferentiable points of a convex function.

Formal correspondence: proxObjective : Objective minimized by the proximity mapping with parameter \(\lambda\). IsProxPoint : \(p\) solves the actual unconstrained proximity minimization problem at \(x\). IsSubgradient : The global supporting-hyperplane characterization of a convex subgradient.

steps.title: The residual characterizes the minimum
steps.body:
A vector \(s\) supports \(g_2\) at \(p\) when \(g_2(p)+\langle s,y-p\rangle\le g_2(y)\) for every \(y\). For positive proximal parameter, minimization is equivalent to the residual support condition

\[ p=P_\lambda(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{x-p}{\lambda}\in\partial g_2(p). \]

For necessity, compare the objective at a minimizer \(p\) with its value at \(p+t(y-p)\). Convexity bounds the function increment, and division by positive \(t\) followed by a limit gives the support inequality. For sufficiency, substitute that support in the difference of the quadratic objectives. The remaining squared norm is nonnegative, proving global minimality without differentiability of \(g_2\).

Monotonicity applied to the two residual supports gives

\[ \|P_\lambda(x)-P_\lambda(y)\|^2 \le\langle x-y,P_\lambda(x)-P_\lambda(y)\rangle. \]

Cauchy–Schwarz proves nonexpansiveness of \(P_\lambda\). Expansion of the residual squared difference proves nonexpansiveness of \(I-P_\lambda\). To state the necessity calculation explicitly, fix competitor \(y\) and put \(d=y-p\). Compare the objective at \(p\) and \(p+td\) for \(0<t\le1\). Convexity bounds \(f(p+td)\) by \((1-t)f(p)+tf(y)\). Expansion of the quadratic and division by \(t\) gives

\[f(y)-f(p)\ge\left\langle\frac{x-p}{\lambda},d\right\rangle-\frac{t}{2\lambda}\|d\|^2.\]

Letting \(t\downarrow0\) proves the support. Conversely the same support gives \(Q_{\lambda,x}(y)-Q_{\lambda,x}(p)\ge\|y-p\|^2/(2\lambda)\) at \(p\), quantitatively bounding the objective increase away from \(p\). Thus the support condition proves both optimality and quadratic growth of the penalized objective.

Formal correspondence: isProxPoint_of_subgradient : A residual subgradient is sufficient for proximal optimality. subgradient_of_isProxPoint : Convex proximal minimizers satisfy the residual subgradient inequality. isProxPoint_iff_subgradient : Exact convex proximal optimality condition.

steps.title: Uniqueness and nonexpansiveness of the proximal and residual maps
steps.body:
Apply subgradient monotonicity to \((x-p)/\lambda\) and \((y-q)/\lambda\). Multiplication by positive \(\lambda\) and expansion give \(\|p-q\|^2\le\langle x-y,p-q\rangle\). For equal inputs this forces \(p=q\), proving uniqueness. Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(\|p-q\|\le\|x-y\|\). Expanding \(\|(x-y)-(p-q)\|^2\) and using the same firm inequality gives \(\|(x-p)-(y-q)\|\le\|x-y\|\).

In the notation \(u=x-y\) and \(v=p-q\), firmness states \(\langle u,v\rangle\ge\|v\|^2\). Therefore \(\|u-v\|^2\le\|u\|^2-\|v\|^2\le\|u\|^2\). This proves the unit Lipschitz bound for the residual map \(I-P_\lambda\). For equal inputs, \(v=0\) gives uniqueness separately from the existence argument.

Formal correspondence: IsProxPoint.firm : Firm nonexpansiveness follows from convex proximal optimality. IsProxPoint.nonexpansive : Proximal minimizers are nonexpansive in the input. IsProxPoint.residual_nonexpansive : The residual of the proximal mapping is also nonexpansive.

steps.title: Existence by compact minimization
steps.body:
Assume \(\lambda>0\) and define

\[ Q_{\lambda,x}(p)=g_2(p)+\frac{\|p-x\|^2}{2\lambda},\qquad P_\lambda(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_p Q_{\lambda,x}(p). \]

A finite convex function on a finite-dimensional real space is continuous. If \(g_2\ge b\), the positive quadratic term forces \(Q_{\lambda,x}(p)\) above the competitor value \(Q_{\lambda,x}(x)=g_2(x)\) outside a large ball. A suitable radius is \(\sqrt{2\lambda(g_2(x)-b)}+1\). Compactness and continuity give a minimizer inside that ball, and the outside bound makes it global.

More precisely, center the ball at \(x\) and choose it to contain every point whose objective can be smaller than the value at \(x\). The lower bound on the function and positivity of the quadratic coefficient give this containment. The compact minimizer is therefore also a global minimizer, and the residual support condition proves that it is unique.

The Lean definition chooses a minimizer when one exists and assigns zero outside that domain. All mathematical endpoints establish existence from convexity, the lower bound, and positive \(\lambda\); their conclusions do not depend on that fallback value. Strict convexity of the quadratic, expressed through the variational characterization below, gives uniqueness.

The existence argument first uses finite-dimensional convexity of a finite-valued function to obtain continuity. If \(f\ge b\), a radius \(R>\sqrt{2\lambda(f(x)-b)}\) ensures \(Q_{\lambda,x}(p)>f(x)=Q_{\lambda,x}(x)\) whenever \(\|p-x\|>R\). A minimum on the compact closed ball is therefore global. The chosen-map theorem invokes this existence result under its explicit assumptions, then uniqueness identifies all minimizers. Consequently later occurrences of prox denote the actual unique minimizer on the positive-parameter domain.

Formal correspondence: exists_proxPoint : Existence of proximal minimizers for finite-valued convex potentials bounded below. Finite-valued convex functions are automatically continuous in finite dimensions. prox : Choice of a true proximal minimizer, with zero as a harmless value off the existence domain. prox_isProxPoint : On its mathematical domain, prox attains the quadratic minimum.

ProximalLangevin/Moreau.lean.title: Moreau envelope: gradient, smoothness and finite bias
ProximalLangevin/Moreau.lean.summary: Let \(f\) be finite, convex, and bounded below on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, and let \(\lambda>0\). Set \(P=P_\lambda\), \(f^\lambda(x)=Q_{\lambda,x}(P x)\), and \(r(x)=(x-Px)/\lambda\). Comparison of minimizing objectives at neighboring inputs gives a two-sided quadratic remainder, proving that the envelope gradient is the scaled proximal residual. A global Lipschitz bound on the original function also bounds the residual and the uniform difference between the original function and its envelope.

steps.title: Value bounds and the exact residual
steps.body:
The envelope is the minimum objective value. Using competitor \(p=x\) gives \(f^\lambda(x)\le f(x)\). If \(f\ge b\), nonnegativity of the quadratic term gives \(f^\lambda\ge b\). These comparisons prove that the envelope is finite and satisfies the same lower bound at every input.

The residual at a minimizing point is a subgradient of the original function. Identification with the derivative of the envelope requires the two neighboring-objective comparisons below; it does not follow from the value bounds alone.

Formal correspondence: moreau : Moreau envelope, evaluated at the selected true proximal point. residual : The proximal residual, which is the actual Moreau gradient on its domain. moreau_le : The Moreau envelope lies below the original potential. le_moreau : The Moreau envelope is above every common lower bound of the potential.

steps.title: Global supports and quadratic upper remainder
steps.body:
Use the residual support at \(P x\) with competitor \(P y\). Addition of the two quadratic penalties leaves a nonnegative squared norm, giving \(f^\lambda(x)+\langle r(x),y-x\rangle\le f^\lambda(y)\). In the other direction, use \(P x\) as competitor for the objective at \(y\). Expanding its penalty gives upper remainder \(\|y-x\|^2/(2\lambda)\).

For \(z=ax+by\), apply the global envelope supports based at \(z\) to the two endpoints. Multiply by weights \(a,b\ge0\) satisfying \(a+b=1\). Their linear terms cancel, proving convexity. The lower comparison uses the support of the original function at \(P_\lambda x\), whereas the upper comparison uses only the old minimizer as an admissible competitor. Its quadratic remainder is \(\|y-x\|^2/(2\lambda)\).

Formal correspondence: moreau_support : The proximal residual supports the Moreau envelope globally. moreau_upper : Quadratic upper Taylor bound for the Moreau envelope. moreau_convex : Convexity of the envelope is a consequence of its global supports.

steps.title: Nonexpansiveness and the derivative
steps.body:
Define \(g_2^\lambda(x)=Q_{\lambda,x}(P_\lambda(x))\) and \(r_\lambda(x)=\lambda^{-1}(x-P_\lambda(x))\). The residual support gives the lower comparison and the old minimizer as competitor gives the upper comparison:

\[ 0\le g_2^\lambda(y)-g_2^\lambda(x) -\langle r_\lambda(x),y-x\rangle \le\frac{\|y-x\|^2}{2\lambda}. \]

The upper remainder is \(o(\|y-x\|)\), so \(\nabla g_2^\lambda=r_\lambda\). The global supports also give convexity. Nonexpansiveness of \(I-P_\lambda\) yields

\[ \|\nabla g_2^\lambda(x)-\nabla g_2^\lambda(y)\| \le\lambda^{-1}\|x-y\|. \]

For \(y=x+h\), the remainder divided by \(\|h\|\) is bounded by \(\|h\|/(2\lambda)\), which tends to zero. Thus the Fréchet derivative is \(h\mapsto\langle r_\lambda(x),h\rangle\). The residual-map inequality gives gradient Lipschitz constant \(1/\lambda\), hence continuity of the gradient. These facts justify smooth Langevin analysis for the envelope even when the original function is nonsmooth.

The key derivative estimate is the two-sided remainder \[0\le f^\lambda(x+h)-f^\lambda(x)-\langle r_\lambda(x),h\rangle\le\frac{\|h\|^2}{2\lambda}.\] Dividing by \(\|h\|\) makes the upper bound \(\|h\|/(2\lambda)\to0\). The declaration moreau_hasGradientAt packages this Fréchet remainder estimate, moreau_differentiable forgets the derivative value, and gradient_moreau identifies the derivative's Riesz vector with the residual. The continuity of that residual, already obtained from nonexpansiveness of \(I-P_\lambda\), upgrades differentiability to \(C^1\).

Formal correspondence: prox_lipschitz : The selected proximal mapping is nonexpansive. residual_lipschitz : The actual envelope residual has the sharp \(1/\lambda\) Lipschitz constant. moreau_hasGradientAt : The Moreau envelope is differentiable, with gradient equal to its proximal residual. moreau_differentiable : Differentiability of the actual Moreau envelope. gradient_moreau : Exact formula for the actual Moreau gradient. moreau_contDiff : The envelope is continuously differentiable, even when \(f\) is nonsmooth.

steps.title: Bounded residual and a sharp uniform gap
steps.body:
Assume \(f\) is convex, bounded below, and globally \(K\)-Lipschitz, with \(K\ge0\) and \(\lambda>0\). At input \(x\), write \(p=P_\lambda(x)\) and \(r=(x-p)/\lambda\). The optimality condition gives \(r\in\partial f(p)\). Test this support at \(p+r\) and apply the Lipschitz bound:

\[ \|r\|^2\le f(p+r)-f(p)\le K\|r\|. \]

For \(r=0\) the residual bound is immediate; otherwise cancellation of its positive norm gives \(\|r\|\le K\). From \(x-p=\lambda r\) one obtains \(\|x-p\|\le\lambda K\).

To bound the value gap, competitor \(p=x\) gives \(f^\lambda(x)\le f(x)\). Set \(d=\|p-x\|\) and subtract the minimizing objective value:

\[ \begin{aligned} f(x)-f^\lambda(x) &=f(x)-f(p)-\frac{d^2}{2\lambda}\\ &\le Kd-\frac{d^2}{2\lambda}\\ &=\frac{\lambda K^2}{2}-\frac{(d-\lambda K)^2}{2\lambda} \le\frac{\lambda K^2}{2}. \end{aligned} \]

The squared remainder has a positive denominator because \(\lambda>0\). Together with the upper comparison this proves \(0\le f(x)-f^\lambda(x)\le\lambda K^2/2\) at every input. For \(U=g_1+f\) and \(V_\lambda=g_1+f^\lambda\) the same estimate becomes \(V_\lambda\le U\le V_\lambda+\lambda K^2/2\). Exponentiation and latent integration then compare marginal potentials by the same finite gap. No asymptotic expansion or interchange of an unbounded remainder with integration is required.

Formal correspondence: residual_norm_le : The Moreau gradient has norm at most the Lipschitz constant of \(f\). prox_displacement_le : A Lipschitz potential moves each proximal point by at most \(\lambda K\). moreau_lower_of_lipschitz : Sharp uniform approximation bound for a \(K\)-Lipschitz potential. moreau_gap_of_lipschitz : The pointwise Moreau correction is nonnegative and at most \(\lambda K^2/2\).

ProximalLangevin/StrongMoreau.lean.title: Strong convexity after full Moreau smoothing
ProximalLangevin/StrongMoreau.lean.summary: Full Moreau smoothing reduces the curvature by factor \(1+m\lambda\). Specifically an \(m\)-strongly convex potential has envelope curvature \(m_\lambda=m/(1+m\lambda)\) under \(m\ge0\) and \(\lambda>0\). Compare the envelope at a convex combination of inputs with the objective at the corresponding combination of proximal minimizers. Combining the potential and quadratic-penalty deficits and completing a square proves the result. Existence of those minimizers follows from finite-dimensional convexity and the lower bound; differentiability of the original potential is not required.

steps.title: Quadratic identities for envelope curvature
steps.body:
For \(a+b=1\), inner-product expansion gives \(\|au+bv\|^2=a\|u\|^2+b\|v\|^2-ab\|u-v\|^2\). The same expansion and completion of a square give

\[m\|u\|^2+\frac{\|u-v\|^2}{\lambda}-\frac{m\|v\|^2}{1+m\lambda}=\frac{\|(1+m\lambda)u-v\|^2}{\lambda(1+m\lambda)}\ge0.\]

The denominator \(\lambda(1+m\lambda)\) is positive under \(\lambda>0\) and \(m\ge0\). Dropping the nonnegative square therefore bounds a quadratic in the input difference by the sum of a quadratic in the proximal-output difference and a quadratic in the residual difference. This is the precise coefficient needed in the convexity comparison.

Formal correspondence: norm_convexCombo_sq : Exact square identity for a convex combination in a real inner product space. weighted_quadratic_lower : The quadratic infimal convolution has the sharp effective modulus.

steps.title: Strong convexity from the proximal minimizer comparison
steps.body:
Let \(U\) be \(m\)-strongly convex. Its full Moreau envelope is

\[ m_\lambda=\frac{m}{1+m\lambda}\text{-strongly convex}. \]

Use the convex combination of the two proximal minimizers as a competitor. Strong convexity of \(U\) and the quadratic-combination identity give two nonnegative deficits. Their required bound is

\[ \frac{m}{1+m\lambda}\|v\|^2 \le m\|u\|^2+\frac{\|u-v\|^2}{\lambda}. \]

The completed-square identity proves this coefficient without differentiability of \(U\). By comparison, smoothing only \(g_2\) and adding it to an unsmoothed strongly convex \(g_1\) preserves the curvature of the latter term.

In detail, put \(p=P_\lambda(x)\), \(q=P_\lambda(y)\), and \(z=ax+by\), and test at \(ap+bq\) for \(a+b=1\). The potential deficit is \(\frac{mab}{2}\|p-q\|^2\) and the penalty deficit is \(\frac{ab}{2\lambda}\|(p-q)-(x-y)\|^2\). Their sum is at least \(\frac{ab}{2}\frac{m}{1+m\lambda}\|x-y\|^2\) because \(\lambda(1+m\lambda)\) is positive. Equivalently, with \(u=p-q\) and \(v=x-y\), the two quadratic expressions are \(m\|u\|^2\) and \(\|u-v\|^2/\lambda\); their sum is bounded below by \(m\|v\|^2/(1+m\lambda)\). This is exactly the strong-convexity correction at the original inputs.

Formal correspondence: moreau_strongConvex : The actual Moreau envelope preserves strong convexity with the exact reduced modulus.

ProximalLangevin/ProximalEnergy.lean.title: A proximal distance–energy inequality
ProximalLangevin/ProximalEnergy.lean.summary: Let \(f\) be convex, \(p=P_\eta(x)\) its proximal point at positive scale \(\eta\), and \(s\in\partial f(x)\) a subgradient at the input. The support at the proximal point bounds its squared distance to an arbitrary comparator. The input support then replaces the proximal function value by the input value. Completion of a square bounds the remaining term by the squared scale times the squared subgradient norm.

steps.title: The support and completed-square estimates
steps.body:
Let \(p=P_\lambda(y)\), \(s\in\partial g_2(y)\), and comparator \(a\) be given. The residual subgradient at \(p\) supplies a support evaluated at \(a\). Evaluate the support of \(s\) at \(p\) and combine the inequalities with the squared-distance expansion. Nonnegativity of \(\|(y-p)-\lambda s\|^2\) gives the inequality corresponding to Lemma A.8 of the source paper:

\[ \|p-a\|^2\le\|y-a\|^2 -2\lambda\bigl(g_2(y)-g_2(a)\bigr)+\lambda^2\|s\|^2. \]

Under \(\|s\|^2\le C\), the last term is at most \(\lambda^2C\). The selected minimal subgradient in the source assumption is one possible choice; any supporting subgradient with the same norm bound suffices.

In equivalent notation, put \(d=x-p\). The support at \(p\) gives \(2\eta[f(p)-f(a)]\le2\langle d,p-a\rangle\), and the input support gives \(f(x)-f(p)\le\langle s,d\rangle\). Their addition to the distance expansion leaves \(2\eta\langle s,d\rangle-\|d\|^2\le\eta^2\|s\|^2\), which follows from \(\|d-\eta s\|^2\ge0\). This proves the energy estimate directly from proximal optimality and the input subgradient bound.

Formal correspondence: isProxPoint_energy_le : Proximity decreases squared distance and nonsmooth energy, up to the squared norm of any subgradient at the input point.

steps.title: The energy inequality for the proximal map
steps.body:
The existence theorem supplies a minimizer \(P_\eta(x)\), so the variational estimate gives \(\|P_\eta(x)-a\|^2\le\|x-a\|^2-2\eta(f(x)-f(a))+\eta^2\|s\|^2\). If \(\|s\|^2\le C\), multiplication by nonnegative \(\eta^2\) bounds its remainder by \(\eta^2 C\).

The underlying expansion is \(\|p-y\|^2=\|x-y\|^2-2\langle x-p,x-y\rangle+\|x-p\|^2\). The residual support at \(p\) bounds the associated inner product by the function difference. A subgradient \(s_x\in\partial f(x)\) bounds \(f(x)-f(p)\) by \(\langle s_x,x-p\rangle\). Completing the square then gives \(2\lambda\langle s_x,x-p\rangle-\|x-p\|^2\le\lambda^2\|s_x\|^2\). Thus \(\|s_x\|^2\le C\) yields remainder \(\lambda^2C\).

The comparator is arbitrary, so a random reference point may later be substituted pointwise. A numerical bound on \(\|s\|^2\) controls only the remainder; \(s\) must still satisfy the global support condition. Positivity of the scale ensures both minimizer existence and the residual optimality characterization.

Formal correspondence: prox_energy_le : The deterministic nonsmooth energy estimate for the actual chosen minimizer of the proximal objective. prox_energy_le_of_subgradient_bound : A squared-subgradient bound supplies the forcing term in Lemma A.8.

ProximalLangevin/ParticleEnergy.lean.title: Energy estimates for averaged pairwise proximal outputs
ProximalLangevin/ParticleEnergy.lean.summary:
The pairwise algorithm averages the proposed parameter outputs and rescales the proposed latent outputs. It generally differs from a proximal minimizer of one objective on the shared state. Nevertheless Jensen’s inequality bounds its squared parameter error, and the latent squared errors satisfy exact scaling identities. Summing the single-pair proximal inequalities therefore gives the required full-state energy estimate for the stated algorithm.

The scaled state is \(z=(\theta,x_1/\sqrt N,\ldots,x_N/\sqrt N)\), with \(N>0\), and \(J_i z=(\theta,x_i)\). The actual algorithm averages proximal parameter outputs; this module proves its energy inequality directly.

steps.title: Averaging squares in the shared parameter
steps.body:
For each parameter coordinate, Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(N(N^{-1}\sum_i b_i)^2\le\sum_i b_i^2\). Each latent coordinate instead has an exact squared scaling identity after multiplication by \(N\), using \((\sqrt N)^2=N\). Adding all coordinate inequalities gives

\[\|\operatorname{Pair}_P(z)-a\|^2\le\frac1N\sum_i\|P(J_i z)-J_i a\|^2.\]\[N\left|\frac1N\sum_i p_{i,\theta,j}-a_{\theta,j}\right|^2\le\sum_i|p_{i,\theta,j}-a_{\theta,j}|^2.\]

For latent coordinate \((i,j)\) the identity is

\[N|N^{-1/2}p_{i,x,j}-a_{i,j}|^2=|p_{i,x,j}-\sqrt N a_{i,j}|^2.\]

For vectors \(b_i\), the parameter estimate is Jensen’s inequality \(\|N^{-1}\sum_i b_i\|^2\le N^{-1}\sum_i\|b_i\|^2\). Here \(b_i\) denotes the parameter difference between the \(i\)-th pair output and the common comparator. Its latent contribution is exactly \(N^{-1}\|p_{i,x}-\sqrt N a_i\|^2\). Thus the bound holds for any pair map, independently of convexity or proximal optimality.

The first declaration is the scalar Jensen inequality \(N\bar b^2\le\sum_i b_i^2\), with \(\bar b=N^{-1}\sum_i b_i\). It follows by multiplying the average-of-squares inequality by positive \(N\); hn supplies exactly that sign and the nonzero denominator.

For the state-space comparison, write \(p_i=P(A_i z)\), with \(A_i z=(\theta,\sqrt N z_i)\), and let the comparison state be \(a\). In parameter coordinate \(j\), the discrepancy is the average of \(p_{i,\theta,j}-a_{\theta,j}\), since the common comparison parameter is the same for every pair. The local identity hid inside hθ moves that constant through the average, and scalar Jensen gives

This is hx, using \((\sqrt N)^2=N\). Expand the two Euclidean squared norms into finite coordinate sums, exchange the parameter and particle summations, and add the parameter inequalities to the exact latent identities. The result is \(N\|\operatorname{Pair}P(z)-a\|^2\le\sum_i\|p_i-A_i a\|^2\); division by \(N>0\) proves the displayed bound. No convexity or proximal property of \(P\) is used at this geometric stage.

Formal correspondence: average_sq_le : Jensen's inequality for an average of real coordinates. pairwiseMap_sq_dist_le : Squared distance of the actual averaged output is bounded by the average of the separate pairwise squared distances. This holds for every joint map.

steps.title: Summation of the pairwise proximal energy inequalities
steps.body:
The averaged pairwise output need not minimize the shared-state proximal objective. The valid comparison is instead

\[ \|\operatorname{Pair}_P(z)-a\|^2 \le\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\|P(J_i z)-J_i a\|^2. \]

Apply the single-pair energy inequality to each term. The identities \(\sum_i\|J_i(z-a)\|^2=N\|z-a\|^2\) and \(G_2=N^{-1}\sum_i g_2\circ J_i\) give

\[ \|\operatorname{Pair}_{P_\lambda}(z)-a\|^2 \le\|z-a\|^2-2\lambda\bigl(G_2(z)-G_2(a)\bigr)+\lambda^2C. \]

This estimate uses the minimizing property only for each individual pair. It is the deterministic energy statement required in the splitting analysis; it is not by itself a stochastic convergence theorem.

A counterexample to shared-state proximal optimality has \(N=2\), \(g_2(\theta,x)=|\theta-x|\), proximal scale one, common parameter \(1\), and physical latent values \((0,4)\). The pair minimizers are \((1/2,1/2)\) and \((2,3)\), so averaging their parameter components gives \((5/4,1/2,3)\). The feasible shared-state competitor \((1,1,3)\) has objective \(3/2\), strictly below the pairwise output value \(51/32\).

To derive the valid estimate, apply the pair inequality at \(A_i z\) against \(A_i y\) and sum its \(N\) instances. The identity \(\sum_i\|A_i(z-y)\|^2=N\|z-y\|^2\) controls the initial squared distances. Divide by positive \(N\); the potential term becomes \(N^{-1}\sum_i[f(A_i z)-f(A_i y)]\). Equivalently the initial sum is \(N\|z-a\|^2\) and the potential sum is \(N[G_2(z)-G_2(a)]\), whose division by \(N>0\) gives the displayed full-state expression. Jensen supplies the parameter inequality, exact latent scaling supplies the other coordinates, and the averaged subgradient bounds supply the remainder.

Formal correspondence: pairwise_prox_energy_le : The actual averaged pairwise proximal update satisfies the lifted energy estimate for the original nonsmooth potential. This proves the bridge needed in v3 Corollary A.13 directly, without a false prox -of-a-sum identity. The bound only needs one bounded subgradient at each pair input. In particular the paper's bound on the least-norm subgradient supplies this hypothesis whenever that minimal section is available.

ProximalLangevin/Algorithms.lean.title: Exact maps for MYIPLA, PIPULA and PIPGLA
ProximalLangevin/Algorithms.lean.summary:
MYIPLA, PIPULA, and PIPGLA use the same scaled parameter–particle space but apply drift, proximal maps, and Gaussian perturbations in different orders. Define these update maps first for arbitrary deterministic inputs. The residual identity identifies MYIPLA and its PIPULA specialization with Euler updates for suitable envelopes. PIPGLA applies proximity after the noisy drift and therefore requires its own splitting estimate.

Write \(F_g(z)=\sum_i g(J_i z)\), \(h=\gamma/N\), and \(a=\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\). This module first defines pointwise algorithms for an arbitrary joint map \(P\); probabilistic assumptions enter later modules.

steps.title: The averaged pair map in coordinates
steps.body:
Define the parameter and latent coordinates of the pair map by \(\operatorname{Pair}_P(z)_\theta=N^{-1}\sum_i(P(J_i z))_\theta\) and \(\operatorname{Pair}_P(z)_{x_i}=N^{-1/2}(P(J_i z))_x\). Every pair is evaluated at the same preceding parameter. The proposed parameters are averaged, and each proposed latent coordinate returns to its own block.

The coefficient \(1/N\) averages the common parameter, while \(1/\sqrt N\) converts each physical latent output to a scaled coordinate. These definitions specify one shared parameter rather than separate evolving parameter copies. They do not assert minimization of a full-state proximal objective.

Formal correspondence: pairwiseMap : Apply a joint map to each common-parameter/particle pair, then average its parameter outputs and rescale its particle outputs.

steps.title: The order of drift, proximity, and noise
steps.body:
PIPGLA first takes the noisy gradient step for \(g_1\) and then applies the pairwise proximal map:

\[ y_n=z_n-\frac\gamma N\nabla\!\left(\sum_i g_1(J_i z_n)\right) +\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}{N}}\xi_n, \qquad z_{n+1}=\operatorname{Pair}_{P_\lambda}(y_n). \]

PIPULA is the MYIPLA specialization with \(g_1=0\) and \(\lambda=\gamma\), in which proximity precedes the added Gaussian perturbation. The expanded MYIPLA update is

\[T_{\mathrm{MY}}(z,\xi)=(1-\gamma/\eta)z-\frac\gamma N\nabla F_{g_1}(z)+\frac\gamma\eta\operatorname{Pair}_P(z)+\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\xi.\]

In MYIPLA the pairwise proximal value is evaluated at the preceding state and contributes through an explicit residual drift. In PIPGLA it is evaluated at the already perturbed smooth step. These compositions give different outputs for the same innovation. Their update identities must therefore be proved separately. In the source convergence analysis PIPGLA is compared with the original nonsmooth Gibbs model; the MYIPLA theorem cannot be applied merely by changing the update’s name.

Formal correspondence: pipulaUpdate : PIPULA: pairwise proximity, followed by noise. myiplaUpdate : MYIPLA, with independent smoothing and time steps. pipglaUpdate : PIPGLA: the noisy smooth forward step is followed by the pairwise proximal map. The common parameter is averaged only at the end.

steps.title: Recursion with a supplied innovation sequence
steps.body:
For an update function \(T\), define \(Z_0=z_0\) and \(Z_{n+1}=T(Z_n,\xi_n)\). Induction determines a unique finite-time sequence from the initial state and innovation sequence. Substitution of the three update maps defines the three particle algorithms.

This deterministic definition requires no Gaussian law or measurability assumption. When those properties and input independence are imposed, the same finite recursion becomes a measurable function of the inputs and defines its probability law. This permits the update equalities to be used on any probability space chosen for a coupling argument.

Formal correspondence: algorithmChain : Iterate the displayed state update against a specified innovation sequence. myiplaChain : The full MYIPLA recursion, without any convergence assumption.

steps.title: Equality of PIPULA and the specified MYIPLA specialization
steps.body:
The PIPULA parameter update is \(N^{-1}\sum_i(P(J_i z))_\theta+a\xi_\theta\). Specialize MYIPLA to \(g_1=0\) and \(\eta=\gamma\ne0\). The smooth gradient vanishes, \(1-\gamma/\gamma=0\) removes the old-state term, and \(\gamma/\gamma=1\) gives the pairwise proximal term with coefficient one. Thus the two updates agree for every state and innovation.

Induction in the common recursion gives equality of every finite iterate. Any probability law on the inputs consequently gives equal output laws. The identity uses equality and positivity of the relevant scales, rather than a limiting approximation.

Formal correspondence: pipulaUpdate_parameter : PIPULA's parameter component is precisely the averaged joint proximal parameter output, followed by the parameter Gaussian noise. pipulaUpdate_eq_myiplaUpdate : Removing the smooth part and equating the two time scales recovers PIPULA exactly, including its noise placement. pipulaChain_eq_myiplaChain : The exact PIPULA/MYIPLA specialization holds for every iteration.

steps.title: The physical parameter and latent-coordinate equations
steps.body:
The lifted smooth gradient has parameter block \(\sum_i\nabla_\theta g_1(J_i z)\) and latent block \(\sqrt N\nabla_x g_1(J_i z)\). Substitute these formulas into the state update. Multiplication of a latent coordinate by \(\sqrt N\) changes the Gaussian coefficient to \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\) and the smooth drift coefficient to \(\gamma\), using \(\sqrt N\sqrt{2\gamma/N}=\sqrt{2\gamma}\).

The parameter equation contains the average smooth force and average proximal parameter output. The physical latent equation contains the force and proximal output of its own pair. Multiplication by \(\sqrt N\) affects only the latent block. The resulting equations have parameter variance divided by particle count and the usual physical latent variance.

Formal correspondence: myiplaUpdate_parameter : The MYIPLA parameter coordinate is the displayed averaged pairwise formula. myiplaUpdate_particle : The MYIPLA physical-particle coordinate is exactly the displayed physical-particle formula.

steps.title: The residual identity and the smoothed Euler update
steps.body:
For a joint-pair map \(P\), apply \(P\) to each \(J_i z\), average the parameter outputs, and divide the physical latent outputs by \(\sqrt N\). This retains one common parameter rather than \(N\) parameter variables. For \(P=P_\lambda\), MYIPLA is the Euler update for \(V_\lambda=g_1+g_2^\lambda\) because

\[ \operatorname{Pair}_P(z)=z-\frac\lambda N\nabla\!\left(\sum_i g_2^\lambda(J_i z)\right). \]

Substitution into the expanded update cancels the extra multiples of \(z\) and gives

\[ z_{n+1}=z_n-\frac\gamma N\nabla\mathcal V_\lambda(z_n) +\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}{N}}\,\xi_n. \]

The parameter and physical latent Gaussian coefficients are \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\) and \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\). More explicitly, substituting \(P_\eta(v)=v-\eta\nabla g_2^\eta(v)\) in each pair makes the averaged and rescaled residual exactly \((\eta/N)\nabla F_{g_2^\eta}\). Addition of the smooth gradient then gives the force of \(g_1+g_2^\eta\). The Gaussian perturbation is unchanged. Equality of the complete chains follows by induction from equality of the update maps.

The recursion declarations include the initial and successor identities for each supplied innovation sequence. All pointwise identities concern the explicit state update, before any stochastic convergence theorem is applied.

For \(P(x)=x-\lambda r(x)\), the parameter coordinate of the pairwise map is its original parameter minus \(\lambda\) times the average parameter residual. Each latent coordinate similarly loses \(\lambda/\sqrt N\) times its pair residual. These are exactly the blocks of \((\lambda/N)\nabla V_N(r)\), using the previously proved lifted-gradient identities. Add \(\nabla g_1+\nabla e=\nabla(g_1+e)\) under differentiability and set the proximal scale to the Euler scale to identify the MYIPLA update with scaledUpdate. Induction then identifies the entire pointwise chain, not merely its first step.

Formal correspondence: pairwiseMap_eq_gradient_step : A pairwise residual gradient becomes the corresponding lifted Euler step. This is an equality of actual coordinate maps, not an assumed law identity. gradient_add_of_differentiable : The gradient of a sum, with the differentiability hypotheses explicit. myiplaUpdate_eq_scaledUpdate : The expanded MYIPLA step is exactly IPLA for \(g_1+e\) whenever \(e\) has the genuine proximal residual gradient. myiplaChain_eq_scaledChain : The entire expanded recursion agrees pointwise with the existing IPLA recursion for the smoothed potential.

ProximalLangevin/MYIPLA.lean.title: Smoothed-model MYIPLA laws and finite-time convergence
ProximalLangevin/MYIPLA.lean.summary: The expanded MYIPLA recursion equals Gaussian IPLA for \(V_\eta=g_1+g_2^\eta\). The Moreau gradient adds gradient constant \(1/\eta\) while preserving the curvature supplied by the smooth term. Write \(V_\eta=g_1+g_2^\eta\) and \(L_\eta=L_1+\eta^{-1}\), where \(g_1\) is differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex and \(g_2\) is convex and bounded below. Applying the transport and sharp concentration estimates to \(V_\eta\) gives a finite-time parameter bound about its marginal maximizer.

steps.title: Curvature and gradient regularity of the smoothed sum
steps.body:
The convexity inequality for the envelope adds no negative curvature to that of the smooth term. Its sum with the smooth term is therefore strongly convex with modulus \(m\). The triangle inequality for gradient differences gives gradient constant \(L_\eta=L_1+1/\eta\). These are constants in the joint-pair space; the replicated-pair norm identity multiplies both by particle count when forming the full-state potential.

The scalar potential is \(V_\eta=g_1+g_2^\eta\). Its envelope is convex, so adding the two convex-combination inequalities preserves strong convexity \(m\). Differentiability of both terms proves \( abla V_\eta= abla g_1+ abla g_2^\eta\); the triangle inequality then adds gradient constants. The nonnegative-real constant used by Lean equals \(L_1+\eta^{-1}\) when \(\eta>0\).

Formal correspondence: smoothedPotential : The pair potential of MYIPLA, with only its nonsmooth part regularized. smoothingLipschitz : Smoothing adds the inverse smoothing scale to the smooth gradient bound. smoothed_strongConvex : Adding a convex envelope preserves the strong convexity of the smooth part. smoothed_gradient_lipschitz : The gradient Lipschitz constants of the smooth part and envelope add.

steps.title: Equality of the recursion laws and finite parameter moments
steps.body:
Define \(\rho_n=Q\circ Z_n^{-1}\) from the expanded recursion. The residual-gradient identity makes this recursion pointwise equal to IPLA for any differentiable envelope satisfying that identity. The corresponding state is an \(L^2\) random vector. Bounded parameter projection and subtraction of a deterministic center preserve \(L^2\).

More explicitly, a globally Lipschitz gradient has at most linear growth, so \(L^2\) initial data and \(L^2\) innovations give finite second moments at every finite step. The resulting parameter error belongs to \(L^2\). Almost-sure equality of representatives gives equality of pushforward laws. These moment and law statements are established independently of the convergence estimate and justify its ordinary square-root expectation.

Formal correspondence: myiplaLaws : The law of the expanded MYIPLA recursion, for arbitrary supplied maps. myiplaLaws_eq_iplaLaws : Pointwise equivalence identifies the actual MYIPLA law with the IPLA law. myiplaLaws_parameter_memLp : Every projected MYIPLA error has a finite second moment whenever the initialization and innovations are in \(L^2\). This is derived from the actual chain, without Gaussianity, equilibrium, or an error bound assumption.

steps.title: The smoothed parameter-error estimate
steps.body:
Add the convex envelope to the \(m\)-strongly convex function \(g_1\). The sum retains modulus \(m\), and its gradient constant is \(L_\lambda=L_1+1/\lambda\). The identity \(\sum_i\|J_i v\|^2=N\|v\|^2\) gives full-state curvature \(Nm\), gradient constant \(NL_\lambda\), and dimension \(d_\theta+Nd_x\). Gaussian ULA at step \(\gamma/N\) therefore gives contraction \((1-m\gamma)^n\) and discretization term

\[ \frac{33}{20}\frac{L_\lambda}{m} \sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\sqrt\gamma. \]

The physical restriction \(\gamma\le2/(m+L_\lambda)\) is precisely the scaled ULA restriction. The prescribed Gaussian independence and finite initial moments give the required probability laws and finite transport. The parameter error at any fixed center belongs to \(L^2\). For smoothed marginal maximizer \(\theta_\eta\) and Gibbs target \(\Pi_{N,\eta}\), sharp concentration and projection give

\[\left(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_\eta\|^2\right)^{1/2}\le\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}+(1-m\gamma)^nW_2(\rho_0,\Pi_{N,\eta})+\frac{33}{20}\frac{L_\eta}{m}\sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\sqrt\gamma.\]

The general statement applies to any convex differentiable envelope with the residual-gradient identity and gradient constant \(\eta^{-1}\). For the Moreau envelope these properties are proved separately. The equilibrium radius is \(\sqrt{d_\theta/(Nm)}\), and the discretization coefficient depends on \(L_\eta/m\). Cancellation of \(N\) gives the physical step restriction. Thus particle count reduces equilibrium spread, but choosing a smaller smoothing scale also increases the gradient constant and restricts the step. The stationary reference and target moments are derived in the Gaussian transport theorem.

Formal correspondence: myipla_parameter_rms_smoothed : An explicit finite-time RMS parameter bound for MYIPLA around the maximizer of its smoothed marginal likelihood. All Gaussian-law hypotheses describe the algorithm's actual innovations. The dependence on the smoothing scale is explicit through \(L_1+\eta^{-1}\).

steps.title: The theorem for the Moreau envelope
steps.body:
For the Moreau envelope, proximal optimality and the neighboring-objective comparisons prove convexity, differentiability, \(\nabla g_2^\eta=\eta^{-1}(I-P_\eta)\), and gradient constant \(\eta^{-1}\). Substitution gives the stated smoothed convergence estimate. A measurable \(L^2\) representative pushes the initial probability space forward to a probability law.

The nonexpansive residual map gives the constant \(1/\eta\). These established envelope properties replace the general envelope assumptions. Linear growth of the update proves finite moments, and measurable pushforward proves mass one, independently of the numerical transport estimate.

For the genuine envelope, the proximal module supplies the residual identity \(\nabla g_2^\eta=(I-P_\eta)/\eta\), its differentiability and convexity, and the score Lipschitz constant \(\eta^{-1}\). Adding the smooth part gives \(V_\eta=g_1+g_2^\eta\), modulus \(m\) and score constant \(L_1+\eta^{-1}\). The theorem therefore discharges each abstract envelope assumption before applying the sharp IPLA estimate. The associated probability and moment declarations establish that the final law has total mass one and a finite projected RMS, independently of merely writing its integral.

Formal correspondence: moreau_myipla_parameter_rms : MYIPLA with the actual proximity minimizer and its actual Moreau envelope. Every analytic envelope property used by the stochastic theorem is derived from convexity and a lower bound on \(g_2\). In particular, no residual-gradient identity, stationarity result, concentration bound, or convergence estimate is an additional hypothesis of this theorem. moreau_myipla_parameter_memLp : Finite moments for MYIPLA with its genuine Moreau/proximal construction. moreau_myipla_isProbability : The actual MYIPLA output is a probability law. Measurability follows from the identified \(L^2\) recursion, rather than being assumed for the map.

ProximalLangevin/Theorem.lean.title: MYIPLA about the original nonsmooth marginal maximizer
ProximalLangevin/Theorem.lean.summary: Assume \(g_1\) is differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(L_1\)-Lipschitz gradient, and \(g_2\) is convex, bounded below, and \(K\)-Lipschitz. Let \(m,\eta,\gamma>0\), \(N>0\), and \(\gamma\le2/(m+L_1+\eta^{-1})\). Assume initialization in \(L^2\) and independent standard Gaussian innovation coordinates, independent of initialization. A finite uniform envelope gap bounds the displacement of the original and smoothed marginal maximizers. Adding this displacement to the smoothed-model estimate gives the four error terms below.

steps.title: Existence of an original marginal maximizer
steps.body:
The envelope estimate gives \(V_\eta\le U\le V_\eta+\eta K^2/2\) for \(U=g_1+g_2\). Since the smoothed potential is smooth and strongly convex, it has a Gaussian majorant controlling the latent integral \(k_U(\theta)=\int e^{-U(\theta,x)}dx\). In particular

\(e^{-\eta K^2/2}e^{-V_\eta}\le e^{-U}\le e^{-V_\eta}\).

These pointwise inequalities give positive finite original marginal values and an upper Gaussian bound with parameter decay. Continuity follows by dominated convergence, using continuity of the original potential and the common latent majorant. The positive continuous marginal tends to zero at infinity and therefore attains a maximum on a sufficiently large closed ball. Thus existence of an original marginal maximizer follows from the potential assumptions.

Formal correspondence: smoothedPotential_gap : The true smoothed pair potential is a one-sided uniform approximation of the original pair potential, with the sharp Lipschitz Moreau value gap. moreau_original_maximizer_exists : The original nonsmooth model has an actual marginal maximizer under the primitive MYIPLA assumptions; no maximizer existence assumption is hidden.

steps.title: The marginal-center displacement estimate
steps.body:
For the split Moreau approximation the uniform gap is \(\delta=\lambda K^2/2\). The marginal-potential comparison and strong convexity consequently give

\[ \|\theta_\star-\theta_{\lambda,\star}\| \le\sqrt{\frac{\lambda K^2}{m}}. \]

Both marginal maximizers exist. Once finite algorithmic second moments are established, Minkowski’s inequality gives

\[ \left(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_\star\|^2\right)^{1/2} \le\left(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_{\lambda,\star}\|^2\right)^{1/2} +\|\theta_{\lambda,\star}-\theta_\star\|. \]

To derive the deterministic displacement, compare \(F_{V_\eta}(\theta_U)\) and \(F_{V_\eta}(\theta_\eta)\). The marginal sandwich and minimality of \(\theta_U\) bound their difference by \(\eta K^2/2\). Strong-convexity growth bounds it below by \((m/2)\|\theta_U-\theta_\eta\|^2\). Comparing these bounds gives the finite \(O(\sqrt\eta)\) estimate. This differs from the source’s claimed linear smoothing expansion: no Hessian along a parameter fiber or uniform Taylor domination is assumed, so a linear rate is not substituted into the result.

The finite envelope gap is \(0\le U-V_\eta\le\delta=\eta K^2/2\). Integrating the corresponding exponential inequalities in the latent variable and taking logarithms gives a parameter-marginal potential gap of the same size. If \(\theta_\eta\) minimizes the smoothed marginal potential, strong convexity yields \[\frac m2\|\theta_U-\theta_\eta\|^2\le\delta,\qquad\|\theta_U-\theta_\eta\|\le\sqrt{\eta K^2/m}.\] The hypotheses hmaxU and hmaxη identify the actual two marginal maximizers, so this is a bound on their displacement rather than the choice of an arbitrary comparison center.

Formal correspondence: moreau_marginal_center_distance : A genuine finite smoothing-bias bound for marginal maximizers. It holds without twice differentiability, a fibrewise Hessian premise, or Taylor remainders: squared displacement is at most \(\eta K^2/m\).

steps.title: The MYIPLA bound about the original marginal maximizer
steps.body:
Let \(U=g_1+g_2\) on \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta+d_x}\). Assume \(g_1\) is differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(m>0\) and \(L_1\)-Lipschitz gradient. Assume \(g_2\) is finite, convex, bounded below, and \(K\)-Lipschitz. For \(\lambda>0\) put

\[ V_\lambda=g_1+g_2^\lambda,\qquad L_\lambda=L_1+\lambda^{-1}. \]

Take \(N>0\), finite-second-moment initialization, mutually independent standard Gaussian innovations independent of initialization, and

\[ 0<\gamma\le\frac{2}{m+L_\lambda}. \]

Let \(\mu_n\) be the scaled MYIPLA law, \(\Pi_{\lambda,N}\) the smoothed Gibbs law, and \(\theta_\star\) a maximizer of \(\int e^{-U(\theta,x)}dx\). Then

\[ \begin{aligned} \left(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_\star\|^2\right)^{1/2} \le{}&\sqrt{\frac{\lambda K^2}{m}} +\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}\\ &+(1-m\gamma)^n W_2(\mu_0,\Pi_{\lambda,N})\\ &+\frac{33}{20}\frac{L_\lambda}{m} \sqrt{d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}}\sqrt\gamma. \end{aligned} \]

Normalization, stationary comparison, finite transport moments, and sharp equilibrium concentration follow from the preceding transport and particle results. The last term depends on \(\lambda\). The source’s claimed \(O(\lambda)+O(\lambda^2)\) smoothing expression is replaced here by the proved finite \(O(\sqrt\lambda)\) bound; the statement is therefore a qualified version of that source theorem.

Apply the smoothed-model estimate at \(\theta_\eta\) and use its finite second moment in

\[\bigl(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_U\|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\le\bigl(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_\eta\|^2\bigr)^{1/2}+\|\theta_\eta-\theta_U\|.\]

The decomposition \(\theta_n-\theta_U=(\theta_n-\theta_\eta)+(\theta_\eta-\theta_U)\) gives this inequality by Minkowski. The deterministic term is bounded by the center comparison. Hence the four contributions are smoothing, equilibrium concentration, initial transport, and discretization. The coefficient still contains \(L_1+1/\eta\), so the admissible step and smoothing scale remain coupled.

In Lean the proof first establishes that the actual MYIPLA law is probability-valued and its error about the smoothed center is square integrable. The center-change inequality then has valid finite real square-root integrals. Add the proved center displacement to the smoothed theorem, giving exactly the displayed four terms.

Formal correspondence: moreau_myipla_parameter_rms_original : A fully proved finite-time theorem for the actual MYIPLA iterates and the original nonsmooth model's marginal maximizer. This is a finite replacement for the Taylor-based statement in v3 Theorem 4.1: the smoothing bias is \(\sqrt{\eta K^2/m}\), and the discretization constant explicitly depends on \(\eta\). There are no interpolation, entropy-production, or convergence hypotheses.

ProximalLangevin/ProjectionCenter.lean.title: Changing the deterministic center in a projected second moment
ProximalLangevin/ProjectionCenter.lean.summary: For probability \(\mu\) and bounded linear map \(T\), define \(R_\mu(a)=\|T(\cdot)-a\|_{L^2(\mu)}\) initially as an extended nonnegative norm. Minkowski’s inequality bounds the error about a new deterministic center by the old error plus the distance between centers. A finite old-center norm makes the new one finite, after which both are ordinary square-root integrals.

steps.title: Minkowski’s inequality and finiteness
steps.body:
The decomposition \(Tx-a=(Tx-b)+(b-a)\) and Minkowski’s inequality give \(R_\mu(a)\le R_\mu(b)+\|b-a\|\). The constant vector has the stated \(L^2\) norm because \(\mu\) has mass one. Thus \(R_\mu(b)<\infty\) implies finiteness of the error about \(a\).

For a measure of mass \(M\) the same constant would have \(L^2\) norm \(\sqrt M\|b-a\|\). Here \(M=1\) gives the coefficient one in the center-distance term. The extended norm inequality is valid before finiteness is known, so existence of the new-center moment is a consequence of this estimate.

Write \(R_a=\|Tx-a\|_{L^2(\mu)}\). The code's heq is the pointwise identity \(Tx-a=(Tx-b)+(b-a)\). Since \(\mu\) has mass one, the constant function \(b-a\) has \(L^2\) norm exactly \(\|b-a\|\). Thus eLpNorm_add_le gives \(R_a\le R_b+\|b-a\|\) even if \(R_b=\infty\). The second declaration uses the finite right-hand side to prove \(R_a<\infty\); it does not assume a second moment about the new center.

Formal correspondence: projectedRMS_center_le : Minkowski controls the change of a parameter center, with infinite moments still represented by the extended norm. projectedRMS_center_finite : A finite error about one center implies finiteness about every center.

steps.title: The inequality for ordinary square-root integrals
steps.body:
After finiteness is proved, the extended norm equals \(\sqrt{\int\|Tx-a\|^2d\mu}\) at the new center and \(\sqrt{\int\|Tx-b\|^2d\mu}\) at the old center. Monotonicity of conversion for a finite upper bound therefore gives \(R_\mu(a)\le R_\mu(b)+\|a-b\|\) as an ordinary real inequality.

This order of argument ensures that the displayed square-root integrals are finite second moments. A real-valued integral or extended-to-real conversion without the finiteness conclusion would not justify the same interpretation.

The order of operations matters: first prove finiteness at \(b\), then at \(a\), then apply ENNReal.toReal_mono. Only after these guards does projectedRMSReal_eq_sqrt_integral identify both real norms with \((\int\|Tx-a\|^2d\mu)^{1/2}\) and \((\int\|Tx-b\|^2d\mu)^{1/2}\). This prevents an infinite moment from being silently converted to the real number zero.

Formal correspondence: projectedRMSReal_center_le : The usual real-valued center-change inequality, guarded by a proved finite moment at the comparison center. sqrt_integral_center_le : The integral form follows after both finite quadratic moments have been established.

ProximalLangevin/Perturbation.lean.title: Uniform potential gaps and marginal-center displacement
ProximalLangevin/Perturbation.lean.summary:
Assume one potential lies between a smooth strongly convex potential and that potential plus a finite constant. Exponentiation and integration preserve a multiplicative comparison of the latent marginals; negative logarithms then give the same additive constant between marginal potentials. Strong-convexity growth at the comparison minimizer converts this value difference into a quantitative bound on the distance between marginal maximizers. Gaussian domination also proves existence of the original marginal maximizer.

Let \(V\le U\le V+\delta\), with \(V\) differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex, \(m>0\), and \(U\) continuous. Write \(k_W(\theta)=\int e^{-W(\theta,x)}dx\) and \(F_W=-\log k_W\). This module derives positive finite marginals and actual maximizers before comparing centers.

steps.title: Quadratic growth from strong convexity and minimality
steps.body:
Let \(F\) be \(m\)-strongly convex with \(m\ge0\) and global minimizer \(z\). For any \(x\) set

\[ A=\frac m2\|x-z\|^2,\qquad G=F(x)-F(z). \]

Both quantities are nonnegative. For \(0<t<1\), the convex-combination inequality between \(z\) and \(x\) and minimality give

\[ F(z)\le F((1-t)z+tx) \le (1-t)F(z)+tF(x)-t(1-t)A. \]

Subtract \(F(z)\) and divide by \(t\) to obtain \((1-t)A\le G\) for every admissible \(t\). If \(G<A\), then \(A>0\) and the finite choice

\[ t=\frac{A-G}{2A}\in(0,1/2] \]

gives \((1-t)A=(A+G)/2>G\), a contradiction. Therefore \(A\le G\), or

\[ F(x)\ge F(z)+\frac m2\|x-z\|^2. \]

The proof uses only strong convexity and global minimality, without differentiating \(F\). Applied to the comparison marginal potential, this inequality bounds squared center distance by its increase above the minimum.

Formal correspondence: strongConvex_minimum_growth : A global minimizer of a strongly convex function has the sharp quadratic growth bound, even when the function is not differentiable.

steps.title: Marginal-potential comparison from a uniform gap
steps.body:
Suppose \(U\) is continuous and \(V\) is differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex, with \(m>0\), and assume \(V\le U\le V+\delta\). Exponentiation reverses order, and integration over each latent fiber gives

\[ e^{-\delta}k_V(\theta)\le k_U(\theta)\le k_V(\theta), \qquad k_W(\theta)=\int e^{-W(\theta,x)}dx. \]

The strongly convex comparison \(V\) gives positive finite slice integrals and a Gaussian bound that is integrable in the latent variable, locally uniformly in the parameter. The displayed inequalities give positivity, finiteness, and decay of the original marginal as the parameter norm tends to infinity. Continuity of \(U\) and dominated convergence give continuity of that marginal. Its positivity, continuity, and decay then imply that it attains a maximum. Taking negative logarithms gives

\[ F_V(\theta)\le F_U(\theta)\le F_V(\theta)+\delta, \qquad F_W=-\log k_W. \]

Let \(\theta_U\) minimize \(F_U\) and let \(\theta_V\) minimize the \(m\)-strongly convex potential \(F_V\). The potential bounds and minimality give \(F_V(\theta_U)-F_V(\theta_V)\le\delta\). The quadratic-growth inequality therefore yields

\[ \frac m2\|\theta_U-\theta_V\|^2\le\delta. \]

In the equivalent notation \(V\le U\le V+\delta\), the pointwise weights satisfy \(e^{-\delta}e^{-V}\le e^{-U}\le e^{-V}\), and integration gives \(e^{-\delta}M_V(\theta)\le M_U(\theta)\le M_V(\theta)\). The positive finite comparison marginal makes \(M_U\) positive and finite. Thus logarithmic monotonicity legitimately yields \(F_V\le F_U\le F_V+\delta\) with \(F=-\log M\). The additive gap is still \(\delta\) because the logarithm is taken after integration. No differentiation of the original marginal or integration of an asymptotic remainder is used.

Formal correspondence: marginalDensity_sandwich : A one-sided uniform perturbation transfers directly to the actual extended-valued latent integrals. No real conversion or normalization is used. marginalPotential_sandwich : The two negative log marginal likelihoods differ by at most the same uniform potential gap. Integrability of the nonsmooth original weight is derived by domination by the smooth strongly convex comparison potential.

steps.title: Existence of an original marginal maximizer
steps.body:
The inequality \(e^{-U}\le e^{-V}\) bounds every original latent weight by an integrable comparison weight. The stronger Gaussian bound gives a common latent majorant for convergent parameter sequences and a decaying Gaussian factor in the parameter. Dominated convergence, applied to the continuous original weights, therefore proves marginal continuity; the parameter factor proves decay at infinity.

The marginal is strictly positive and finite at each parameter. Choose a ball large enough that all outside values are smaller than one fixed positive inside value. Continuity gives a maximum on that compact ball, which is then a global maximum. Hence the original center exists under the comparison assumptions, without an additional optimizer-existence hypothesis.

Formal correspondence: integrable_original_marginal : A continuous nonsmooth original potential has finite latent integrals when it dominates the smooth strongly convex comparison potential. continuous_original_marginal : The original marginal is continuous by a Gaussian dominated convergence argument, even though its joint potential may be nonsmooth. exists_original_marginalMaximizer : A maximizer of the actual nonsmooth marginal exists; existence is not an extra statistical premise added to the Moreau comparison argument.

steps.title: Quadratic growth and the center displacement
steps.body:
On positive finite marginal densities, \(-\log\) reverses order. Thus an original likelihood maximizer minimizes \(F_U\). At the two minimizers \(\theta_U,\theta_V\), the sandwich gives \(F_V(\theta_U)\le F_U(\theta_U)\le F_U(\theta_V)\le F_V(\theta_V)+\delta\). The comparison potential’s quadratic growth then gives \(\|\theta_U-\theta_V\|^2\le2\delta/m\).

The minimality used in this chain is at \(\theta_U\) and states \(F_U(\theta_U)\le F_U(\theta_V)\). The uniform gap controls the other comparisons, so the increase of the comparison potential at \(\theta_U\) is at most \(\delta\). Taking the nonnegative square root yields distance at most \(\sqrt{2\delta/m}\). The original potential requires no differentiability or globally Lipschitz gradient in this step.

Formal correspondence: original_maximizer_minimizes : Marginal maximization for the actual nonsmooth model is equivalent to minimization of its finite negative log marginal likelihood. marginal_center_distance_sq : A fully nonasymptotic marginal-center perturbation bound. Only the comparison model is assumed smooth. The centers maximize the actual marginal integrals; they are not joint modes. marginal_center_distance : The square-root form of the uniform-gap marginal-center estimate.

ProximalLangevin/PIPULA.lean.title: PIPULA for the full envelope and its smoothed marginal maximizer
ProximalLangevin/PIPULA.lean.summary: PIPULA applies the full-potential pairwise proximal map and then adds Gaussian noise. The residual identity makes it Euler Langevin for the full Moreau envelope at the same scale. The envelope has reduced curvature \(m_\gamma=m/(1+m\gamma)\). Assume the original potential \(U\) is \(m\)-strongly convex and bounded below, with \(m,\gamma>0\). No global Lipschitz assumption is imposed on \(U\). The resulting estimate concerns the marginal maximizer of \(U^\gamma\) and retains the scale dependence of the generic Euler error.

steps.title: The full-envelope curvature and admissible step
steps.body:
Set \(m_\gamma=m/(1+m\gamma)>0\). The inequality \(\gamma m_\gamma=m\gamma/(1+m\gamma)\le1\) gives \(\gamma(m_\gamma+\gamma^{-1})\le2\), equivalently \(\gamma\le2/(m_\gamma+\gamma^{-1})\). Positivity of the denominators justifies the multiplications and divisions.

More specifically, \(m\gamma/(1+m\gamma)<1\) implies \(\gamma m_\gamma+1\le2\). Since the envelope gradient constant is \(1/\gamma\), this is precisely the required Euler restriction. The contraction factor is \(1-m_\gamma\gamma=1/(1+m\gamma)>0\). These facts follow from strong convexity of the original potential and envelope regularity, without a global Lipschitz bound on the original potential’s values.

Formal correspondence: fullSmoothingModulus : Strong convexity after smoothing the entire potential. pipula_admissible_step : With smoothing equal to the time step, the envelope always meets the proved Gaussian ULA step restriction.

steps.title: Equality of the proximal-noise and envelope Euler laws
steps.body:
In the MYIPLA update set \(g_1=0\) and \(\eta=\gamma\). Proximal optimality gives \(P_\gamma=I-\gamma\nabla U^\gamma\), so the resulting recursion is IPLA for \(U^\gamma\).

The pointwise identity \(P_\gamma(v)=v-\gamma\nabla U^\gamma(v)\), applied to every pair, gives the scaled Euler drift. Adding the same Gaussian vector after proximity gives the PIPULA update. Equality at initialization and at each successor proves equality of all finite iterates; their measurable pushforwards therefore agree as probability laws.

Formal correspondence: pipulaLaws : The probability law defined by the paper's pairwise PIPULA recursion. pipulaLaws_eq_iplaLaws : Exact equality between the displayed PIPULA law and IPLA for the genuine full Moreau envelope.

steps.title: The proved estimate about the smoothed marginal center
steps.body:
The update specialization \(g_1=0\) and \(\lambda=\gamma\) identifies PIPULA with full-envelope IPLA. The source’s claim about error relative to the original marginal maximizer requires additional analysis: its proximal inner-product deficit \(\mu\) gives envelope-gradient monotonicity coefficient \(\mu/\gamma\) because the residual is divided by \(\gamma\). A scale-uniform discretization estimate and the source’s rate relative to the original marginal maximizer are not established by substituting smoothness \(1/\gamma\) into a generic Euler bound.

The proved estimate instead assumes a bounded-below \(m\)-strongly convex full potential. For \(\gamma>0\) its envelope curvature is \(m_\gamma=m/(1+m\gamma)\) and its gradient constant is \(1/\gamma\). The generic error term is \((33/20)(1/(\gamma m_\gamma))\sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\sqrt\gamma\), which diverges as \(\gamma\downarrow0\). It therefore does not reproduce the claimed rate \(O(\sqrt\gamma)\) relative to the original marginal maximizer.

Write \(m_\gamma=m/(1+m\gamma)\), let \(\Pi_{N,\gamma}\) be the envelope Gibbs law, and let \(\theta_\gamma\) be its marginal maximizer. Sharp concentration and the Gaussian particle estimate give

\[\left(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_\gamma\|^2\right)^{1/2}\le\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm_\gamma}}+(1-m_\gamma\gamma)^nW_2(\rho_0,\Pi_{N,\gamma})+\frac{33}{20}\frac{\gamma^{-1}}{m_\gamma}\sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\sqrt\gamma.\]

The theorem uses gradient constant \(\gamma^{-1}\). For a separately denoted envelope scale, the curvature is \(m_\eta=m/(1+m\eta)\) rather than \(m\) and the gradient constant is \(1/\eta\); the required restriction is \(\gamma\le2/(m_\eta+1/\eta)\). At equal proximal and Euler scales, the preceding algebra proves it automatically. The equilibrium radius uses this reduced curvature, and the error coefficient uses \((1/\gamma)/m_\gamma\). Consequently the valid finite-step estimate is about the smoothed center and does not prove vanishing error as \(\gamma\downarrow0\). A uniform conclusion relative to the original marginal maximizer would require a stronger envelope analysis.

Formal correspondence: pipula_parameter_rms_smoothed : A complete finite-time bound for PIPULA around the maximizer of the smoothed marginal. The original potential may be nonsmooth and need not be globally Lipschitz. All envelope properties, the time-step restriction, normalization, finite transport moments, and equilibrium concentration are proved from the displayed assumptions and the actual Gaussian innovations.

ProximalLangevin/PIPULAConsistency.lean.title: Bounded fields and positive global strong monotonicity
ProximalLangevin/PIPULAConsistency.lean.summary: A globally bounded vector field on a nontrivial real Hilbert space cannot have a positive global strong-monotonicity constant. The Moreau gradient of a globally Lipschitz convex function is bounded. Hence the conjunction of full-potential value Lipschitzness and a positive global proximal-residual deficit is inconsistent. The conclusion concerns that literal conjunction of assumptions; it does not apply to a decomposition in which only the nonsmooth summand is Lipschitz.

steps.title: Incompatibility of boundedness and positive global monotonicity
steps.body:
Assume \(\|R(x)\|\le K\) and \(c\|x-y\|^2\le\langle x-y,R(x)-R(y)\rangle\) with \(c>0\). Cauchy–Schwarz and the triangle inequality give \(c\|x-y\|^2\le2K\|x-y\|\). A nonzero direction can be scaled to have length greater than \(2K/c\), contradicting this bound.

In the alternative notation \(\|b(x)\|\le K\) and \(\langle b(x)-b(y),x-y\rangle\ge q\|x-y\|^2\) with \(q>0\) imply \(q\|x-y\|\le2K\) for every distinct pair. Explicitly choose separation \(r>2K/c\). Strong monotonicity bounds the inner product below by \(cr^2\), while boundedness bounds it above by \(2Kr\). Division by \(r\) gives \(cr\le2K\). A nontrivial space has arbitrarily large such separations \(r\), so the assumptions cannot both hold. The nontrivial-space qualification is essential.

Formal correspondence: bounded_field_not_stronglyMonotone : A globally bounded field cannot have a positive strong-monotonicity constant on a nontrivial real Hilbert space.

steps.title: The obstruction for a globally bounded proximal residual
steps.body:
Consider the reading of the source reduction in which \(g_1=0\) also applies the value-Lipschitz assumption to \(U=g_2\). Then \(U\) is globally \(K\)-Lipschitz, so its Moreau gradient \(R_\gamma=\gamma^{-1}(I-P_\gamma)\) satisfies \(\|R_\gamma(x)\|\le K\). A positive proximal deficit gives

\[ \frac{\mu}{\gamma}\|x-y\|^2 \le\langle x-y,R_\gamma(x)-R_\gamma(y)\rangle \le2K\|x-y\|. \]

The preceding obstruction contradicts these simultaneous global conditions on a nontrivial space. If the Lipschitz assumption instead concerns the nonsmooth term in an independent decomposition \(U=g_1+g_2\), it does not make the full \(U\) Lipschitz and the contradiction does not follow.

The residual \(R_\gamma=(I-P_\gamma)/\gamma\) is bounded in the first reading, while the deficit makes it strongly monotone with coefficient \(\mu/\gamma\). Under \(\mu>0\) these are incompatible. This is a conditional consistency result about the specified assumptions, not a general refutation of the source corollary. The separate full-potential PIPULA theorem assumes strong convexity and a lower bound without global value Lipschitzness.

Formal correspondence: lipschitz_full_potential_not_proximal_deficit : Under a literal full-potential globally Lipschitz reading, B1 cannot hold with positive deficit in positive dimension. The separate PIPULA theorem therefore does not assume global Lipschitzness of the full strongly convex \(U\).

ProximalLangevin/SharpConcentration.lean.title: Sharp Gibbs concentration by dilation
ProximalLangevin/SharpConcentration.lean.summary: Let \(F\) be continuous and \(q\)-strongly convex in dimension \(d\), with \(q>0\) and global minimizer \(z\). A contraction toward the minimizer compares the Gibbs partition with its unnormalized second moment. The left derivative at unit dilation gives the dimension-over-curvature bound. Gaussian domination ensures all integrals are finite, and only an explicit scalar expression is differentiated; no derivative of the potential is required.

steps.title: The partition comparison under radial contraction
steps.body:
Strong convexity and minimality give \(F(z+r(x-z))\le F(x)-\frac q2(1-r^2)\|x-z\|^2\) for \(0\[Z+\frac q2(1-r^2)M\le r^{-d}Z,\qquad Z=\int e^{-F},\quad M=\int\|x-z\|^2e^{-F}.\]

In the notation \(w(x)=e^{-F(x)}\), \(Z=\int w\), \(M=\int\|x-z\|^2w(x)\,dx\), and \(d=\dim H\), Gaussian domination first proves integrability of \(w\) and \(\|x-z\|^2w\). Strong convexity combined with quadratic growth at the mode gives

\[F(z+r(x-z))\le F(x)-\tfrac q2(1-r^2)\|x-z\|^2.\]

Using \(e^u\ge1+u\) after exponentiation gives

\[w(z+r(x-z))\ge w(x)+\tfrac q2(1-r^2)\|x-z\|^2w(x).\]

Indeed the strong-convexity segment from the minimizer to \(x\) contributes radial deficit \(q(1-r^2)\|x-z\|^2/2\). Inequality \(e^u\ge1+u\) turns it into a density-plus-moment bound. The determinant is \(r^d\), so the integral of the dilated density is \(r^{-d}Z\). This proves the partition comparison with all terms finite.

The local fact hpoint is exactly this last inequality. hip separately proves that the dilated weight is integrable, using translation invariance and nonzero scalar dilation. htrans computes its integral as \(r^{-d}Z\). Integrating hpoint now proves \(Z+\frac q2(1-r^2)M\le r^{-d}Z\), with every integral finite before the comparison.

Formal correspondence: sharp_gibbs_mode_dilation_inequality : The dilation inequality before taking the tangent limit.

steps.title: The limiting derivative and the normalized moment
steps.body:
Multiply the partition comparison by \(r^d\) and define \(\Phi(r)=r^d[Z+(q/2)(1-r^2)M]\). It satisfies \(\Phi(r)\le Z=\Phi(1)\) for \(0\[\int\|x-z\|^2\pi(dx)=M/Z\le d/q,\qquad\pi(dx)=Z^{-1}e^{-F(x)}dx.\]

The argument does not differentiate \(F\). Equivalently, \(qM\le dZ\) may be divided by positive \(Z\). The normalized second moment is \(M/Z\) and is bounded by \(d/q\). This permits the estimate for continuous nonsmooth strongly convex potentials without an integration-by-parts assumption.

Here hZ proves \(Z>0\), and hpart identifies the extended partition function with \(\iota Z\). The density change in heq therefore gives \[\int\|x-z\|^2\,d\pi(x)=Z^{-1}M.\] Multiplication of the unnormalized inequality by the nonnegative \(Z^{-1}\), followed by \(Z^{-1}Z=1\), yields \(\int\|x-z\|^2d\pi\le d/q\). Positive normalization is proved from the potential assumptions, rather than supplied as a moment or probability premise.

Formal correspondence: sharp_integral_sq_dist_gibbs_le : A continuous \(q\)-strongly convex Gibbs potential concentrates around its minimizer with sharp second moment at most \(\operatorname{dim}/q\). Every normalization and integrability fact used in the conclusion is proved from the stated inputs.

steps.title: The left derivative giving the \(d/q\) bound
steps.body:
With \(Z,M,d\) from the partition comparison define

\[\Phi(r)=r^d\bigl[Z+\tfrac q2(1-r^2)M\bigr].\]

For \(0<r<1\) one has \(\Phi(r)\le Z=\Phi(1)\). Thus when \(-1<u<0\), the difference quotient \((\Phi(1+u)-\Phi(1))/u\) is nonnegative: its numerator and denominator are both nonpositive.

For negative \(u\) tending to zero, \(\Phi(1+u)-\Phi(1)\) and \(u\) retain these signs. The quotient converges to \(dZ-qM\) by differentiation of the explicit scalar expression. Its limit is nonnegative, giving the desired moment bound. The comparison only needs contractions \(r<1\) because their left derivative already determines the derivative inequality at \(r=1\).

Differentiate this explicit scalar polynomial, rather than differentiating \(F\): \[\Phi'(1)=dZ-qM.\] In Lean, hinner differentiates the bracket, hder applies the product rule, and hnonneg records the sign of the left difference quotient. Its limit is \(\Phi'(1)\), so hbound gives \(dZ-qM\ge0\). Since \(q>0\), divide to obtain \(M\le(d/q)Z\).

Formal correspondence: sharp_integral_sq_dist_mul_exp_neg_le : Taking the tangent limit of the dilation inequality gives the exact dimension dependence, without differentiating the potential.

ProximalLangevin/SharpIPLA.lean.title: Sharp parameter concentration and the IPLA RMS bound
ProximalLangevin/SharpIPLA.lean.summary: Apply the continuous-potential concentration estimate to the parameter marginal, whose curvature has factor \(N\) from particle count. For a differentiable \(m\)-strongly convex pair potential \(U\) with \(m>0\), Prékopa–Leindler gives the marginal curvature. Its \(N\)-power target has curvature \(Nm\), so its parameter second moment is at most \(d_\theta/(Nm)\). This improves the equilibrium term in the earlier estimate while keeping the transport and discretization terms unchanged.

steps.title: Sharp concentration of the parameter marginal
steps.body:
For continuous \(a\)-strongly convex potential \(f\) with minimizer \(x_\star\), the dilation argument gives

\[ \int\|x-x_\star\|^2\,\pi(dx)\le\frac d a, \qquad\pi(dx)\propto e^{-f(x)}dx. \]

Only continuity, strong convexity, and a minimizing point are needed; no nonsmooth integration-by-parts formula is assumed. Prékopa–Leindler gives strong convexity of the parameter marginal potential. Raising the marginal likelihood to its \(N\)-th power multiplies that curvature by \(N\). Thus

\[ W_2(\Pi_{\lambda,N}^{\theta},\delta_{\theta_{\lambda,\star}}) \le\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}. \]

This is the factor in the source’s equilibrium estimate. The earlier radius \(\sqrt{2d_\theta/(Nm)}\) was a valid weaker bound.

The parameter density is proportional to \(M(\theta)^N\) and has negative log potential \(NF(\theta)\). Its curvature is \(Nm\), with minimizer \(\theta_*\). The sharp theorem in dimension \(d_\theta\) gives \(\int\|\theta-\theta_*\|^2d\Pi_N\le d_\theta/(Nm)\). In the equivalent notation, density \(e^{-N\Phi}\) has curvature \(Nm\), so dimension \(d_\theta\) gives second moment \(d_\theta/(Nm)\). The exact projection identity transfers that same moment to the full Gibbs law; its nonnegative square root is the equilibrium root mean square radius.

Formal correspondence: sharp_marginalTarget_secondMoment_le : Sharp equilibrium second moment of the actual powered marginal density. sharp_gibbsTarget_parameter_secondMoment_le : The exact parameter-marginal identity transfers sharp concentration to the full lifted Gibbs measure. sharp_gibbsTarget_parameter_concentration : The parameter RMS radius with the sharp dimension constant.

steps.title: The Gaussian particle estimate with sharp equilibrium radius
steps.body:
Assume \(N>0\), \(\gamma>0\), \(\gamma\le2/(m+L)\), independent Gaussian innovations, and \(L^2\) initialization. The scaled Gaussian Euler estimate, parameter projection, and the sharp equilibrium moment give

\[\operatorname{RMS}_n\le\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}+(1-m\gamma)^nW_2(\rho_0,\Pi_N)+\frac{33}{20}\frac Lm\sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\sqrt\gamma.\]

For any coupling of the current state and Gibbs target, projection does not increase quadratic cost. Minkowski adds the Gibbs parameter error about the center. Taking the coupling infimum gives transport plus the sharp radius, and substitution yields the displayed estimate. If the parameter dimension is zero its error is zero; if the state is a singleton its transport is zero. Thus the same inequality holds for arbitrary nonnegative parameter and latent dimensions.

For \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\), the lifted state has score constant \(NL\), convexity \(Nm\) and step \(\gamma/N\). The shared Gaussian ULA theorem controls its \(W_2\) error, while the parameter projection has norm at most one. The projected RMS therefore is at most the sharp equilibrium scale \(\sqrt{d_\theta/(Nm)}\) plus that transport error. The nonempty-dimensional case proves this combination directly; the final declaration splits off zero-dimensional cases so that no unspoken positive-dimension premise remains.

Formal correspondence: sharp_ipla_parameter_rms : A complete actual Gaussian IPLA parameter bound with sharp concentration. This theorem includes zero parameter/latent dimensions.

ProximalLangevin/MYPGDNoise.lean.title: Orthogonal masks and the exact removed-noise cost
ProximalLangevin/MYPGDNoise.lean.summary: Let \(P_\theta\) be the orthogonal projection onto the common parameter block and \(P_x=I-P_\theta\) the complementary latent projection. For standard Gaussian \(\xi\), the parameter projection has mean zero and squared moment \(d_\theta\). Coupling the latent-only and full-noise updates with the same Gaussian vector leaves exactly this omitted parameter block. Independence makes its mixed term with the preceding discrepancy vanish.

steps.title: Complementary parameter and latent projections
steps.body:
Define \(P_\theta(\theta,x)=(\theta,0)\) and \(P_x(\theta,x)=(0,x)\). These bounded linear maps preserve square integrability, so an \(L^2\) innovation remains an \(L^2\) random vector after either projection.

Coordinate evaluation gives \(P_\theta+P_x=I\), \(P_\theta P_x=0\), \(P_\theta^2=P_\theta\), and \(P_x^2=P_x\). Their ranges are therefore complementary orthogonal parameter and latent subspaces. Applying \(P_x\) to the noise removes its parameter component and leaves the deterministic drift unchanged, which is the update difference in the MYPGD comparison.

Denote the two maps by \(P_\theta\) and \(P_x=I-P_\theta\). On a scaled particle state, \(P_\theta(\theta,z_1,\ldots,z_N)=(\theta,0,\ldots,0)\), while \(P_x(\theta,z_1,\ldots,z_N)=(0,z_1,\ldots,z_N)\). The four coordinate lemmas establish these formulas directly; the subtraction defining latentNoiseCLM is an equality of continuous linear maps, so all later compositions are measurable.

Formal correspondence: parameterNoiseCLM : Retain the parameter coordinates and erase the latent coordinates. latentNoiseCLM : Retain precisely the latent noise of the original particle scheme.

steps.title: Projection norms and Gaussian moments
steps.body:
The parameter projection satisfies \(\|P_\theta z\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^{d_\theta}z_j^2\) and hence \(\|P_\theta z\|\le\|z\|\). Linearity of expectation gives \(\mathbb E P_\theta\xi=0\); the unit second moment of each standard Gaussian coordinate gives \(\mathbb E\|P_\theta\xi\|^2=d_\theta\).

In the coordinate expansion \(\sum_{j=1}^{d_\theta}z_j^2\), each summand is integrable because the Gaussian vector belongs to \(L^2\). The identities \(\mathbb E z_j^2=1\) and \(\mathbb E P_\theta Z=P_\theta\mathbb EZ=0\) therefore give \(\mathbb E\|P_\theta Z\|^2=d_\theta\) by a finite sum. No factor \(N\) occurs: the projection retains exactly \(d_\theta\) scalar coordinates and their variances sum to \(d_\theta\). The particle count enters only when this noise block is multiplied by amplitude \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\).

steps.title: The zero mixed expectation and omitted-noise variance
steps.body:
Let \(g\) be square-integrable and independent of standard Gaussian \(\xi\). Expansion of \(\|g+bP_\theta\xi\|^2\) is integrable term by term by Cauchy–Schwarz. Fubini and bilinearity identify the mixed expectation as \(\langle\mathbb E g,\mathbb E P_\theta\xi\rangle=0\), so

\[\mathbb E\|g+bP_\theta\xi\|^2=\mathbb E\|g\|^2+b^2d_\theta.\]

The independence is between the fresh Gaussian and \(g\); the discrepancy \(g\) need not be centered. In particular \(\mathbb E\langle g,P_\theta\xi\rangle\) factors into the inner product of the two means, and the Gaussian mean is zero. Either sign of the removed parameter block therefore adds exactly \(b^2d_\theta\) to the squared error.

For a general \(g\in L^2(\mu)\), use the actual product law \(\mu\otimes\mathcal N(0,I)\), and expand \[\|g(x)+bP_\theta z\|^2=\|g(x)\|^2+2b\langle g(x),P_\theta z\rangle+b^2\|P_\theta z\|^2.\] The facts hgsq and hzsq prove integrability of the two squares on the product; hcross proves integrability of the bilinear term, so splitting the integral is justified. Independence here is the product-measure construction itself: integral_prod_bilin factors the mixed integral as \(\langle\mathbb Eg,\mathbb E P_\theta Z\rangle=0\). Hence \(\mathbb E\|g+bP_\theta Z\|^2=\mathbb E\|g\|^2+b^2d_\theta\), with no assumption that \(g\) is centered.

Formal correspondence: integral_add_parameterNoise_sq : Exact independent-noise identity, for an arbitrary square-integrable source. The mixed term vanishes by the actual product Gaussian law.

ProximalLangevin/MYPGDTransport.lean.title: A coupling of latent-only and full Gaussian transitions
ProximalLangevin/MYPGDTransport.lean.summary: Let \(r\)-Lipschitz map \(D\) define the common deterministic update. Compare \(D(x)+aP_x\xi\) and \(D(y)+a\xi\) using the same independent standard Gaussian vector. The omitted parameter block has a known variance, and its mixed expectation with the input discrepancy is zero. For probability input laws with finite second moments, this constructs a finite-cost coupling of the two transition laws.

steps.title: Finite moments of Lipschitz images and finite coupling costs
steps.body:
For map \(D\), the bound \(\|D(x)-D(0)\|\le r\|x\|\) and addition of its constant value at zero show preservation of \(L^2\). If two \(L^2\) vectors are defined on one probability space, their joint distribution is a coupling. Its quadratic cost bounds \(W_2\) and yields \(W_2(\mathcal L(X),\mathcal L(Y))^2\le\mathbb E\|X-Y\|^2\).
