A joint realization \((X,Y)\) is thus an admissible candidate in the infimum defining \(W_2\). The same finite squared separation proves transport finiteness and the numerical upper bound. The map need not vanish at zero because its constant part has finite second moment under a probability measure.

A globally Lipschitz map \(D\) need not vanish at zero. The first lemma writes \(D(X)=[D(X)-D(0)]+D(0)\): the centered map preserves \(L^2\), and the constant belongs to \(L^2\) because the measure is a probability. For the transport lemma, convert \(X,Y\) to their \(L^2\) classes. Their joint realization is an admissible coupling of their pushforwards, so \[W_2(X_\#P,Y_\#P)^2\le\|X-Y\|_{L^2(P)}^2=\int\|X-Y\|^2dP.\] The representative equalities hx, hy prove that these pushforwards are the original laws, and the finite norm bound proves finite Wasserstein distance before squaring its real value.

Formal correspondence: memLp_lipschitz_comp : Globally Lipschitz maps preserve finite quadratic moments on a probability space. wasserstein_sq_le_integral_pair : Direct finite-cost transport estimate for an actual \(L^2\) pair.

steps.title: Measurability and moments of the two Gaussian transitions
steps.body:
The transition maps are \(T_x(u,\xi)=D(u)+aP_x\xi\) and \(T(u,\xi)=D(u)+a\xi\). Continuity of \(D\), linearity of \(P_x\), and continuity of addition make them jointly measurable. On \(\mu\otimes\mathcal N(0,I)\) both summands belong to \(L^2\).

The squared norm of a sum is at most twice the sum of squared norms, so both output distributions have finite second moments. This integrability also justifies expansion and Fubini in the subsequent exact mixed-term calculation. The product distribution explicitly separates the input from the fresh noise.

Both updates use a fresh \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\), independent of the input: \(D(x)+aP_xZ\) and \(D(x)+aZ\). Their measurability follows by composing continuous \(D\), the coordinate projections, addition and scalar multiplication. For moment propagation, comp_fst pulls the \(L^2\) drift onto the input–Gaussian product and comp_snd pulls the Gaussian noise onto that same space. The sum is in \(L^2\); memLp_map_measure_iff then transfers this fact to the output law. Thus the next coupling argument has actual finite-moment marginals.

Formal correspondence: latentGaussianUpdate : The deterministic map followed by latent-only Gaussian noise. fullGaussianUpdate : The same map followed by full Gaussian noise.

steps.title: Extension of an input coupling by independent Gaussian noise
steps.body:
Given any finite-cost input coupling \(c\) of \(\mu,\nu\), extend it independently to \(c\otimes\mathcal N(0,I)\). The output marginals are the latent-only and full Gaussian transitions. Their difference is \(D(x)-D(y)-aP_\theta\xi\). The zero mixed-term identity gives squared cost \(\mathbb E_c\|D(x)-D(y)\|^2+a^2d_\theta\), at most \(r^2\operatorname{cost}(c)^2+a^2d_\theta\) by Lipschitz continuity.

The first marginal uses law \(\mu\) and latent Gaussian noise, while the second uses \(\nu\) and full Gaussian noise. In random-vector notation the difference is \(D(X)-D(Y)-aP_\theta\xi\). Independence gives mean square at most \(r^2\mathbb E\|X-Y\|^2+a^2d_\theta\). Thus the same bound holds for every finite-cost input coupling, which permits the Wasserstein infimum without choosing an optimal coupling.

Start from any input coupling \(c\) of \(\mu,\nu\), and work on \(c\otimes\mathcal N(0,I)\). Define \(F=D(X)+aP_xZ\) and \(H=D(Y)+aZ\). The facts hFlaw and hHlaw check separately that their marginals are the desired two Markov transitions; this ensures the constructed pair is a coupling of the actual algorithms.

The cancellation in hid is \[F-H=D(X)-D(Y)-aP_\theta Z.\] By the product Gaussian identity, its mean square is \(\mathbb E_c\|D(X)-D(Y)\|^2+a^2d_\theta\). If \(D\) is \(r\)-Lipschitz, the first term is bounded by \(r^2\mathbb E_c\|X-Y\|^2\). Finally hnorm identifies the latter integral with the square of the coupling cost. All three random variables are proved square integrable before any of these integral identities is used.

Formal correspondence: latent_full_markov_coupling_sq : Actual latent-noise and full-noise one-step laws admit the stated squared coupling bound. The independent centered parameter noise supplies exactly \(a^2d_\theta\), and has no mixed contribution.

ProximalLangevin/MYPGD.lean.title: Iterated finite-particle noise-removal comparison
ProximalLangevin/MYPGD.lean.summary: Consider finite-second-moment latent-only and full-noise chains with the same deterministic \(r\)-contractive map \(D\) and noise amplitude \(a\). The one-step coupling gives a squared Wasserstein recurrence. From a common initial law, geometric summation bounds their separation uniformly over finite iteration counts. For the smoothed gradient map this yields an explicit radius depending on parameter dimension and particle count.

steps.title: The transition estimate after the coupling infimum
steps.body:
For every finite-cost input coupling the transition estimate is \(W_2(T_x\mu,T u)^2\le r^2\operatorname{cost}(c)^2+a^2d_ heta\). Finite input second moments give \(W_2(\mu, u)<\infty\), so taking the coupling infimum yields \(W_2(T_x\mu,T u)^2\le r^2W_2(\mu, u)^2+a^2d_ heta\).

The additive term \(a^2d_ heta\) is independent of the chosen coupling. Since \(W_2(\mu, u)<\infty\), the infimum is finite and the equivalent kernel notation gives

\[W_2(\mu P_x, u P)^2\le r^2W_2(\mu, u)^2+a^2d_ heta.\]

The infimum replaces the squared input cost by \(W_2(\mu, u)^2\), with nonnegative coefficient \(r^2\). One finite input coupling already proves a finite output cost. Thus neither finiteness nor the recurrence assumes attainment of the optimal coupling.

Formal correspondence: latent_full_markov_sq : The finite-moment independent Gaussian transition satisfies the derived squared transport recurrence.

steps.title: The geometric comparison from a common initial law
steps.body:
Measurable transitions preserve probability, and their linear-growth moment bounds preserve \(L^2\) at every finite iteration. Starting both chains from \(\mu\) gives zero initial transport by the diagonal coupling. Under \(0\le r<1\), geometric summation yields \(W_2(\rho_n^x,\rho_n)^2\le a^2d_\theta/(1-r^2)\).

For recurrence \(E_{k+1}\le r^2E_k+a^2d_\theta\) with zero initial value, induction gives \(E_k\le a^2d_\theta\sum_{j

Let \(E_k=W_2(\mu_k^x,\mu_k^{\mathrm{full}})^2\), with the same initial law. The two inductions hMm and hIm propagate finite second moments, while hMp and hIp propagate probability mass. Therefore the one-step theorem applies at every \(k\), giving \(E_{k+1}\le r^2E_k+a^2d_\theta\). A diagonal realization proves \(E_0=0\). Since \(0\le r<1\), the affine-recurrence sum yields \[E_k\le a^2d_\theta\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}r^{2j}\le\frac{a^2d_\theta}{1-r^2}.\] This recurrence is derived from the transitions, rather than a hypothesis of this theorem.

Formal correspondence: latent_full_markov_laws_sq : The actual iterated independent-Gaussian laws differ by at most the explicit noise-removal floor. No error recurrence is assumed.

steps.title: Contraction of the smoothed gradient step
steps.body:
The smoothed gradient step contracts by \(r=1-m\gamma\) under \(0\[ W_2(\rho^{\mathrm{PGD}}_{k+1},\rho^{\mathrm{IPLA}}_{k+1})^2 \le r^2 W_2(\rho^{\mathrm{PGD}}_k,\rho^{\mathrm{IPLA}}_k)^2 +\frac{2\gamma d_\theta}{N}. \]

Take the input coupling infimum at each step. From the same initial law, \(0\le r<1\) and \(1-r^2=m\gamma(2-m\gamma)\ge m\gamma\) give

\[ W_2(\rho^{\mathrm{PGD}}_n,\rho^{\mathrm{IPLA}}_n)^2 \le\frac{2d_\theta}{Nm}. \]

For \(V_\eta=g_1+g_2^\eta\), the envelope results give curvature \(m\) and gradient constant \(L_\eta=L_1+\eta^{-1}\). Lifting gives \(Nm,NL_\eta\), so the step \(\gamma/N\) has contraction \(r=1-m\gamma\). Restriction \(0<\gamma\le2/(m+L_\eta)\) and \(m\le L_\eta\) imply \(0\le m\gamma\le1\) and thus \(0\le r<1\).

With \(r=1-m\gamma\) and \(a^2=2\gamma/N\), the denominator in the geometric sum is \(1-r^2=m\gamma(2-m\gamma)\). Inequality \(m\gamma\le1\) bounds it below by \(m\gamma>0\). Cancellation of the physical step gives the squared radius \(2d_\theta/(Nm)\). This is an upper bound on the difference between two finite-particle laws. It asserts neither that removing noise worsens the algorithm nor that a mean-field limit has been taken.

Substitute \(a^2=2\gamma/N\) into the preceding floor. The scalar fact hbound is \[1-(1-m\gamma)^2=m\gamma(2-m\gamma)\ge m\gamma.\] Its denominator is positive, so \[\frac{(2\gamma/N)d_\theta}{1-(1-m\gamma)^2}\le\frac{2d_\theta}{Nm}.\] The proof controls removal of parameter noise in a finite-particle algorithm; it does not replace this floor with a mean-field limit assertion.

Formal correspondence: mypgdDriftMap : The smooth Euler map used by both MYPGD and MYIPLA. mypgd_myipla_markov_transport_sq : Genuine MYPGD/MYIPLA comparison with a uniform finite-particle floor. This bound concerns the actual Gaussian Markov transitions. It is a proved replacement for, rather than an assertion of, the source's mean-field estimate.

ProximalLangevin/MYPGDAlgorithm.lean.title: MYPGD recursion and transition laws
ProximalLangevin/MYPGDAlgorithm.lean.summary: MYPGD retains the Moreau residual drift and latent Gaussian noise of MYIPLA while removing its parameter Gaussian component. Equality of the update maps identifies the expanded proximal recursion with the masked-noise Euler recursion. The independent Gaussian-sequence assumptions then identify its laws with the corresponding iterated Markov transition, to which the finite-particle noise comparison applies.

steps.title: The recursion with latent-projected innovations
steps.body:
Replace the innovation \(\xi\) in MYIPLA by \(P_x\xi\). This defines MYPGD. The recursion is MYIPLA driven by sequence \((P_x\xi_k)_k\) because initialization and successor updates agree.

The deterministic terms are identical at every step; only the supplied innovation is projected. Induction therefore proves equality of the pointwise chains before any distributional assumptions are made. Their laws are subsequently the measurable pushforwards of this same recursion.

Formal correspondence: mypgdUpdate : MYPGD removes precisely the parameter noise from the displayed MYIPLA step. mypgdChain : The actual MYPGD chain driven by supplied full innovations. mypgdChain_eq_myiplaChain : MYPGD is exactly MYIPLA applied to the latent-only innovations. mypgdLaws : The output law of the actual MYPGD recursion.

steps.title: The common deterministic smoothed gradient map
steps.body:
Let \(F_\eta=\sum_i(g_1+g_2^\eta)(\theta,x_i)\) and \(h=\gamma/N\). The residual-envelope identity gives the update

\[ X_{k+1}=X_k-h\nabla F_\eta(X_k)+\sqrt{2h}\,P_x\xi_k. \]

The parameter coordinate has no additive Gaussian term, while each physical latent coordinate has coefficient \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\). Finite-second-moment initialization and independent standard Gaussian coordinates, independent of initialization, define the transition laws. The unused parameter Gaussians may remain on the probability space for comparison with MYIPLA; no initial independent-particle assumption is required.

The bound \(\operatorname{Lip}(I-(\gamma/N)\nabla F_\eta)\le1+|\gamma/N|\,NL_\eta\) ensures continuity and measurable finite-moment updates without imposing contraction. In particular the deterministic map is \(D(z)=z-(\gamma/N)\nabla F_\eta(z)\), and the physical latent noise coefficient is \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\). The stricter step restriction is required only for the quantitative contractive comparison.

Formal correspondence: mypgdUpdate_eq_latentGaussianUpdate : The drift/noise formula for the actual Moreau proximal construction. myiplaUpdate_eq_fullGaussianUpdate : The full-noise update used for comparison is the actual MYIPLA update.

steps.title: The Markov transition from independent Gaussian coordinates
steps.body:
Mutual independence of all scalar Gaussian innovations gives independent standard vector innovations, independent of initialization. Consequently the two supplied chains have the Markov transitions \(D+aP_x\xi\) and \(D+a\xi\).

The common deterministic map is \(D(z)=z-(\gamma/N)\nabla V_{N,\eta}(z)\). MYPGD adds \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}P_x\xi\) and MYIPLA adds \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\xi\). At time \(k\) the current state is a measurable function of initialization and preceding innovations, so the next Gaussian vector is independent of it. Projection gives the latent-only kernel; retention of the full vector gives the MYIPLA kernel. Induction identifies their supplied laws with the iterated transition laws used in the comparison theorem.

Formal correspondence: mypgdLaws_eq_markovLaws : The actual Gaussian realization has the proved latent-noise Markov law. myiplaLaws_eq_markovLaws : The same full innovations give the ordinary full-noise MYIPLA Markov law.

ProximalLangevin/MYPGDTheorem.lean.title: MYPGD error about the original marginal maximizer
ProximalLangevin/MYPGDTheorem.lean.summary: Assume the potential, smoothing, initialization, and Gaussian conditions of the MYIPLA theorem relative to the original marginal maximizer, together with \(m\le L_\eta=L_1+\eta^{-1}\), \(N>0\), \(m,\eta,\gamma>0\), and \(\gamma\le2/(m+L_\eta)\). The MYPGD latent-only transition and the MYIPLA full transition have a finite-particle Wasserstein comparison. Parameter projection adds its radius to the MYIPLA estimate, yielding comparison, smoothing, equilibrium, initial-transport, and discretization contributions.

steps.title: The squared transport comparison of the two laws
steps.body:
Both recursions have the same smoothed deterministic map and initial pushforward. The initial representative belongs to \(L^2\), so this law has a finite second moment. Identification of their Gaussian transition laws allows the iterated comparison theorem to give finite transport and \(W_2(\rho_n^{\rm PGD},\rho_n^{\rm IPLA})^2\le2d_\theta/(Nm)\).

The squared comparison radius is \(2d_\theta/(Nm)\). All output moments follow from the finite-moment transition bounds. The comparison therefore applies to the stated algorithm laws, independently of the particular probability space used to realize the innovations.

Formal correspondence: mypgd_myipla_actual_transport_sq : The actual MYPGD and MYIPLA laws have the proved finite transport bound. Their common full Gaussian input is used only to identify the two different Markov transitions; the MYPGD output has latent-only noise.

steps.title: The parameter-error comparison under projection
steps.body:
The parameter projection has operator norm at most one. Projection of a coupling and Minkowski’s inequality give \(\operatorname{RMS}_{\rm PGD}(\theta)\le W_2(\rho_n^{\rm PGD},\rho_n^{\rm IPLA})+\operatorname{RMS}_{\rm IPLA}(\theta)\). The finite comparison distance and finite MYIPLA moment prove finiteness of the MYPGD parameter moment as well. The square root of the squared comparison estimate is \(\sqrt{2d_\theta/(Nm)}\).

In root mean square notation the inequality is

\[R_{\mathrm{MYPGD}}(\theta_*)\le R_{\mathrm{MYIPLA}}(\theta_*)+W_2(\rho_n^{\mathrm{MYPGD}},\rho_n^{\mathrm{MYIPLA}}).\]

The squared last term is at most \(2d_\theta/(Nm)\), and nonnegative square roots bound it by \(\sqrt{2d_\theta/(Nm)}\). Equivalently, minimizing the projected coupling estimate gives the added radius \(\sqrt{2d_\theta/(Nm)}\). Substitution of the MYIPLA theorem relative to the original marginal maximizer retains its finite smoothing displacement, sharp equilibrium radius, initial transport term, and discretization term.

Formal correspondence: mypgd_parameter_rms_le_myipla : Any parameter RMS for actual MYPGD is bounded by the corresponding actual MYIPLA RMS plus an explicit finite-particle noise-removal radius.

steps.title: The MYPGD bound about the original marginal maximizer
steps.body:
Apply the projected transport inequality to the two algorithm laws and substitute the MYIPLA estimate relative to the original marginal maximizer. With \(L_\eta=L_1+1/\eta\),

\[ \begin{aligned} \left(\mathbb E\|\theta^{\mathrm{PGD}}_n-\theta_\star\|^2\right)^{1/2} \le{}&\sqrt{\frac{2d_\theta}{Nm}} +\sqrt{\frac{\eta K^2}{m}}+\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}\\ &+(1-m\gamma)^nW_2(\rho_0,\Pi_{N,\eta})\\ &+\frac{33}{20}\frac{L_\eta}{m} \sqrt{d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}}\sqrt\gamma. \end{aligned} \]

The result is finite under the stated assumptions. It is a finite-particle version related to the source’s Appendix B theorem: its initial transient is measured from the smoothed Gibbs target and it adds a conservative noise-comparison radius. It does not reproduce the source’s mean-field metric, constants, or stronger Taylor smoothing claim. The remaining discretization coefficient contains \(L_1+1/\eta\). Thus the estimate retains its dependence on smoothing scale and does not assert a bound for a path supremum.

Formal correspondence: moreau_mypgd_parameter_rms_original : Fully proved finite-time original-center control for the actual MYPGD Gaussian recursion. The extra \(\sqrt{2d_\theta/(Nm)}\) is a conservative derived comparison radius, not the source's unformalized mean-field constant.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingContraction.le.title: Contraction of the splitting recursion with common innovations
ProximalLangevin/SplittingContraction.le.summary: Assume \(N>0\); let \(g_1\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(L_1\)-Lipschitz gradient, and let \(g_2\) be convex and bounded below. Suppose \(00\), and \(0\le\gamma\le2/(m+L_1)\). Jensen’s inequality transfers pairwise proximal nonexpansiveness to the averaged state map. In two updates driven by the same innovation, the additive perturbations cancel before proximity. The smooth gradient-step contraction therefore also bounds the full splitting update and its finite iterates.

steps.title: Nonexpansiveness of the averaged pair map
steps.body:
Jensen’s inequality for the averaged parameter difference and the exact latent squared scaling give

\[\|\operatorname{Pair}_P(z)-\operatorname{Pair}_P(w)\|^2\le N^{-1}\sum_i\|P(J_i z)-P(J_i w)\|^2.\]

If \(P\) is nonexpansive, each squared summand is at most \(\|J_i(z-w)\|^2\). Their sum is \(N\|z-w\|^2\), so the averaged map is nonexpansive.

Explicitly put \(A_i z=(\theta,\sqrt N z_i)\) and \(\Delta_i=P(A_i z)-P(A_i w)\). The parameter inequality is \(N\|\overline\Delta_\theta\|^2\le\sum_i\|\Delta_{i,\theta}\|^2\), while the latent differences are rescaled by \(N^{-1/2}\). Thus

\[\|\operatorname{Pair}P(z)-\operatorname{Pair}P(w)\|^2\le\frac1N\sum_i\|\Delta_i\|^2.\]

Nonexpansiveness of \(P\) and identity \(\sum_i\|A_i(z-w)\|^2=N\|z-w\|^2\) give the unit full-state Lipschitz bound. Positivity of \(N\) justifies division and rescaling. The argument compares two averaged outputs and does not assume that either minimizes a shared-state proximal objective.

Formal correspondence: pairwiseMap_difference_sq_le : Averaging only the shared parameter contracts the squared difference relative to the average of all separate pairwise squared differences. pairwiseMap_nonexpansive : A nonexpansive pair map remains nonexpansive after the actual shared parameter averaging and physical-particle scaling.

steps.title: Contraction with the same innovation
steps.body:
The lifted smooth potential has curvature \(Nm\) and gradient constant \(NL_1\). At step \(\gamma/N\) its gradient update contracts by \(1-m\gamma\ge0\). For the same innovation the noisy forward difference is this deterministic difference. Composition with the nonexpansive pairwise proximal map yields

\[\|T_\lambda(z,\xi)-T_\lambda(w,\xi)\|\le(1-m\gamma)\|z-w\|.\]

Induction gives factor \((1-m\gamma)^n\). Writing \(q=1-m\gamma\), the step restriction ensures \(q\ge0\). Starting from \(e_0=\|z-w\|\), the induction step is \(e_{k+1}\le q e_k\le q^{k+1}e_0\). Equivalently, with \(q=1-m\gamma\) the discrepancies satisfy \(e_{k+1}\le q e_k\) and are bounded at time \(n\) by \(q^n e_0\).

Only equality of the innovations is used, so this stability statement holds for deterministic sequences as well as Gaussian ones. Convergence to a Gibbs law additionally requires a stationary reference and a local-error estimate.

Formal correspondence: pipglaUpdate_shared_noise_contract : PIPGLA contracts synchronously driven initial states at the smooth forward-step rate. No stochastic or equilibrium hypothesis is needed. pipglaChain_shared_noise_contract : Iterating the actual pathwise inequality controls two PIPGLA runs with the same innovations. It supplies stability, rather than a Gibbs bias bound.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingLaw.lean.title: Probability laws and second moments of the splitting recursion
ProximalLangevin/SplittingLaw.lean.summary: The splitting update is the composition of a noisy smooth-gradient map and the averaged pairwise proximal map. Assume convexity and a lower bound for \(g_2\), positive \(\lambda\), \(N>0\), and a globally Lipschitz smooth gradient. These hypotheses give measurable updates and propagation of finite second moments. Almost-sure equality identifies the pointwise and square-integrable recursions. Independent identically distributed innovations then determine the same finite-time law on any realization with the prescribed initial distribution.

steps.title: Measurability of the splitting update
steps.body:
Proximal nonexpansiveness gives \(\operatorname{Lip}(\operatorname{Pair}_{P_\lambda})\le1\). The forward map

\((z,\xi)\mapsto z-(\gamma/N)\nabla F_{g_1}(z)+\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\xi\)

is jointly continuous because its gradient is Lipschitz. Its composition with the continuous averaged proximal map is therefore measurable. Finite composition proves that each recursive state is a measurable function of initialization and innovations. The custom splitting recursion and the recursion using this same update agree by induction.

Formal correspondence: pipglaUpdate_measurable : The exact splitting update is jointly measurable in the state and noise. pipglaChain_eq_noiseDrivenChain : The pointwise recursion is the existing generic noise-driven chain.

steps.title: Square-integrable realization of the recursion
steps.body:
Define the output law from the pointwise recursion. An \(L^2\) update is obtained by applying the Lipschitz proximal map to the \(L^2\) noisy forward step. Composition and addition in \(L^2\) give representatives equal almost surely to that pointwise composition. Its linear growth preserves square integrability, so every iterate belongs to \(L^2\).

At each finite step, intersect the probability-one events for the preceding representative equality and the update formula. Induction then proves agreement with the explicit recursion. These law and moment conclusions require neither Gaussian innovations nor equilibrium assumptions; square-integrable supplied innovations suffice.

The square-integrable update first applies the Euler drift/noise map and then the genuine pairwise proximal map. Both are Lipschitz, so the result is again an \(L^2\) random variable. The update representative theorem intersects the full-measure sets for these two operations and obtains the pointwise PIPGLA formula. An induction repeats this at each fixed finite time, replacing the previous representative by the pointwise iterate on their common full-measure event. The chain's pushforward law is therefore exactly pipglaLaws, rather than merely a convenient auxiliary recursion.

Formal correspondence: pipglaLaws : The law of the actual PIPGLA state after a supplied innovation sequence. lpPipglaUpdate : The actual noisy forward step followed by the genuine pairwise proximal map, represented in \(L^2\). lpPipglaChain : Every iterate is an actual \(L^2\) random variable.

steps.title: Probability normalization of the output law
steps.body:
Equality almost surely of the two realizations gives \(\rho_n=Q\circ X_n^{-1}\) for the constructed \(L^2\) iterate. Its measurable representative pushes the probability source forward to a probability law: the inverse image of the whole state space has \(Q\)-mass one.

Almost-sure replacement does not change a pushforward law. Thus normalization of the pointwise splitting law follows independently of its second-moment or transport estimates.

steps.title: Equality of laws for independent identically distributed inputs
steps.body:
Assume initialization is independent of the complete innovation sequence and the innovations are independent with common law \(\eta\). The joint input law is \(\mathcal L(X_0)\otimes\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}\). Its pushforward under the measurable finite recursion determines the output distribution.

In initial-law notation that input measure is \(\mu_0\otimes\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}\). The state at time \(n\) depends on finitely many innovation coordinates. Therefore two realizations with the same initial law and innovation law have identical output laws. In particular a product probability space may be used for the coupling proof without changing the distribution of the stated algorithm.

For a measurable update, the time-\(n\) state is a measurable function of initialization and the innovation path. Independence of initialization from that path makes their joint law a product; iid innovations make the path law \(\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}\). Pushing this product through the finite recursion proves the canonical-law equality. The assumptions hinit, hnoise, hind, hiid and hlaw respectively supply these measurability, independence and distribution facts; none is a convergence-rate premise.

Formal correspondence: pipglaLaws_eq_canonical : Any independent iid realization has the canonical splitting law. This proves law transfer across coupling spaces without a convergence assumption.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingGaussianLaw.le.title: Gaussian sequence representations of the splitting laws
ProximalLangevin/SplittingGaussianLaw.le.summary: Mutual independence of the scalar standard Gaussian coordinates specifies an independent sequence of standard state-space Gaussian vectors. Independence of initialization gives a product law for all recursive inputs. The measurable splitting map therefore has the same output distribution whether the Gaussian sequence is represented by a scalar product measure, a vector product measure, or another realization with the same input laws.

steps.title: Independent standard Gaussian vectors from scalar coordinates
steps.body:
The scalar coordinate distributions and their mutual independence give \(\xi_k\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\) as a full vector. Disjoint time-coordinate groups give independence across \(k\). Together with initialization independence, the innovation-sequence law is \(\mathcal N(0,I)^{\otimes\mathbb N}\).

Indeed every finite set of vector coordinates has the product of its scalar Gaussian laws. These finite-coordinate distributions determine the vector-sequence product measure. Applying the general independent-innovation recursion result identifies the finite-time splitting laws without requiring a stationary distribution.

The hypothesis GaussianInnovations specifies laws and independence of all scalar coordinates over all times, as well as independence of initialization from the whole path. gaussianInnovations_vectorLaw groups a finite set of independent standard scalar Gaussians into a standard state-space Gaussian; gaussianInnovations_vectorIndependent groups the time slices into an independent vector family. The measurable recursion can then be pushed forward from the product of the initial law and this iid path law. Equality follows for the actual PIPGLA iterate at every finite time; it requires no invariant target.

Formal correspondence: pipglaLaws_eq_canonicalGaussian : The full iid vector Gaussian algorithm law follows from the original scalar-coordinate Gaussian hypotheses.

steps.title: Equality of scalar and vector sequence representations
steps.body:
The map grouping scalar coordinates into time-indexed vectors is measurable. Its pushforward takes the scalar Gaussian product measure to the vector Gaussian product measure. Applying the same measurable recursion to these equal input distributions gives the same output law at time \(n\).

Consequently any two probability-space realizations with the same initial law and independent standard Gaussian sequence have equal splitting laws. The concrete representatives and the choice of auxiliary product space have no effect on this distributional conclusion.

There are two descriptions of the same noise source: a countable product of scalar coordinates, packed into vectors, or a countable product of standard vector Gaussians. The first law identity uses noisePath_law directly; the second uses vector iid laws. To compare two probability spaces, rewrite both output laws in the vector representation and substitute the equal initial laws. The ambient probability spaces and their concrete random-variable representatives therefore disappear from the conclusion.

Formal correspondence: pipglaLaws_eq_canonicalNoisePath : An equivalent canonical law uses the repository's single countable product of scalar Gaussian coordinates, grouped into vector innovations. pipglaLaws_eq_of_initialLaw_eq : Gaussian realizations on different probability spaces give identical actual PIPGLA output laws when the initialization laws agree.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingMoments.lean.title: Reference drift moments uniform over smoothing scales
ProximalLangevin/SplittingMoments.lean.summary: For \(F=f+e\), assume \(F\) is \(m\)-strongly convex, \(f,e\) are differentiable, \(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, and \(\|\nabla e\|\le K\). Sharp Gibbs concentration and the gradient identity at a global minimizer bound the smooth drift’s second moment using \(L,m,K\). Applied to a Lipschitz convex penalty and its envelope, the gradient-magnitude bound is uniform in the smoothing parameter and avoids its inverse-scale gradient Lipschitz constant.

steps.title: Value Lipschitzness of the envelope
steps.body:
Let \(p=P_\lambda(y)\). At input \(x\) use competitor \(p+x-y\); its quadratic penalty equals that of \(p\) at \(y\). The \(K\)-Lipschitz bound on \(f\) changes its function value by at most \(K\|x-y\|\). Hence \(f^\lambda(x)\le f^\lambda(y)+K\|x-y\|\), and exchanging \(x,y\) proves the absolute-value bound.

Explicitly the minimizer \(p=P_\lambda(y)\) supplies a competitor at \(x\) given by \(p+(x-y)\). Identity \(p+(x-y)-x=p-y\) makes the penalties equal, and the function increment is at most \(K\|x-y\|\). This gives \(f^\lambda(x)\le f^\lambda(y)+K\|x-y\|\). The inherited value Lipschitz constant is independent of \(\lambda\), unlike the gradient Lipschitz constant \(1/\lambda\). The next moment argument uses gradient magnitude rather than gradient variation.

Formal correspondence: moreau_lipschitz_of_lipschitz : A Lipschitz potential has a Moreau envelope with the same Lipschitz constant.

steps.title: The total-potential minimizer and its smooth gradient
steps.body:
Positive strong convexity gives a coercive quadratic lower bound for \(F\). The radius \(2\| abla F(0)\|/m+1\) is large enough that the potential exceeds a fixed competitor outside the ball. Continuity and compactness give a global minimizer \(z\). Differentiability at that minimizer implies \( abla f(z)=- abla e(z)\) and thus \(\| abla f(z)\|\le K\).

The vanishing total gradient is \( abla(f+e)=0\). The smooth gradient is therefore the negative perturbation gradient at this minimizing point, which gives \(\| abla f(z)\|\le K\). Lipschitz growth of the smooth gradient can now be measured from this point and integrated using concentration of the total Gibbs law.

The strong-convexity lower bound forces the total potential above its value at zero outside a finite ball. A minimizer on the compact ball is therefore global; this is the radius construction in exists_strongConvex_minimum. At a global minimizer of \(F=f+e\), the derivative vanishes, giving \( abla f(z)=- abla e(z)\). Thus a pointwise bound \(\| abla e\|\le K\) yields \(\| abla f(z)\|\le K\). This is the only value of the smooth score at a specific point needed in the moment estimate.

Formal correspondence: gradient_eq_zero_at_minimum : A differentiable function has zero gradient at an actual global minimizer. exists_strongConvex_minimum : A smooth strongly convex real-valued function attains its minimum. gradient_smoothPart_at_minimum : At a minimum of the sum, a bounded second gradient bounds the first gradient.

steps.title: The second moment of a bounded gradient
steps.body:
The derivative of a differentiable \(K\)-Lipschitz scalar function has operator norm at most \(K\), as follows by limits of directional difference quotients. Its gradient has the same norm. Thus a pointwise bound \(\|b(x)\|\le K\) implies \(\|b(Y)\|_{L^2}\le K\) on any probability space.

Indeed for value Lipschitz constant \(K\), every unit-direction difference quotient has absolute value at most \(K\). Taking derivatives and then the supremum over unit directions bounds the gradient. Integration gives \(\mathbb E\|b(Y)\|^2\le K^2\). Neither dimension nor an inverse smoothing scale occurs in this estimate.

The derivative of a globally \(K\)-Lipschitz scalar function has operator norm at most \(K\), and the Riesz identification preserves this norm, giving \(\|\nabla f(x)\|\le K\). Separately, if \(\|b(x)\|\le K\) for every input, then the representative equality for lpDrift gives \(\|b(Y(\omega))\|\le K\) almost everywhere. Since \(P\) has mass one, its \(L^2\) norm is at most \(K\). This explains why a state-space uniform bound transfers without a dimension or measure-mass factor.

Formal correspondence: gradient_norm_le_of_lipschitz : Global Lipschitzness bounds the actual gradient norm. lpDrift_norm_le_of_bounded : A pointwise bounded Lipschitz drift is bounded by the same constant in \(L^2\).

steps.title: The smooth-gradient moment under the Gibbs law
steps.body:
The Lipschitz gradient estimate relative to the minimizing point gives \(\| abla f(x)\|\le L\|x-z\|+K\) and hence \(\| abla f(x)\|^2\le2L^2\|x-z\|^2+2K^2\). Sharp concentration gives \(\mathbb E_\pi\|x-z\|^2\le d/m\), so

\[\mathbb E_\pi\| abla f\|^2\le2L^2d/m+2K^2.\]

For a random vector \(Y\) with Gibbs law \(\pi\), the pushforward integral formula and nonnegative square root give \(\| abla f(Y)\|_2\le\sqrt{2L^2d/m+2K^2}\). The minimizing point is for the total potential, so the estimate \(\| abla f(x)\|\le L\|x-z\|+K\) contains the bounded perturbation gradient there. Squaring with \((a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2\) gives the integrable majorant whose expectation is bounded by \(2L^2d/m+2K^2\). The constants are uniform for all smoothing parameters satisfying the same gradient-magnitude bound.

Let \(z\) minimize \(F=f+e\), with \(F\) \(m\)-strongly convex. From the previous stage, \(\| abla f(z)\|\le K\), and score Lipschitzness gives \(\| abla f(x)\|\le L\|x-z\|+K\). Consequently \[\| abla f(x)\|^2\le2L^2\|x-z\|^2+2K^2.\] The Gibbs second moment is integrable by strong convexity; the right side therefore supplies an integrable majorant for the score square. The facts hbound and hgrad discharge that prerequisite before integral_mono is applied.

Sharp concentration yields \(\mathbb E_\pi\|X-z\|^2\le d/m\), so \(\mathbb E_\pi\| abla f(X)\|^2\le2L^2d/m+2K^2\). The next declaration transfers this actual Gibbs-law integral to any random variable with that law and takes its square root, obtaining the \(L^2\) drift bound used in the splitting reference.

Formal correspondence: integral_sq_smooth_gradient_le : A smoothing-uniform second moment for the smooth part of a Gibbs drift. Only the smooth part's own Lipschitz constant enters the bound. lpDrift_smooth_gradient_norm_le : The corresponding actual \(L^2\) smooth-drift bound for a random variable with the proved reference Gibbs law.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingCoupling.lean.title: Lipschitz energy and the averaged lifted potential
ProximalLangevin/SplittingCoupling.lean.summary: Assume \(g\) is convex, bounded below, and \(K\)-Lipschitz, with \(\lambda>0\) and \(N>0\). Proximal optimality and the value bound give the pairwise energy inequality; Jensen transfers it to the averaged particle output. The replicated-pair norm identity also proves that \(G=N^{-1}\sum_i g(J_i z)\) has the same value Lipschitz constant. Neither argument requires the averaged output to minimize a shared-state objective.

steps.title: The proximal energy inequality from value Lipschitzness
steps.body:
For \(p=P_\lambda(x)\), test the residual support at comparator \(a\) to bound \(f(p)-f(a)\). Apply \(f(x)-f(p)\le K\|x-p\|\) in the expansion of \(\|x-a\|^2\). Nonnegativity of \((\|x-p\|-\lambda K)^2\ge0\) gives \(\|p-a\|^2\le\|x-a\|^2-2\lambda(f(x)-f(a))+\lambda^2K^2\). Sum the pair inequalities, use Jensen for the common parameter, and divide by positive \(N\). The resulting full-state remainder is \(\lambda^2K^2\).

At the proximal point \(p\), the residual \(r=(x-p)/\lambda\) is a subgradient at \(p\). Its norm is at most \(K\) for a \(K\)-Lipschitz potential. The support at \(p\), bound \(f(x)-f(p)\le K\|x-p\|\), and squared-distance expansion give

\[\|p-y\|^2\le\|x-y\|^2-2\lambda(f(x)-f(y))+\lambda^2K^2.\]

The required replacement of output energy by input energy is exactly \(f(x)-f(p)\le K\|x-p\|\). Completion of a square bounds the remaining displacement expression by \(\lambda^2K^2\). Thus value Lipschitzness supplies the needed numerical remainder without assuming a bounded input-subgradient selection.

Formal correspondence: isProxPoint_energy_le_of_lipschitz : The proximal energy inequality follows directly from a Lipschitz potential. pairwise_prox_energy_le_lipschitz : The nonsmooth energy bound for the actual averaged pairwise proximal map, with a global Lipschitz hypothesis instead of an assumed subgradient selection.

steps.title: The averaged potential’s value Lipschitz constant
steps.body:
Put \(G(z)=F_g(z)/N\). Cauchy–Schwarz for the finite average and \(\sum_i\|J_i v\|^2=N\|v\|^2\) imply \(N^{-1}\sum_i\|J_i v\|\le\|v\|\). Applying the pairwise value Lipschitz estimate therefore gives

\[|G(z)-G(w)|\le\frac KN\sum_i\|J_i(z-w)\|\le K\|z-w\|.\]

The latent scaling \(N^{-1/2}\) makes the average pair squared distance equal to the state squared distance. Consequently the averaged physical-time potential \(G=F_g/N\) retains value Lipschitz constant \(K\). This bound ensures integrability of its values at square-integrable random states.

Let \(\bar f_N(z)=N^{-1}\sum_i f(A_i z)\). Cauchy–Schwarz and the replication identity give \[\frac1N\sum_i\|A_i v\|\le\left(\frac1N\sum_i\|A_i v\|^2\right)^{1/2}=\|v\|.\] Applying \(|f(a)-f(b)|\le K\|a-b\|\) to each pair and summing proves \(|\bar f_N(z)-\bar f_N(w)|\le K\|z-w\|\). The declarations separate the average norm estimate from the value estimate so that the particle scaling can be checked independently.

Formal correspondence: averagedPotential : The averaged lifted potential in the physical-time Langevin equation. average_joint_norm_le : Average pair distances are controlled by the scaled state norm. averagedPotential_lipschitz : Averaging in the scaled coordinates preserves the pair potential's Lipschitz constant.

ProximalLangevin/ParticleSmoothing.lean.title: Uniform Moreau gaps in scaled particle coordinates
ProximalLangevin/ParticleSmoothing.lean.summary: The lifted envelope gradient has norm at most \(NK\), and its uniform potential gap is at most \(N\eta K^2/2\). These follow by summing the single-pair value estimates and are different from gradient variation with constant involving \(1/\eta\). Write \(F_g(z)=\sum_i g(J_i z)\) with \(N>0\). If \(g\) is convex, bounded below, and \(K\)-Lipschitz, the Moreau value Lipschitz bound yields a gradient-magnitude estimate uniform over positive smoothing parameters.

steps.title: The lifted value bound and envelope-gradient magnitude
steps.body:
The averaged potential has value Lipschitz constant \(K\). Multiplication by \(N\) gives \(\operatorname{Lip}(F_g)\le NK\). Since the envelope retains single-pair value constant \(K\), its lifted sum \(F_{g^\eta}\) has constant \(NK\). Differentiability therefore bounds its gradient norm by \(NK\) for every \(\eta>0\).

Equivalently multiplication by \(N\) gives lifted value constant \(NK\). The envelope’s single-pair constant \(K\) yields \(\|\nabla V_{N,\eta}^{(2)}\|\le NK\). This uses the norm bound for the derivative of a Lipschitz function, rather than the gradient Lipschitz constant \(N/\eta\), and is consequently uniform as \(\eta\downarrow0\). In the averaged notation the constants are \(K\) and \(NK\) for the full sum, giving \(\|\nabla F_{g_2^\eta}\|\le NK\) independently of \(\eta\). Rapid spatial variation of the gradient does not change this bound on its magnitude.

Formal correspondence: potential_lipschitz : Lifting a globally Lipschitz pair potential to the scaled state multiplies its Lipschitz constant by the number of particles. potential_moreau_lipschitz : The lifted true Moreau approximation preserves the particle Lipschitz constant, uniformly over positive smoothing scales. potential_moreau_gradient_norm_le : The actual gradient of the lifted Moreau term is bounded by \(NK\), independently of the smoothing scale.

steps.title: The summed envelope gap and split-potential identity
steps.body:
Apply \(0\le g-g^\eta\le\eta K^2/2\) at each pair and sum the finite inequalities:

\[0\le F_g(z)-F_{g^\eta}(z)\le N\eta K^2/2.\]

Distributivity also gives the function identity \(F_{g_1+g_2^\eta}=F_{g_1}+F_{g_2^\eta}\). In nonsmooth-component notation the bound \(0\le g_2-g_2^\eta\le\eta K^2/2\) has \(N\) summands, so

\[0\le V_N^{(2)}-V_{N,\eta}^{(2)}\le N\eta K^2/2.\]

Expanding \(V_N(g_1+g_2^\eta)\) and distributing the sum gives \(V_N(g_1)+V_N(g_2^\eta)\). Each nonnegative gap is at most \(\eta K^2/2\); summing \(N\) such gaps proves the displayed total gap directly. Differentiating the sum identity, under the established regularity, separates the smooth and envelope reference forces in the splitting argument.

Formal correspondence: potential_moreau_gap : The finite one-sided Moreau gap for the actual sum over particles. potential_smoothed_decomposition : Lifting commutes with the smooth-plus-Moreau decomposition.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingL2Energy.lean.title: Integrated quadratic and convex-energy estimates
ProximalLangevin/SplittingL2Energy.lean.summary: Apply the deterministic energy estimate to \(L^2\) random vectors. Lipschitz growth makes the scalar potential values integrable, and square integrability makes all squared-distance terms integrable. Weighted Young inequalities control the smooth local defect without losing the squared contraction. Integrated convex supports retain the perturbation-force pairing in a form that can be combined with the expected potential difference.

steps.title: Weighted Young inequality and squared contraction
steps.body:
For \(t>0\), expansion and \((t\|v\|-\|r\|)^2\ge0\) give

\[\|v+r\|^2\le(1+t)\|v\|^2+(1+t^{-1})\|r\|^2.\]

If \(0

Choosing the Young parameter as \(mh\) gives \((1+mh)(1-mh)^2\le1-mh\) under \(mh\le1\), while multiplying the squared local defect by \(1+(mh)^{-1}\). Keeping the integrated perturbation force in its inner product permits its convex-energy contribution to combine with the proximal energy difference, rather than estimating each term by an unrelated norm bound.

Expanding \(\|v+r\|^2\) and using \(2\langle v,r\rangle\le t\|v\|^2+t^{-1}\|r\|^2\) gives the weighted inequality. If \(\|v\|\le(1-t)\|e\|\), \(0<t\le1\), then \((1+t)(1-t)^2\le1-t\). This is the scalar inequality proved in hf; it keeps a linear contraction in the squared error instead of doubling the leading term. The final identity rearranges \(\|v+r+b\|^2\) with its cross term paired against the final error, the form needed for convex-energy cancellation.

Formal correspondence: norm_add_sq_le_weighted : A weighted quadratic triangle bound with an explicit positive weight. norm_add_sq_le_of_contraction : The weighted estimate retains a linear contraction in the squared error. norm_sum_rearranged : Moving an integrated nonsmooth drift into a cross term avoids a Lipschitz constant for that drift in the consistency estimate.

steps.title: Integrability of potential and quadratic terms
steps.body:
For globally \(K\)-Lipschitz scalar function \(f\), subtract \(f(0)\). The centered growth is at most \(K\|X\|\), so \(f(X)\in L^2\subset L^1\) on a probability space. The \(L^2\) norm satisfies \(\|X\|_2^2=\int\|X(\omega)\|^2dP\).

For observable \(f\), the direct bound is \(|f(X)|\le K\|X\|+|f(0)|\). Thus an \(L^2\) state gives \(f(X)\in L^2\subset L^1\). Centering \(f\) justifies the composition estimate. The \(L^2\) inner product and identity \(\langle X,X\rangle=\|X\|^2\) give \(\|X\|_{L^2}^2=\int\|X(\omega)\|^2dP\). More generally, bound \(|f(x)|\le|f(0)|+K\|x\|\) makes composition with an \(L^2\) state an \(L^2\) function. Squared differences of \(L^2\) states are also integrable. Hence the potential and quadratic expectations below are finite, and linearity may be applied without subtraction of infinite quantities.

Formal correspondence: integrable_lipschitz_compLp : Every globally Lipschitz scalar observable of an \(L^2\) random variable is integrable. lp_norm_sq_eq_integral : Exact second-moment identity for actual \(L^2\) random variables.

steps.title: The integrated proximal energy inequality
steps.body:
Assume \(\|T(x)-y\|^2\le\|x-y\|^2-2h(f(x)-f(y))+C\) and Lipschitz maps \(T,f\). Substitute \(S,Y\in L^2\) pointwise on a probability-one representative event. The Lipschitz composition represents \(T(S)\) almost surely. Each term is integrable by the preceding growth and moment bounds. Integral monotonicity and linearity therefore give

\[\|T(S)-Y\|_2^2\le\|S-Y\|_2^2-2h(\mathbb E f(S)-\mathbb E f(Y))+C.\]

This is the same energy inequality in \(L^2\). The additive constant is unchanged because the source has mass one. The statement concerns the random output of the actual composed map, as identified by its almost-sure representative.

Apply the deterministic premise at \((S(\omega),Y(\omega))\). The representative facts for lpDrift and subtraction identify its left side almost everywhere with \(\|T(S)-Y\|^2\). The local facts hn, hfS, hfY prove integrability of both quadratic norms and both potential values. Only then does integral_mono_ae integrate the inequality and distribute its finite terms: \[\|T(S)-Y\|_2^2\le\|S-Y\|_2^2-2h(\mathbb Ef(S)-\mathbb Ef(Y))+C.\] The constant remains \(C\) because \(P\) has mass one.

Formal correspondence: lp_energy_of_pointwise : Lift a proved deterministic energy inequality to actual \(L^2\) random variables. This is an integration lemma; the particle instantiation below proves its pointwise premise from the genuine proximal minimization problem.

steps.title: Integrated convex support and the terminal-state difference
steps.body:
The support inequality for a differentiable convex perturbation gives \(\langle S-Y, abla e(Y) angle\le e(S)-e(Y)\) pointwise. Integrability permits the same inequality for the \(L^2\) inner product. For a third vector \(Z\), identity \(S-Z=(S-Y)+(Y-Z)\) leaves additional pairing \(\langle Y-Z, abla e(Y) angle_{L^2}\).

Explicitly, for convex differentiable \(e\) the inequality is \(\langle S-Y, abla e(Y) angle\le e(S)-e(Y)\). The gradient composition and state difference belong to \(L^2\) under the stated bounds, so Cauchy–Schwarz makes their pairing integrable. Integration consequently replaces the reference-force pairing by an expected potential difference, while retaining the endpoint-difference pairing whose future-noise part is shown to vanish separately.

The pointwise supporting-plane inequality is \(e(S)-e(Y)\ge\langle abla e(Y),S-Y angle\). Potential integrability follows from value Lipschitzness; inner-product integrability follows from both vectors belonging to \(L^2\), with score Lipschitzness ensuring \( abla e(Y)\in L^2\). Integration gives the first declaration. For an endpoint \(Z\), write \(S-Z=(S-Y)+(Y-Z)\) and use linearity of the inner product. This produces the energy difference plus the reference-increment cross term, precisely the two contributions used in splitting_cross_energy_le.

Formal correspondence: lp_convex_gradient_support : The actual convex gradient supports every square-integrable comparison variable after integrating the pointwise supporting-plane inequality. lp_convex_gradient_cross : Endpoint comparison split into the convex energy difference and a reference-increment cross term, all in the genuine \(L^2\) inner product.

ProximalLangevin/IndependenceHelpers.lea.title: Independence under grouping of random variables
ProximalLangevin/IndependenceHelpers.lea.summary: Independent source variables may be grouped into an initialized past and a future increment by factoring their joint distributions and reassociating product measures. The results below use joint independence of the specified blocks. Pairwise independence of three separate variables would not imply the required independence of one variable from a pair.

steps.title: An independent family with two indices
steps.body:
Assume \(X\perp Y\) and define \(Z_{\rm false}=X\) and \(Z_{\rm true}=Y\). To verify independence of this two-element family, consider its finite index subsets. The empty subset uses probability mass one, and each singleton gives an identity. For the subset of both indices the condition is exactly \(P(X\in A,Y\in B)=P(X\in A)P(Y\in B)\).

Thus two-variable independence is equivalent to the factorization required for the corresponding two-element independent family. No additional independence condition is introduced by this indexing.

An independent family is defined by factorization for every finite set of indices. For a Boolean index there are four possibilities: neither variable, only \(X\), only \(Y\), or both. The singleton identities are tautological; the empty family has probability one because \(\mu\) is a probability; the two-variable case is exactly the assumed independence of \(X\) and \(Y\). The two membership case splits in Lean exhaust these four possibilities explicitly.

Formal correspondence: iIndepFun_bool_of_indepFun : Two independent random variables form an independent family indexed by Bool . The probability assumption supplies the empty-family identity.

steps.title: Reassociation of a jointly independent triple
steps.body:
Assume measurable variables satisfy \(X\perp(Y,Z)\) and \(Y\perp Z\). Their triple law factors as \(\mu_X\otimes(\mu_Y\otimes\mu_Z)\). Product reassociation gives \((\mu_X\otimes\mu_Y)\otimes\mu_Z\), while projection gives \(\mu_{(X,Y)}=\mu_X\otimes\mu_Y\). Hence \((X,Y)\perp Z\).

Indeed \(X\) is independent of the entire pair \((Y,Z)\), and \(Y\) and \(Z\) are independent. These hypotheses give \(\mu_X\otimes(\mu_Y\otimes\mu_Z)\), whose reassociation is \((\mu_X\otimes\mu_Y)\otimes\mu_Z\). This proves independence of \((X,Y)\) and \(Z\). The first two product marginals are the joint law of \((X,Y)\), so the conclusion is \((X,Y)\perp Z\). Equality of measurable pushforward measures proves the statement also for path-valued variables. The hypotheses are stronger than mere pairwise independence.

Formal correspondence: indepFun_prodMk_left_of_indepFun : Regroup a jointly independent triple from \(X\perp(Y,Z)\) into \((X,Y)\perp Z\). Independence of \(Y\) and \(Z\) is essential; pairwise independence alone is insufficient.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingOrthogonality..title: Orthogonality of future Brownian increments to past observables
ProximalLangevin/SplittingOrthogonality..summary: Assume independent full scalar Brownian paths with measurable evaluations and initialization independent of the entire Brownian family. The integral solution is measurable with respect to initialization and the stopped noise path. A future Brownian increment is independent of this past and centered. Its expected inner product with any square-integrable Lipschitz observable of the reference state is therefore zero. This is an expectation identity, not a samplewise orthogonality claim.

steps.title: Independence of vector stopped past and shifted future
steps.body:
For each scalar coordinate, the shifted future \(B_i(T+s)-B_i(T)\) is independent of the stopped past \(B_i(\min(t,T))\). Independence of the full coordinate paths gives joint independence across these coordinatewise pairs. Selecting and grouping the disjoint past and future indices therefore gives independence of the entire vector-valued past and future path families.

The stopped path records all coordinate values up to time \(t\); the shifted future records increments after \(t\). The resulting independence is between the sigma-algebras generated by these full path blocks. Consequently any measurable function of the entire past is independent of every measurable future increment. This uses full-path independence and Brownian independent increments, rather than unrelated pairwise independence assertions.

Formal correspondence: brownian_future_past_independent : The complete shifted future and the stopped past of independent scalar Brownian coordinates are independent vector-valued path families.

steps.title: The pointwise Brownian vector and its square-integrable representative
steps.body:
Define the pointwise vector noise by \(\mathcal B_t=\sqrt2(B(t_+)-B(0))\) with \(t_+=\max(t,0)\). The constructed \(L^2\) Brownian noise agrees almost surely with this expression. Each scalar evaluation is measurable, and finite vector assembly, subtraction, and scaling preserve measurability. Its Gaussian coordinate second moments prove square integrability.

The \(L^2\) class and the pointwise vector thus have the same laws and integrals. Independence and centering may be transferred by their almost-sure equality. The nonnegative-time definition specifies the domain of Brownian evaluation and does not change the positive-time process.

Formal correspondence: rawBrownianNoise : The pointwise vector presentation of the Langevin noise from time zero.

steps.title: Independence of the initialized past from future increments
steps.body:
The stopped Brownian path is independent of the future increment. Initialization is independent of their joint pair. Reassociation of the product law therefore makes the pair consisting of initialization and stopped past independent of the future increment. Any variable measurable with respect to that initialized past inherits the same independence.

A variable only almost everywhere strongly measurable for the past admits a measurable representative with the same law. Almost-sure equality then transfers the conclusion to its \(L^2\) representative. The grouping relation is \((\text{initial},\text{past})\mid\text{future}\). Thus independence for the later reference observable follows from its past measurability and the input assumptions; it is not added as an independent assertion about the solution.

Formal correspondence: brownian_future_independent_initial_past : A future Brownian increment is independent of the initialization and all earlier actual \(L^2\) Brownian-noise representatives. naturalPast_independent_of_aestronglyMeasurable : Every random variable measurable from the natural initialization/noise past inherits its independence from a supplied future source variable.

steps.title: Expected orthogonality from independence and centering
steps.body:
Scalar Brownian centering and commutation of finite coordinate projections with integration give \(\mathbb E B_t=0\), and subtraction and scaling give \(\mathbb E\mathcal B_t=0\). For independent \(L^2\) vectors \(X,W\), Cauchy–Schwarz proves integrability of the inner product. Independence and bilinear integration give \(\langle X,W\rangle_{L^2}=\langle\mathbb E X,\mathbb E W\rangle\).

When \(W\) is centered, the latter inner product of means is zero. Thus no norm bound on the other mean is needed: independence and centering give exact expected orthogonality.

Formal correspondence: brownianCoordinates_integral_zero : The finite-dimensional Brownian vector has zero mean. brownianNoise_integral_zero : The actual \(L^2\) additive Langevin noise is centered at every real time. independent_centered_lp_inner_zero : Binary independence and zero mean imply genuine \(L^2\) orthogonality.

steps.title: Orthogonality for observables of the adapted integral solution
steps.body:
The integral-equation construction makes \(Y_t\) measurable for the initialized Brownian past. A Lipschitz observable \(b(Y_t)\) remains measurable for that past and belongs to \(L^2\). Independence of future increments and their zero mean imply

\[\langle b(Y_t),\mathcal B_h-\mathcal B_t\rangle_{L^2}=0,\qquad0\le t\le h.\]

For observable \(b(Y_t)\), both factors are in \(L^2\), so their pairing is integrable and

\[\mathbb E\langle b(Y_t),B_h-B_t\rangle=\left\langle\mathbb E b(Y_t),\mathbb E(B_h-B_t)\right\rangle=0.\]

The \(L^2\) inner product is this expectation. The state at time \(t\) depends only on initialization and noise up to \(t\). Composing with the drift observable preserves this dependence, while the increment over \([t,h]\) is independent and centered. This identity removes the contribution that an absolute norm bound would estimate at order \(\sqrt{h-t}\) in the subsequent energy comparison.

Formal correspondence: lp_langevin_future_inner_zero : A Lipschitz function of the actual Langevin solution is orthogonal to every later Brownian increment. Adaptedness is derived from the integral equation by the existing invariant-subspace construction.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingProcess.lean.title: Local smooth drift defect and the future cross term
ProximalLangevin/SplittingProcess.lean.summary: Suppose the continuous Hilbert-valued reference satisfies \(Y_t-Y_0=-\int_0^t g(Y_s)ds+B_t\) with \(\|g(Y_t)\|\le G\) and \(\|B_t\|\le\sigma\sqrt t\). Its increments are bounded by the sum of a term linear in time and a term proportional to the square root of time. The smooth drift’s Lipschitz constant then bounds its integrated local defect. For a bounded perturbation observable, first use orthogonality of the future noise; the remaining drift pairing is linear in the remaining time.

steps.title: The integrated smooth drift defect
steps.body:
The integral equation and the integral norm inequality give \(\|Y_t-Y_0\|\le Gt+\sigma\sqrt t\). If \(a\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, then for \(0\le t\le h\), \(\|a(Y_t)-a(Y_0)\|\le L(Gh+\sigma\sqrt h)\). Integration over length \(h\) therefore yields

\[\left\|\int_0^h(a(Y_t)-a(Y_0))dt ight\|\le Lh(Gh+\sigma\sqrt h).\]

Equivalently, for solution \(Y_t-Y_0=-\int_0^t g(Y_s)ds+B_t\) with \(\|g(Y_s)\|\le G\) and \(\|B_t\|\le u\sqrt t\), one has \(\|Y_t-Y_0\|\le tG+ u\sqrt t\). For smooth component \(a\) with Lipschitz constant \(L\), this gives

\[\left\|\int_0^h(a(Y_t)-a(Y_0))dt ight\|\le Lh(Gh+ u\sqrt h).\]

The estimate replaces both time factors by their endpoint maxima on \(0\le t\le h\), using monotonicity of \(t\) and \(\sqrt t\), and multiplies by interval length. Thus from \(\|Y_t-Y_0\|\le Gt+\sigma\sqrt t\), multiplication by \(L\) controls the smooth force difference; for \(t\in[0,h]\) the factors \(t\) and \(\sqrt t\) are bounded by their endpoint values. Regularity may require Lipschitz continuity of the full drift, but only the smooth component’s constant enters this numerical bound.

Formal correspondence: splitting_localDefect_bound : A coarse local smooth-drift defect bound uses only the smooth part's own Lipschitz constant and the total reference drift moment.

steps.title: The future-drift pairing after noise orthogonality
steps.body:
Subtract the reference equations at \(t,h\) to obtain

\[Y_t-Y_h=\int_t^h g(Y_s)ds-(B_h-B_t).\]

If \(\|b\|\le K\) and \(\langle b,B_h-B_t\rangle=0\), the noise pairing is zero. Cauchy–Schwarz on the remaining drift integral gives \(\langle Y_t-Y_h,b\rangle\le(h-t)GK\), avoiding an order-\(\sqrt{h-t}\) bound.

Splitting the integral at \(t\) gives the same difference identity

\[Y_t-Y_h=\int_t^h g(Y_s)ds-(B_h-B_t).\]

Pairing with \(b\) and applying orthogonality gives

\[\langle Y_t-Y_h,b\rangle\le\left\|\int_t^h g(Y_s)ds\right\|\|b\|\le(h-t)GK.\]

In the application the inner product is in \(L^2\), so this cancellation is of the expected pairing. Subtraction at \(t\) and \(h\) leaves future drift integral of norm at most \((h-t)G\), hence remainder \((h-t)GK\). Brownian sample increments themselves do not vanish.

Formal correspondence: reference_future_inner_le : Future-noise orthogonality turns the reference increment cross term into a drift integral of order \(h-t\), rather than a Brownian norm of order \(\sqrt{h-t}\).

ProximalLangevin/SplittingCrossEnergy.le.title: Expected energy comparison for the perturbation force
ProximalLangevin/SplittingCrossEnergy.le.summary: Let \(e\) be convex and differentiable, assume \(e\le f\le e+\delta\), and let \(Y_t\) have the stated stationary smoothed law, integral equation, and future-noise orthogonality. Assume the value Lipschitz bounds needed for integrability. Convex support bounds the force pairing by an envelope-energy difference. Stationarity identifies the time-dependent reference energy with the terminal energy, and the uniform gap then compares this with the original nonsmooth energy in the proximal estimate.

steps.title: The expected uniform value-gap inequality
steps.body:
Suppose \(f(x)\le e(x)+\delta\) and both functions are Lipschitz. For \(L^2\) variable \(X\) their values are integrable, so integral monotonicity gives \(\mathbb E f(X)-\mathbb E e(X)\le\delta\). In the notation \(f\le e+\delta\) and an \(L^2\) state, the mass-one calculation is \(\mathbb Ef(X)\le\mathbb Ee(X)+\delta P(\Omega)=\mathbb Ee(X)+\delta\).

The subsequent comparison uses \(e\le f\) at the algorithm’s intermediate state and \(f\le e+\delta\) at the reference endpoint. The integrated gap is \(\delta\) because the source is a probability. All expected values are finite before subtraction, and no derivative of the original nonsmooth function is used.

Formal correspondence: expectation_gap_le : A finite uniform value gap controls its actual expectation.

steps.title: The stationary convex-support and future-drift estimates
steps.body:
Convex support bounds \(\langle S-Y_h, abla e(Y_t) angle\) by \(\mathbb E e(S)-\mathbb E e(Y_t)+\langle Y_t-Y_h, abla e(Y_t) angle\). Stationarity gives equality of \(\mathbb E e(Y_t)\) and \(\mathbb E e(Y_h)\). The future-noise estimate bounds the remaining drift pairing by \(hGK\). The gap \(e\le f\le e+\delta\) changes the difference of the two energies by at most \(\delta\). Integration therefore gives

\[2\left\langle S-Y_h,\int_0^h abla e(Y_t)dt ight angle-2h(\mathbb E f(S)-\mathbb E f(Y_h))\le2h\delta+2h^2GK.\]

More explicitly, for \(b_t= abla e(Y_t)\) in \(L^2\) the support and future-increment bounds give

\[\langle S-Y_h,b_t angle\le\mathbb Ee(S)-\mathbb Ee(Y_t)+(h-t)GK.\]

Stationarity replaces \(\mathbb Ee(Y_t)\) by \(\mathbb Ee(Y_h)\). Integration over \([0,h]\) is legitimate because \(b_t\) is continuous and the fixed inner-product functional commutes with the Bochner integral. A valid upper bound is \(h[\mathbb Ee(S)-\mathbb Ee(Y_h)]+h^2GK\).

The decomposition \(S-Y_h=(S-Y_t)+(Y_t-Y_h)\) separates the convex support term from the future-increment term. Again \(\mathbb E e(Y_t)\) equals \(\mathbb E e(Y_h)\). At \(S\) use \(e\le f\), and at \(Y_h\) use \(f\le e+\delta\). Only one additive gap \(\delta\) remains. This is the energy comparison used to cancel the original potential difference in the splitting estimate.

The two value comparisons give \([\mathbb Ee(S)-\mathbb Ee(Y_h)]-[\mathbb Ef(S)-\mathbb Ef(Y_h)]\le\delta\). Multiply by \(2h\) and combine to obtain the displayed \(2h\delta+2h^2GK\) remainder. In Lean, hpoint is the pointwise-in-time estimate, hi its integral, and hsum the finite value-gap cancellation. The conclusion never substitutes \(\operatorname{Lip}( abla e)\) into this remainder.

Formal correspondence: splitting_cross_energy_le : The integrated reference-gradient cross term cancels the original nonsmooth energy up to a finite value gap and a drift error of order \(h^2\). The orthogonality premise is instantiated by the actual Brownian construction in lp_langevin_future_inner_zero , not by a convergence assumption.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingOneStep.lean.title: The synchronous one-step splitting estimate
ProximalLangevin/SplittingOneStep.lean.summary: In the Hilbert space \(L^2\), suppose \(f_1\) is \(m\)-strongly convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Let a Lipschitz map \(T\) satisfy the proximal energy inequality for \(f\). Assume the stationary reference satisfies the integral equation for \(f_1+e\) and \(e\le f\le e+\delta\), together with the stated moment and orthogonality conditions. Subtraction from the numerical forward step decomposes the discrepancy into a contractive smooth difference, a local smooth defect, and an integrated envelope force. The energy comparison and weighted Young inequality then give the one-step squared-error bound.

steps.title: The four local forcing terms
steps.body:
For \(m,h>0\), drift bound \(G\), noise coefficient \(\sigma\), perturbation-gradient bound \(K\), and potential gap \(\delta\), set

\[\mathcal F=(1+(mh)^{-1})[Lh(Gh+\sigma\sqrt h)]^2+2h\delta+2h^2GK+h^2K^2.\]

The first term is the squared smooth local defect with Young factor \(1+(mh)^{-1}\). The other terms are, respectively, the finite potential-gap contribution, the reference drift paired with the bounded perturbation gradient, and the proximal quadratic remainder. These distinct estimates will bound the sum by a constant times the squared step.

Formal correspondence: splittingCouplingForcing : Explicit local forcing in the synchronous splitting proof.

steps.title: The error decomposition and energy comparison
steps.body:
Define \(S=X-h abla f_1(X)+B_h\), \(v=(X-h abla f_1(X))-(Y_0-h abla f_1(Y_0))\), \(R=\int_0^h[ abla f_1(Y_t)- abla f_1(Y_0)]dt\), and \(H=\int_0^h abla e(Y_t)dt\). The shared noise and reference integral equation give \(S-Y_h=v+R+H\). Expand its square and integrate the energy inequality for \(T(S)\). The expected \(f\) difference cancels with the corresponding force pairing up to the cross-energy bound. Smooth-step contraction and weighted Young control \(\|v+R\|^2\), while the local estimate controls \(R\). Discarding \(-\|H\|^2\le0\) gives

\[\|T(S)-Y_h\|_2^2\le(1-mh)\|X-Y_0\|_2^2+\mathcal F.\]

The conditions \(m\le L\) and \(h\le2/(m+L)\) imply \(mh\le1\), as required in the weighted contraction estimate. In the shorter notation \(a= abla f_1\), \(b= abla e\), \(S=X-ha(X)+B_h\), \(v=[X-ha(X)]-[Y_0-ha(Y_0)]\), \(R=\int_0^h[a(Y_t)-a(Y_0)]dt\), and \(H=\int_0^h b(Y_t)dt\), the exact difference is \(S-Y_h=v+R+H\) and its squared rearrangement is

\[\|S-Y_h\|^2=\|v+R\|^2+2\langle S-Y_h,H angle-\|H\|^2.\]

This identity retains the integrated envelope force until its energy comparison is applied. The nonpositive square can then be dropped. Weighted Young leaves coefficient \(1-mh\) on the preceding squared error. The forcing is derived from these inequalities rather than assumed as a stochastic recurrence; the Gaussian reference construction supplies the stated reference premises.

Apply the genuine proximal energy estimate to \(T(S)\), then control \(\|v+R\|^2\) using the weighted inequality with \(t=mh\). Strong smooth convexity gives \(\|v\|\le(1-mh)\|X-Y_0\|\), and the step restriction proves \(mh\le1\). The local smooth drift estimate bounds \(\|R\|\), while the preceding cross-energy theorem cancels the original nonsmooth potential difference up to \(2h\delta+2h^2GK\). Discarding \(-\|H\|^2\le0\) leaves exactly the four displayed terms in splittingCouplingForcing. The facts hdecomp, hweighted, hRweighted and hcross correspond to these four stages.

Formal correspondence: splitting_one_step_of_integral_solution : One splitting step compared with an actual smooth stationary reference. The pointwise energy premise is proved for the actual averaged joint proximal map; the reference hypotheses are discharged by its canonical Brownian construction. No stochastic error recurrence is assumed.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingCanonical.lean.title: A stationary coupling for the splitting transition
ProximalLangevin/SplittingCanonical.lean.summary: For splitting transition \(\mathcal T_h(x,\xi)=T(x-h\nabla f_1(x)+\sqrt{2h}\xi)\) and Gibbs reference potential \(F=f_1+e\), extend an arbitrary finite-cost initial coupling by an independent Brownian source. The Langevin solution started in the Gibbs marginal remains stationary. Its drift moments and independence from future increments supply the one-step comparison assumptions. The normalized Brownian endpoint gives the numerical transition its required independent Gaussian law.

steps.title: The measurable transition and sum-gradient identity
steps.body:
The Gaussian forward map is jointly continuous, and the following map \(T\) is Lipschitz. Their composition is measurable and defines the splitting transition. Differentiability of the two potential components gives \( abla(f_1+e)= abla f_1+ abla e\).

Composition with square-integrable vectors preserves this identity almost surely, so the corresponding \(L^2\) drift maps add as \(L^2\) elements. Hence the reference drift used in the integral equation is the gradient of the stated sum potential.

Formal correspondence: splittingUpdate : The actual forward, noise, backward splitting transition. lpDrift_gradient_add : The lifted drift of an actual sum is the sum of its lifted gradients.

steps.title: The stationary comparison from an arbitrary finite-cost coupling
steps.body:
Let \(c\) be any finite-cost coupling of input law \(\mu\) and the Gibbs target. Its product with an independent Brownian probability space gives square-integrable initial variables with the prescribed marginals. The Langevin solution started at the target coordinate is stationary. Its adaptedness, future-increment independence, and moment bounds give

\[G=\sqrt{2L^2d/m+2K^2}+K,\qquad\sigma=\sqrt{2d}.\]

The normalized increment over \([0,h]\) is independent standard Gaussian noise for the numerical transition. The resulting output pair is a finite-cost coupling, and the one-step theorem gives

\[W_2(\mu\mathcal T_h,\pi)^2\le(1-mh)\operatorname{cost}(c)^2+\mathcal F(m,h,L,G,\sigma,K,\delta).\]

More explicitly, the initial coupling \(c\) has reference marginal \(\pi\propto e^{-(f_1+e)}\) and gives initial variables \(X,Z\). The integral solution \(Y_t\) starts from \(Z\) and satisfies \(\operatorname{Law}(Y_t)=\pi\). Thus stationarity, Gaussian laws, moments, and orthogonality follow from the construction under the potential assumptions, rather than being extra assumptions of the final convergence theorem.

The bound on the total reference force is \[G=\sqrt{2L_1^2d/m+2K^2}+K,\] combining the proved smooth-score Gibbs moment with the uniformly bounded envelope score. The Brownian moment gives \(\|B_t\|_2\le\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t\). Adaptedness and future-increment independence prove horth; stationarity proves equality of the envelope expectations in hstationary. These facts discharge the analytic one-step theorem's stochastic inputs.

Finally, the normalized Brownian increment \(V\) has the standard Gaussian law and is independent of \(X\). The representative identity hX'coe identifies the updated random variable with \(T(X-h\nabla f_1(X)+\sqrt{2h}V)\); hX'law proves its law is the actual independent-Gaussian Markov step. The pair \((X',Y_h)\) therefore provides a finite transport coupling. This proves both output finiteness and the squared estimate for the original arbitrary \(c\).

Formal correspondence: splitting_markov_step_coupling_bound : A genuine canonical coupling estimate for one actual independent Gaussian splitting step. All stochastic inputs of the analytic one-step theorem are constructed here from the potential assumptions.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingTransport.lean.title: The infimum of squared coupling estimates
ProximalLangevin/SplittingTransport.lean.summary: Assume \(W_2(\mu, u)<\infty\) and \(q,c\ge0\). Suppose \(W_2(\mu', u')^2\le q\operatorname{cost}(p)^2+c\) holds for every finite-cost coupling \(p\) of \(\mu, u\). The same coefficient and forcing then bound the output squared Wasserstein distance in terms of the input squared distance. The proof below treats zero coefficients separately and otherwise uses the greatest-lower-bound property of the input cost infimum.

steps.title: The greatest-lower-bound argument
steps.body:
If \(q=0\), choose one finite-cost input coupling. If the output square is at most \(c\), nonnegativity of the other term already proves the claim. Otherwise the coefficient is positive and one may set \(r=\sqrt{(W_2(\mu', u')^2-c)/q}\). Each finite coupling estimate implies \(r\le\operatorname{cost}(p)\), and infinite-cost couplings satisfy the same extended lower bound. Hence \(r\le\inf_p\operatorname{cost}(p)=W_2(\mu, u)\). Squaring and multiplying by \(q\) gives

\[W_2(\mu', u')^2\le qW_2(\mu, u)^2+c.\]

In the notation \(A=W_2(\mu', u')^2\), the hypothesis is \(A\le qC^2+c\) for all finite costs. The case \(q=0\) gives \(A\le c\) directly. The case \(A\le c\) follows using \(q\ge0\). Otherwise \(r=\sqrt{(A-c)/q}\) is real and positive, and all coupling costs are at least \(r\).

Equivalently, costs may approach the finite infimum from above; continuity of squaring makes their squared costs tend to \(W_2(\mu, u)^2\). The fixed output bound survives that limit. These arguments require neither an optimal coupling nor division by a coefficient without first proving its positivity. One finite-cost comparison also establishes output finiteness.

The operation le_iInf now proves \(r\le W_2(\mu, u)\) directly from the definition as an infimum. The finite-distance hypothesis justifies passing to real values. Squaring and multiplying by \(q\) gives \(A\le qW_2(\mu, u)^2+c\). This is why the proof does not need existence of an optimal transport plan.

Formal correspondence: wasserstein2_sq_bound_of_finite_couplings : A uniform squared estimate for actual finite-cost couplings passes to the square of the genuine Wasserstein distance.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingRate.lean.title: A finite coefficient for the splitting error floor
ProximalLangevin/SplittingRate.lean.summary: The explicit local forcing is at most \(mh^2C\) when its potential gap is at most \(hK^2/2\). Its coefficient uses curvature, smooth-gradient regularity, drift and noise moments, and the bounded perturbation-gradient magnitude. It contains no inverse envelope gradient constant. Thus the one-step squared forcing is \(O(h^2)\) under \(\delta\le hK^2/2\), as required for a transport error tending to zero with the step.

steps.title: The explicit nonnegative coefficient
steps.body:
For \(m>0\) and \(G,K\ge0\) define

\[C(m,L,G,\sigma,K)=\frac{4L^2}{m^2}\left(\frac{G^2}{m}+\sigma^2\right)+\frac2m(GK+K^2).\]

Every squared term is nonnegative and the denominators are positive, giving \(C\ge0\). Each summand of \(C\) is finite under \(m>0\) and the stated nonnegative magnitude bounds. The coefficient is not asserted optimal; its explicit dependence on dimension, curvature, and particle factors is retained in the quantitative estimate.

Formal correspondence: splittingRMSConstant : A finite coefficient for the squared splitting error floor. splittingRMSConstant_nonneg : The coefficient is nonnegative under the actual moment-bound hypotheses.

steps.title: The quadratic-step bound on local forcing
steps.body:
Assume \(h\le1/m\) and the stated gap bound. The estimates \((Gh+\sigma\sqrt h)^2\le2G^2h^2+2\sigma^2h\le2h(G^2/m+\sigma^2)\) and \(h+1/m\le2/m\) bound the weighted smooth defect by \(4L^2h^2(G^2/m+\sigma^2)/m\). The gap contributes \(2h\delta\le h^2K^2\). Adding \(2h^2GK+h^2K^2\) proves \(\mathcal F\le mh^2C\), whose geometric sum has floor \(hC\).

For the expression \((Gh+\sigma\sqrt h)^2\), apply \((u+v)^2\le2u^2+2v^2\) and \(h\le1/m\) to obtain

\[(Gh+\sigma\sqrt h)^2\le2h(G^2/m+\sigma^2).\]

The remaining weighted factor satisfies \((1+(mh)^{-1})h^2\cdot2h=2h^2(h+1/m)\le4h^2/m\). The gap bound is \(2h\delta\le h^2K^2\); addition of \(h^2K^2\) and \(2h^2GK\) gives exactly \(mh^2\,C\). Positivity \(m,h>0\) justifies all denominators.

The use of \((a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2\) separates drift and noise. Under \(h\le1/m\) the additional powers of \(h\) are bounded by curvature constants, leaving a coefficient times \(h^2\). The gap contributes \(h^2K^2\), and the sum is \(mh^2C\). Division by the later contraction gap \(mh\) gives a squared transport error linear in the step.

Formal correspondence: splittingCouplingForcing_le : With a gap of at most \(hK^2/2\), the derived one-step forcing is bounded by \(mh^2C\), where \(C\) is independent of the smoothing parameter.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingEndpoint.lean.title: Transport convergence for equal forward and proximal scales
ProximalLangevin/SplittingEndpoint.lean.summary:
The stationary one-step coupling gives an estimate for each input coupling. Taking the coupling infimum makes it a recurrence for the Gaussian transition laws. At equal forward and proximal scales, the potential gap meets the required linear-step bound, and the forcing is quadratic in the step with a finite step-independent coefficient. Geometric summation and the particle scaling then give the stated squared transport estimate.

For \(f_1\) strongly convex and smooth, a bounded convex envelope term \(e\), and a genuine energy map \(T\), this module first proves convergence of actual Gaussian Markov laws. It then instantiates the result with the true averaged particle proximity and equal proximal/forward steps.

steps.title: The one-step transport recurrence
steps.body:
The admissible step and \(m\le L\) give \(mh\le1\). For each finite-cost input coupling the stationary construction gives a finite output coupling with the same forcing. Taking the cost infimum yields

\[W_2(\rho_{k+1},\pi)^2\le(1-mh)W_2(\rho_k,\pi)^2+\mathcal F.\]

The forcing is nonnegative because \(e\le f\le e+\delta\) implies \(\delta\ge0\). In the smooth-part notation, \(m\le L_1\) and step admissibility give \(0<mh\le1\), hence \(q=1-mh\ge0\). The transition estimate is

\[W_2(\mu P,\pi)^2\le qW_2(\mu,\pi)^2+\mathcal F.\]

The reference target is fixed during iteration at the chosen scale. One finite input coupling proves finite output transport, while the estimate for every coupling gives the infimum bound. The condition \(mh\le1\) ensures its preceding-error coefficient is nonnegative, permitting iteration.

Formal correspondence: splitting_markov_step_sq_bound : The squared transport recurrence for one actual independent Gaussian transition, with canonical stationarity and the coupling infimum discharged.

steps.title: The finite-time geometric estimate
steps.body:
Measurability preserves probability, and the one-step bound preserves finite distance to the target. Under \(\delta\le hK^2/2\) the forcing is at most \(mh^2C\). For \(q=1-mh\in[0,1)\), geometric summation gives

\[W_2(\rho_n,\pi)^2\le(1-mh)^nW_2(\rho_0,\pi)^2+hC.\]

The denominator is \(1-q=mh>0\). Explicitly \(\delta\le hK^2/2\) gives \(\mathcal F\le mh^2C\), so the recurrence \(E_{n+1}\le(1-mh)E_n+mh^2C\) has geometric error term \((mh^2C)/(mh)=hC\) and conclusion

\[E_n\le(1-mh)^nE_0+hC.\]

Cancellation is valid because \(m,h>0\). For \(E_{k+1}\le qE_k+mh^2C\) and \(q=1-mh\), the finite-sum formula is \(E_n\le q^nE_0+mh^2C(1-q^n)/(1-q)\). Identity \(1-q=mh>0\) bounds its added term by \(hC\). The same induction proves normalization and finiteness needed to reapply the transition estimate at every step.
