Formal correspondence: splitting_markov_laws_sq_bound : Fully derived convergence for the actual iterated Gaussian splitting laws. The coefficient is uniform in the smoothing scale whenever the value gap is at most \(hK^2/2\).

steps.title: The lifted particle coefficient
steps.body:
Let \(d=d_\theta+Nd_x\) and substitute \(\bar m=Nm\), \(\bar L=NL_1\), \(\bar K=NK\), \(\sigma=\sqrt{2d}\), and

\[G_N=\sqrt{2(NL_1)^2d/(Nm)+2(NK)^2}+NK.\]

The resulting coefficient is \(C_N=C(Nm,NL_1,G_N,\sqrt{2d},NK)\). Its nonnegativity follows from \(N,m>0\) and the scalar coefficient inequality. Both lifted force constants have factor \(N\), and the moment uses dimension \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\). This defines \(C_N\) with all particle dependence explicit before the forward step is varied. Independence of the step does not imply independence of particle count.

Formal correspondence: pipglaReferenceG : Smoothing-uniform moment bound in the scaled particle coordinates. pipglaTransportConstant : A finite explicit coefficient for the equal-step PIPGLA transport floor. pipglaTransportConstant_nonneg : The explicit transport coefficient is nonnegative in the intended regime.

steps.title: The equal-step PIPGLA estimate
steps.body:
For \(\lambda=\gamma>0\) take \(h=\gamma/N\), \(T=\operatorname{Pair}_{P_\gamma}\), and \(\pi=\Pi_{N,\gamma}\), the Gibbs law of \(g_1+g_2^\gamma\). The summed envelope gap \(N\gamma K^2/2\) equals \(h(NK)^2/2\), as required by the forcing estimate. Identification with the Gaussian transition laws then gives

\[W_2(\rho_n,\Pi_{N,\gamma})^2\le(1-m\gamma)^nW_2(\rho_0,\Pi_{N,\gamma})^2+\frac\gamma N C_N.\]

Coefficient \(C_N\) does not depend on \(\gamma\), although the target itself uses envelope scale \(\gamma\). In detail the gap \(N\gamma K^2/2\), with \(h=\gamma/N\) and \(K_N=NK\), is exactly \(hK_N^2/2\). The contraction factor is \(1-m\gamma\) and the floor is \((\gamma/N)C_N\). These are substitutions into the proved recurrence for the output laws, which equal those of the supplied splitting recursion.

For the particle application substitute lifted modulus \(Nm\), smooth score constant \(NL_1\), time step \(h=\gamma/N\), dimension \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\), and envelope scale \(\eta=\gamma\). The lifted score-magnitude bound is \(K_N=NK\) and the value gap is \(N\gamma K^2/2=hK_N^2/2\), exactly the required equal-step gap. The definitions pipglaReferenceG and pipglaTransportConstant retain every resulting factor. The exact Gaussian-law identities transfer the Markov-law result to the supplied PIPGLA innovations, so the theorem concludes a rate for the implemented algorithm.

Formal correspondence: pipgla_equal_step_transport_sq : The actual PIPGLA Gaussian recursion, with equal proximal and forward steps, converges to within a proved \(O(\sqrt\gamma)\) transport radius of the true smooth reference Gibbs law. No invariant-law or convergence hypothesis is assumed.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingProjection.lea.title: Project splitting transport to the original parameter center
ProximalLangevin/SplittingProjection.lea.summary:
Finite moments of the splitting recursion justify parameter root mean square errors about any deterministic center. Projection converts full-state transport to the smoothed Gibbs law into parameter error about its maximizer. The finite potential-gap estimate then changes that center to the original marginal maximizer. The resulting inequality retains the transport distance until its quantitative splitting estimate is substituted.

Let \(\rho_n\) be the actual PIPGLA law with any positive proximal parameter \(\lambda\), and compare it with the Gibbs target for \(V_\eta=g_1+g_2^\eta\), \(\eta>0\). This module does not assume the algorithm already has a transport convergence rate.

steps.title: State and projected second moments
steps.body:
The splitting law is the pushforward of its \(L^2\) iterate. Change of variables gives \(z\mapsto z\in L^2(\rho_n)\). Bounded parameter projection and subtraction of a constant give \(\theta(z)-a\in L^2(\rho_n)\) for every \(a\).

Indeed the \(L^2\) state is sent into \(L^2\) by the linear projection. A deterministic center is an \(L^2\) constant under a probability measure, so their difference has finite second moment. These moment conclusions hold for every positive proximal scale before the more restrictive convergence-step condition is imposed.

The law equals the pushforward of lpPipglaChain, so the identity observable under that law has a finite second moment. The continuous parameter projection preserves \(L^2\), and subtracting a constant center also preserves it because the law is a probability. These two declarations establish finiteness before the later comparison writes a real square-root integral.

Formal correspondence: pipglaLaws_state_memLp : Every actual output law has a finite state second moment, without Gaussianity or a convergence assumption. pipglaLaws_parameter_memLp : The actual parameter error has finite second moment about every center.

steps.title: Transport, equilibrium concentration, and center displacement
steps.body:
The smoothed target has sharp equilibrium radius \(\sqrt{d_\theta/(Nm)}\), and the uniform gap gives \(\|\theta_U-\theta_\eta\|\le\sqrt{\eta K^2/m}\). Projection of a coupling and Minkowski’s inequality therefore yield

\[\operatorname{RMS}_{\rho_n}(\theta_U)\le\sqrt{\eta K^2/m}+\sqrt{d_\theta/(Nm)}+W_2(\rho_n,\Pi_{N,\eta}).\]

For algorithm law \(\rho_n\) and reference \(\Pi_{N,\eta}\), finite second moments ensure finite transport. The intermediate estimate is

\[R_{\theta_\eta}(\rho_n)\le W_2(\rho_n,\Pi_{N,\eta})+\sqrt{d_\theta/(Nm)}.\]

Changing the center by its deterministic displacement gives

\[R_{\theta_U}(\rho_n)\le W_2(\rho_n,\Pi_{N,\eta})+\sqrt{d_\theta/(Nm)}+\sqrt{\eta K^2/m}.\]

For each coupling the projection does not increase its quadratic cost, and the reference parameter error is bounded by \(\sqrt{d_\theta/(Nm)}\). Taking the coupling infimum gives the transport contribution. The center change is at most \(\sqrt{\eta K^2/m}\) by the finite smoothing gap. These operations use the same smoothed target, and the subsequent splitting transport theorem supplies the remaining numerical bound.

Formal correspondence: pipgla_parameter_rms_original_le_transport : A rigorous original-center comparison for the actual PIPGLA law. The remaining transport term is its genuine Wasserstein distance to the smoothed Gibbs target; this statement alone is not a convergence rate.

ProximalLangevin/ProxParameter.lean.title: Sensitivity to the proximal parameter
ProximalLangevin/ProxParameter.lean.summary: For a convex bounded-below \(K\)-Lipschitz function, the proximal map satisfies \(\|P_\lambda(x)-P_\eta(x)\|\le K|\lambda-\eta|\) at positive scales. The bound follows by representing one proximal point as a proximal point at the other scale with a shifted input. Jensen transfers this bound to the averaged particle map without an extra particle factor. Combined with common-innovation contraction, it gives finite-time and uniform-iteration comparisons of splitting chains at two scales.

steps.title: Value Lipschitzness from bounded supporting subgradients
steps.body:
Suppose a subgradient \(s_x\) is chosen at every point with \(\|s_x\|\le K\). Its support evaluated at \(y\) and Cauchy–Schwarz give \(f(x)-f(y)\le\langle s_x,x-y\rangle\le K\|x-y\|\). Exchange \(x,y\) to bound the absolute difference.

Thus a subgradient section bounded by \(K\) gives value Lipschitz constant \(K\). Every selected vector must satisfy the supporting inequality; the norm bound alone is insufficient. No derivative of the potential is required.

Formal correspondence: lipschitz_of_bounded_subgradients : A bounded genuine subgradient at every input implies global Lipschitzness. In particular, the paper's uniformly bounded minimal section supplies this hypothesis, without adding a separate Lipschitz assumption to Assumption C1.

steps.title: Comparison of proximal minimizers at two positive scales
steps.body:
Write \(q=P_\eta(x)\) and \(s=(x-q)/\eta\). The residual characterization gives \(s\in\partial f(q)\) and \(\|s\|\le K\). The same support makes \(q\) the \(\lambda\)-proximal point of \(q+\lambda s\). Nonexpansiveness at scale \(\lambda\) yields

\[\|P_\lambda(x)-q\|\le\|x-(q+\lambda s)\|=|\eta-\lambda|\|s\|\le K|\lambda-\eta|.\]

In residual notation \(s=(x-P_\eta x)/\eta\), the second minimizer is also the \(\lambda\)-proximal point at \(P_\eta x+\lambda s\). Its comparison input is \(x=P_\eta x+\eta s\), so their separation is the scale difference times \(\|s\|\). The uniform residual bound gives \(K|\lambda-\eta|\) for every pair of positive scales.

Let \(q=P_\eta(x)\) and \(s=(x-q)/\eta\). The optimality theorem gives \(s\in\partial f(q)\), and global value Lipschitzness gives \(\|s\|\le K\). Reversing the optimality characterization shows that the same \(q\) is \(P_\lambda(q+\lambda s)\). Nonexpansiveness at parameter \(\lambda\) therefore gives \[\|P_\lambda(x)-P_\eta(x)\|\le\|x-(q+\lambda s)\|=|\eta-\lambda|\|s\|\le K|\lambda-\eta|.\] The local identities hq, hxs and hid implement exactly these substitutions; both parameters must be positive to cancel their residual denominators.

Formal correspondence: prox_parameter_sensitivity : The actual proximal point changes by at most \(K|\lambda-\eta|\) when the positive smoothing parameter changes.

steps.title: Uniform comparison of the averaged pair maps
steps.body:
Linearity in the supplied pair map gives \(\operatorname{Pair}_{P-Q}=\operatorname{Pair}_P-\operatorname{Pair}_Q\). If \(\sup_x\|P(x)-Q(x)\|\le c\), the averaged-square inequality bounds every summand by \(c^2\) and hence the state norm by \(c\). Proximal scale sensitivity therefore transfers with bound \(K|\lambda-\eta|\).

Explicitly \(\operatorname{Pair}(P-Q)=\operatorname{Pair}(P)-\operatorname{Pair}(Q)\). Under \(\|P(x)-Q(x)\|\le c\), Jensen and latent scaling give squared state difference at most \(N^{-1}\sum_i c^2=c^2\). Taking nonnegative square roots gives \(c\); substitute \(c=K|\lambda-\eta|\). Every pair difference is bounded by \(c\), and the state square is bounded by \(N^{-1}\sum_i c^2=c^2\), so the same constant \(c\) applies despite the common-parameter average.

Formal correspondence: pairwiseMap_sub : Pairwise averaging is linear in the supplied joint map. pairwiseMap_uniform_difference_le : A uniform difference of joint maps stays uniformly bounded after the common-parameter averaging and latent-coordinate scaling. pairwise_prox_parameter_sensitivity : The proximal-parameter sensitivity has no particle-number loss.

steps.title: The finite-time and uniform scale-perturbation estimates
steps.body:
Insert an update at the first scale and the second current state. Common-innovation contraction controls the change of state, and proximal sensitivity controls the change of scale. Thus

\[e_{n+1}\le(1-m\gamma)e_n+K|\lambda-\eta|.\]

Induction gives \(e_n\le(1-m\gamma)^ne_0+K|\lambda-\eta|\sum_{j0\), the step restriction gives \(0\le1-m\gamma<1\), so the geometric sum is at most \(1/(m\gamma)\).

With intermediate input \(w\) and scale \(\lambda\) the same triangle inequality gives

\[e_{k+1}\le(1-m\gamma)e_k+K|\lambda-\eta|.\]

Under \(\gamma>0\), factor \(1-m\gamma<1\) gives floor \(K|\lambda-\eta|/(m\gamma)\). More precisely the two update changes are bounded by \(q e_k\) and \(K|\lambda-\eta|\). Summing under \(q=1-m\gamma<1\) yields \(K|\lambda-\eta|/(m\gamma)\). A common initialization removes the transient term. Since the innovations only need to agree, no distribution or independence assumption enters this pathwise estimate.

Formal correspondence: pipglaUpdate_parameter_comparison : One step of two actual splitting schemes with different proximal parameters, the same time step, and the same supplied innovation. pipglaChain_parameter_comparison_sum : Exact finite-horizon comparison of two actual splitting recursions. pipglaChain_parameter_comparison_bound : The resulting pathwise difference floor is valid for any two positive proximal parameters; it is not assumed to be an algorithm error bound.

steps.title: A scale comparison within the specified interval
steps.body:
Suppose \(0

The width of the allowed scale interval is \(\gamma/(1-m\gamma)-\gamma=m\gamma^2/(1-m\gamma)\). Its lower endpoint \(\gamma\) makes the absolute difference from the reference scale equal to the nonnegative difference. Division by \(m\gamma>0\) gives the bound. The strict condition \(m\gamma<1\) is required because the denominator vanishes at equality.

In the corridor \(\gamma\le\lambda\le\gamma/(1-m\gamma)\), positivity of \(1-m\gamma\) gives \[0\le\lambda-\gamma\le\frac{m\gamma^2}{1-m\gamma}.\] Therefore \(K|\lambda-\gamma|/(m\gamma)\le K\gamma/(1-m\gamma)\). The Lean proof first removes the absolute value using the lower corridor inequality, then clears the two positive denominators. This term measures the additional error incurred by changing the proximal parameter away from the equal-step algorithm.

Formal correspondence: prox_parameter_corridor_floor : In the paper's proximal-parameter corridor, the additional comparison floor against \(\eta=\gamma\) is of order \(\gamma\), with every denominator displayed.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingTheorem.lean.title: PIPGLA about the original center for every positive proximal scale
ProximalLangevin/SplittingTheorem.lean.summary: Assume the stated strong convexity and smoothness of \(g_1\), and convexity, a lower bound, and \(K\)-Lipschitz values for \(g_2\). Let \(N>0\), \(00\), and \(\gamma\le2/(m+L_1)\). Initialization belongs to \(L^2\) and all Gaussian innovation coordinates are mutually independent and independent of initialization. Compare the chain at its chosen proximal scale with the equal-step chain. Its transport bound, parameter concentration, and finite center displacement then give the error estimate relative to the original marginal maximizer with the scale-mismatch contribution retained.

steps.title: The root mean square comparison of two scales
steps.body:
Use the same initial variable and innovations for the \(\lambda\) and \(\eta\) chains. Their uniform state separation is at most \(K|\lambda-\eta|/(m\gamma)\). Parameter projection is nonexpansive, and both chains have finite second moments. Minkowski therefore gives

\[\operatorname{RMS}_\lambda(a)\le\operatorname{RMS}_\eta(a)+\frac{K|\lambda-\eta|}{m\gamma}.\]

This is an inequality for their \(L^2\) realizations. More explicitly, let \(X\) and \(Y\) be the \(L^2\) iterates at scales \(\lambda\) and \(\eta\). The pathwise bound is

\[\|X(\omega)-Y(\omega)\|\le c:=\frac{K|\lambda-\eta|}{m\gamma}\quad\text{almost surely}.\]

Its \(L^2\) norm is at most the same constant because the source has mass one. Projection followed by Minkowski adds the reference-center error. Pushforward integration identifies the two ordinary law integrals, both finite by the moment result.

The transient term vanishes because both initial states agree. The full-measure representative equalities for the two chains and their subtraction justify this substitution in hpoint. Since \(Q\) has total mass one, integrating the uniform bound gives \(\|X-Y\|_{L^2}\le c\); this is hXY.

Define \(A=P_\theta X-\theta\) and \(B=P_\theta Y-\theta\) as \(L^2\) variables. Linearity gives \(A-B=P_\theta(X-Y)\), and the projection norm bound gives \(\|A-B\|_2\le\|X-Y\|_2\). Thus \(\|A\|_2\le\|B\|_2+c\), the inequality hn. Finally, hnorm first identifies each actual law as the pushforward of its \(L^2\) iterate, then changes variables in the quadratic integral and uses \(\sqrt{\|A\|_2^2}=\|A\|_2\). All these norms are finite by construction. Substituting those two identities into hn proves the stated RMS comparison.

Formal correspondence: pipgla_parameter_rms_prox_comparison : Actual PIPGLA parameter RMS values at two positive proximal parameters are separated by the proved pathwise parameter-sensitivity floor.

steps.title: The PIPGLA estimate about the original marginal maximizer
steps.body:
Choose comparison scale \(\eta=\gamma\). The equal-step transport estimate and parameter projection relative to the original marginal maximizer give

\[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{RMS}_\lambda(\theta_U)\le{}&\frac{K|\lambda-\gamma|}{m\gamma}+\sqrt{\frac{\gamma K^2}{m}}+\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}\\&+\sqrt{(1-m\gamma)^nW_2(\rho_0,\Pi_{N,\gamma})^2+\frac\gamma N C_N}.\end{aligned}\]

The explicit finite coefficient \(C_N\) is independent of the forward step. Every positive \(\lambda\) is allowed, with its displayed mismatch term. Convergence as \(\gamma\to0\) additionally requires control of that term. The coefficient is the proved one and does not reproduce the source’s printed heat-flow constants.

At reference scale \(\gamma\), the transport estimate gives the square root of the transient squared distance plus its floor. Sharp equilibrium concentration and the finite smoothing displacement add the other terms. For chosen scale \(\lambda\), common-innovation sensitivity gives \(K|\lambda-\gamma|/(m\gamma)\). Its constant bound has the same root mean square value under a probability source, giving the addition \(K|\lambda-\gamma|/(m\gamma)\). Thus allowance of all positive \(\lambda\) is distinct from a bound uniform as the forward step tends to zero. The preceding scale-interval estimate gives a simpler mismatch bound when that interval condition holds.

Formal correspondence: pipgla_parameter_rms_original : A genuine finite-time original-center theorem for PIPGLA, for any positive proximal parameter. In the paper's corridor the additional sensitivity term is \(O(\gamma)\); the derived transport and center-bias terms are \(O(\sqrt\gamma)\). All stationarity, moment, Brownian, and law-recurrence obligations are proved in the imported endpoints rather than assumed here.

ProximalLangevin/Recurrence.lean.title: Scalar affine recurrences for the proposed splitting coefficients
ProximalLangevin/Recurrence.lean.summary:
Assume a scalar affine inequality with the coefficients specified below. Nonnegative multiplication and induction give its finite geometric sum. A strict ratio below one gives a uniform error bound; ratio one gives only the finite-horizon linear bound. These are conditional scalar conclusions. A stochastic one-step estimate must be proved separately before this recurrence can describe an algorithmic error.

This file proves scalar consequences of an explicitly supplied recurrence. It does not supply the stochastic one-step law estimate for the paper’s coefficient. The independently proved PIPGLA law theorem uses the constructed coupling route.

steps.title: The proposed coefficients and their sign conditions
steps.body:
Define

\[q=\frac{\lambda(1-\mu\gamma)}\gamma,\qquad c=\lambda\left(\frac{2\gamma LD}{N}+\lambda C\right).\]

The stated sign assumptions give \(q,c\ge0\). Under \(\gamma>0\) and \(\mu\gamma<1\), multiplication through positive denominators gives \(q<1\iff\lambda<\gamma/(1-\mu\gamma)\). The strict inequality is needed for the geometric denominator. The subgradient contribution is \(\lambda^2C\) and has no further division by \(N\).

Equivalently let \(q=\lambda(1-\mu\gamma)/\gamma\) and \(c=2\lambda\gamma LD/N+\lambda^2C\). Positivity of \(\gamma\) and \(1-\mu\gamma\) makes \(q<1\) equivalent to \(\lambda<\gamma/(1-\mu\gamma)\). Division by \(1-q\) is consequently permitted only under that strict condition; the signs of \(q,c\) follow separately. In particular \(q<1\) fails at the limiting scale, where \(q=1\). Only the Gaussian part of the forcing contains \(1/N\), so its particle scaling differs from the subgradient part.

Formal correspondence: splittingRatio : The contraction coefficient used in the paper's splitting argument. splittingForcing : Correct scaling for noise variance \(2\gamma/N\) and the unscaled squared-norm bound \(C\) on the convex potential's selected subgradient in v3. splittingRatio_lt_one_iff : The upper endpoint has to be strict for a geometric error floor.

steps.title: The finite geometric bound for an assumed recurrence
steps.body:
Assume \(e_{n+1}\le q e_n+c\) and \(q\ge0\). Repeated substitution gives \(e_n\le q^ne_0+c\sum_{j

The induction is over \(n\). Multiply the preceding bound by nonnegative \(q\) and add \(c\). When \(q<1\) the geometric denominator is positive; when \(c\ge0\) its negative tail may be discarded. Each statement keeps the original recurrence as an explicit hypothesis.

Assume explicitly the scalar recurrence \(e_{n+1}\le qe_n+c\). Induction expands it to \(e_n\le q^ne_0+c\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}q^j\); each induction step multiplies by \(q\ge0\). When \(q<1\), the geometric sum is \((1-q^n)/(1-q)\), and \(c\ge0\) allows the simpler floor \(c/(1-q)\). These three declarations instantiate the shared affine-recurrence lemmas with the displayed corrected coefficients. They are scalar consequences of a supplied recurrence, independently of the later stochastic theorem.

Formal correspondence: splitting_recurrence_sum : The finite sum is meaningful at the endpoint \(q=1\), too. splitting_recurrence_exact : Exact finite-horizon bound in the strict contraction regime. splitting_recurrence_bound : Corrected error floor. The forcing's gradient contribution is \(\lambda^2C\), whereas its Gaussian contribution is \(2\lambda\gamma LD/N\).

steps.title: The unit ratio and the equal-scale formula
steps.body:
When \(q=1\), induction gives \(e_n\le e_0+nc\). Under \(\lambda=\gamma\) and the nonzero-denominator assumptions, algebra instead gives

\[\frac c{1-q}=\frac\gamma\mu\left(\frac{2LD}{N}+C\right).\]

The \(C\) contribution is unscaled by particle count. At unit ratio the finite sum is \(n\), giving \(e_n\le e_0+nc\) rather than a bounded geometric error. Under equal positive scales and strict contraction, cancellation in \(c/(1-q)\) produces the displayed identity. This scalar computation does not establish that a stochastic error satisfies the assumed recurrence.

At \(q=1\), retain the finite sum: the induction gives \(e_n\le e_0+nc\). For \(\lambda=\gamma\), cancellation in the strict regime gives \[\frac{c}{1-q}=\frac\gamma\mu\left(\frac{2LD}{N}+C\right).\] The \(C\) term is not divided by \(N\): its numerator was \(\lambda^2 C\), whereas the Gaussian contribution was \(2\lambda\gamma LD/N\). The nonzero assumptions in splitting_bias_equal_steps justify exactly these algebraic cancellations.

Formal correspondence: splitting_recurrence_endpoint : At the noncontracting endpoint, retain the linear finite-horizon bound. splitting_bias_equal_steps : When \(\lambda=\gamma\), the corrected error floor takes this particularly simple form, with no \(1/N\) multiplying \(C\).

ProximalLangevin/Corrections.lean.title: Exact algebraic corrections and an averaged-proximity counterexample
ProximalLangevin/Corrections.lean.summary:
The examples below establish specific algebraic facts used to qualify the source arguments: the sign of a quadratic proximal expansion, scaling of a squared norm, the inverse-step factor in residual monotonicity, and failure of shared-state proximal optimality for averaged pairwise outputs. The convergence results use the finite potential-gap and summed energy inequalities proved above. Each example has only the scope stated for its own assumptions.

This module contains explicit mathematical certificates. Each claim is limited to its stated algebraic example or implication; these certificates do not claim that every stronger result in the reference paper is false.

steps.title: The second-order sign in the quadratic proximal expansion
steps.body:
The proximal equation \(p+\lambda\nabla g_2(p)=x\) gives a positive second-order coefficient in the scalar quadratic example:

\[ \operatorname{prox}_{u^2/2}^\lambda(x) =\frac{x}{1+\lambda} =x-\lambda x+\lambda^2x-\frac{\lambda^3x}{1+\lambda}. \]

The negative coefficient printed in the source leaves error at least \(\lambda^2\) at \(x=1\) and therefore cannot be its third-order expansion. The quadratic is not globally value Lipschitz, so this calculation diagnoses the displayed algebra rather than refuting a full theorem under that assumption.

Almost-everywhere twice differentiability and the stated moment condition also do not provide the uniform integrable third-order remainder needed for the claimed order \(O(\lambda)\) for displacement of the original marginal maximizer. The proved finite-gap result gives \(\sqrt{\lambda K^2/m}\); this difference in established scope does not prove the stronger assertion false. For \(f(u)=u^2/2\) the minimizer equation is \((1+\lambda)p=x\). Division gives the exact resolvent and its positive \(\lambda^2x\) term with the displayed third-order remainder.

Formal correspondence: quadratic_prox_minimizes : The proximal point of \(u\mapsto u^2/2\) is \(x/(1+\lambda)\). The difference of objectives is a nonnegative square; no differentiability of an argmin map is assumed. quadratic_prox_expansion : The second-order coefficient in the proximal expansion has a positive sign. This exact identity diagnoses the opposite sign in v1 equation (25) and v3 equation (22). negative_second_order_residual : The negative second-order term printed in v1 equation (25) / v3 equation (22) leaves an error of order \(\lambda^2\), already for the scalar quadratic.

steps.title: Squared scaling and the unit recurrence ratio
steps.body:
Multiplication of a vector by \(N\) multiplies its squared norm by \(N^2\), by norm homogeneity and squaring. Separately, an affine recurrence with unit ratio has finite sum \(n\) and therefore a linear-in-iteration additive bound, rather than a bounded geometric sum. These identities determine the particle powers and the strict positive-denominator condition needed in an energy or transport estimate.

Norm homogeneity gives \(\|Ng\|^2=N^2\|g\|^2\). The numerical case \(N=2,\|g\|=1\) disproves linear squared-gradient scaling. Substituting \(\lambda=\gamma/(1-\mu\gamma)\) gives \(1-q=0\). Lean’s total real division has \(1/0=0\); the numerical certificate \(1\not\le0+1/(1-1)\) shows why an unguarded formula at that endpoint cannot express an error floor.

Formal correspondence: squared_gradient_scaling : Scaling a gradient by \(N\) scales its squared norm by \(N^2\), not \(N\). This corrects v1 Corollary A.5; v3 Corollary A.12 already uses this scaling. linear_squared_gradient_scaling_fails : A numerical witness to the invalid \(NC\) bound from the valid \(C\) bound when the gradient is multiplied by \(N\). endpoint_denominator_zero : The geometric-series denominator is zero at the upper endpoint allowed in v1 Corollaries A.4--A.6 and v3 Corollaries A.11--A.13. A finite error floor requires a strict inequality. endpoint_error_floor_fails : At \(q=1\), the recurrence \(e(n+1)=e(n)+1\) has linear growth. Interpreting real division by zero cannot rescue the printed error floor.

steps.title: The inverse-step factor in residual monotonicity
steps.body:
Assume \(\langle x-y,p(x)-p(y)\rangle\le(1-\mu)\|x-y\|^2\) and define the residual difference by \(R(x)-R(y)=\gamma^{-1}[(x-y)-(p(x)-p(y))]\). For \(\gamma>0\), expansion gives \(\langle x-y,R(x)-R(y)\rangle\ge(\mu/\gamma)\|x-y\|^2\). Hence the strong-monotonicity coefficient is \(\mu/\gamma\) rather than \(\mu\).

Explicitly the inner product expands as \(\langle x-y,R(x)-R(y)\rangle=\gamma^{-1}(\|x-y\|^2-\langle x-y,p(x)-p(y)\rangle)\). Substitution of the proximal deficit bounds it below by \((\mu/\gamma)\|x-y\|^2\). Division by \(\gamma\) in the residual definition is the source of this inverse-step factor.

Formal correspondence: proximal_displacement_strong_monotonicity : If the proximal displacement satisfies the paper's assumption B1, the envelope gradient inherits the constant \(\mu/\gamma\).

steps.title: A counterexample to shared-state proximal optimality
steps.body:
Take \(g(\theta,x)=|\theta-x|\) and proximal scale one. The pair inputs \((1,0)\) and \((1,4)\) have proximal minimizers \((1/2,1/2)\) and \((2,3)\). Averaging their parameter components gives \((5/4,1/2,3)\). The shared-state objective is

\[\tfrac12(|\theta-x_1|+|\theta-x_2|)+\tfrac12(\theta-1)^2+\tfrac14(x_1^2+(x_2-4)^2).\]

The competitor \((1,1,3)\) has strictly smaller objective, as follows from direct absolute-value evaluation. Each pair was allowed its own proposed parameter, whereas the shared objective permits only one. Averaging the proposals need not solve that common minimization problem.

In particular the averaged output has value \(51/32\) and the feasible comparator has value \(3/2=48/32\). This strict comparison disproves the shared-state proximal identity in general. The splitting proof instead sums the valid single-pair energy inequalities and applies Jensen’s inequality to the parameter average.

Formal correspondence: pairAbsObjective : The pair objective for the convex, globally Lipschitz penalty \(g_2(\theta,x)=|\theta-x|\) with smoothing parameter one. pairAbs_first_prox : At pair input \((1,0)\), the true proximal point is \((1/2,1/2)\). pairAbs_second_prox : At pair input \((1,4)\), the true proximal point is \((2,3)\). sharedAbsObjective : The two-particle lifted objective in physical particle coordinates. The quadratic penalty uses precisely the scaled state norm with \(N=2\). averaged_pair_prox_not_lifted_minimizer : Averaging the two true pairwise proximal outputs gives parameter \(5/4\) and particles \((1/2,3)\). A feasible competitor \((1,1,3)\) has strictly smaller lifted objective. Thus the pairwise average cannot be a lifted proximal minimizer, even for a convex globally Lipschitz penalty.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldDrift.lean.title: Wasserstein regularity of the integrated parameter force
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldDrift.lean.summary: For pair potential \(V\) with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, define the parameter force by \(b_V(\theta,\mu)=\int\nabla_\theta V(\theta,x)\mu(dx)\). Finite latent second moments and linear gradient growth make this a Bochner integral. Comparing the integrands on arbitrary couplings gives a bound in quadratic Wasserstein distance. Parameter projection is a contraction, so the joint-gradient regularity constant also controls this force.

steps.title: Expectation differences for a Lipschitz observable
steps.body:
For a Lipschitz observable \(\phi\), subtract \(\phi(0)\). Its centered growth is bounded by \(K\|x\|\), giving \(\phi(X)\in L^2\subset L^1\). For any finite-cost coupling \(c\) of \(\mu, u\), the norm-of-integral inequality and Cauchy–Schwarz give

\[\left\|\int\phi\,d\mu-\int\phi\,d u ight\|\le K\left(\int\|x-y\|^2dc ight)^{1/2}.\]

The infimum of coupling costs gives \(K W_2(\mu, u)\). The coupling integral identity is

\[\int\varphi\,d\mu-\int\varphi\,d u=\int[\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)]\,dc(x,y).\]

Integrability includes the observable’s value at zero. Its Lipschitz constant bounds the integrand difference by the pair distance, and \(\|\cdot\|_1\le\|\cdot\|_2\) bounds its first moment by its quadratic cost. The input second moments make the infimum finite; no optimal coupling is required.

The nonzero value \(\varphi(0)\) must be retained when proving integrability. Write \(\varphi(X)=[\varphi(X)-\varphi(0)]+\varphi(0)\). The first term is in \(L^2\) because its Lipschitz map vanishes at zero; the second is a constant in \(L^2\) on a probability space. This proves memLp_lipschitz_observable, including the offset.

For the transport estimate, take any coupling \(c\) of \(\mu, u\). Its marginal identities pull the given second moments onto its two coordinate random variables. Applying the observable lemma to both coordinates proves their \(L^2\) membership and hence their Bochner integrability. The fact hid then changes variables using those marginals and combines the two integrals:

The successive inequalities in hfamily are the integral triangle inequality, the probability-space comparison \(\|F\|_1\le\|F\|_2\), and the pointwise Lipschitz bound \(\|\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)\|\le K\|x-y\|\). They give the same upper bound \(K\,\operatorname{cost}(c)\) for every coupling. Taking the infimum in the extended nonnegative reals proves hbound. Finite input second moments already imply finite \(W_2\), so the product \(KW_2\) is finite and the final conversion to real numbers preserves the inequality.

Formal correspondence: memLp_lipschitz_observable : A Lipschitz observable with a nonzero offset still preserves finite second moments on a probability space. integral_lipschitz_wasserstein2 : Actual expectations of a Lipschitz observable are Lipschitz in \(W_2\). Both input probability laws have finite second moment; infinity is never removed by an unguarded real conversion.

steps.title: The parameter block of the joint gradient
steps.body:
The orthogonal projection \(P_\theta\) keeps the parameter coordinates and satisfies \(\|P_\theta z\|\le\|z\|\) because their squared norm is a subsum of the full squared norm. Define \(\phi_\theta(x)=P_\theta\nabla V(\theta,x)\) and integrate this observable against the latent law.

Projection preserves the joint-gradient Lipschitz and linear-growth bounds. Finite latent second moment implies finite first moment, so the resulting parameter force is a finite Bochner expectation. It is the integrated parameter block of the specified potential gradient, rather than an independently assumed vector field.

Formal correspondence: jointParameterCLM : The parameter block of a parameter/latent joint vector. parameterGradient : The parameter component of the actual joint gradient. meanFieldDrift : The actual averaged parameter drift, as a Bochner integral.

steps.title: The two-coordinate gradient perturbation bound
steps.body:
Decomposing the pair difference into parameter and latent inclusions gives \(\|(\theta,x)-(\theta',x')\|\le\|\theta-\theta'\|+\|x-x'\|\). The joint-gradient Lipschitz estimate followed by the parameter contraction gives

\[\|\phi_\theta(x)-\phi_{\theta'}(x')\|\le L(\|\theta-\theta'\|+\|x-x'\|).\]

For \(\theta=\theta'\) the latent observable is \(L\)-Lipschitz. Fixing the latent coordinate similarly gives the separate parameter bound. The sum on the right comes from the triangle inequality on the two orthogonal coordinate inclusions.

steps.title: Separate parameter and probability-law perturbations
steps.body:
For differentiable \(V\) define

\[ b_V( heta,\mu)=\int abla_ heta V( heta,x)\,\mu(dx). \]

Assume \( abla V\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(\mu, u\) have finite second moments. Linear growth gives integrability. Comparison on a finite-cost coupling, Cauchy–Schwarz, and the cost infimum then give

\[ \|b_V( heta,\mu)-b_V( heta', u)\| \le L igl(\| heta- heta'\|+W_2(\mu, u) igr). \]

For split envelope \(V=g_1+g_2^\eta\) the gradient constant is \(L_1+1/\eta\). The source’s \(1/\eta\) constant is the full-envelope constant and is not in general sufficient for this split potential. Moreover the present estimate is in quadratic Wasserstein distance, a weaker conclusion than the source’s first-Wasserstein assertion. It does not alone establish the later propositions cited there.

For arbitrary coupling \((X,Y)\), the \(L\)-Lipschitz joint gradient gives \(\| abla_ heta U( heta,x)- abla_ heta U(\vartheta,y)\|\le L(\| heta-\vartheta\|+\|x-y\|)\). Integration and Cauchy–Schwarz on \(\mathbb E\|X-Y\|\) yield

\[\|b( heta,\mu)-b(\vartheta, u)\|\le L\| heta-\vartheta\|+LW_2(\mu, u).\]

The Moreau substitution gives \(L_1+\eta^{-1}\). Alternatively insert intermediate force \(b_V( heta',\mu)\): its parameter change is at most \(L\| heta- heta'\|\) and its law change at most \(LW_2(\mu, u)\). Their sum proves the claim with constant \(L_1+1/\eta\) for split smoothing.

Formal correspondence: meanFieldDrift_lipschitz_wasserstein2 : Corrected \(W_2\) version of Lemma C.1 for an actual gradient-Lipschitz joint potential and actual finite-second-moment latent probability laws. moreau_meanFieldDrift_lipschitz_wasserstein2 : For split Moreau smoothing, the actual averaged drift has coefficient \(L_1+1/\eta\); the finite moments and all integral guards remain explicit.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldProcess.lean.title: Mean-field integral equations in the space of square-integrable states
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldProcess.lean.summary: On probability space \(Q\) let \(H=L^2(Q;\mathbb R^{d_\theta+d_x})\). A potential \(V\) with globally \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient induces a Lipschitz composition map on this Hilbert space. A bounded linear operator replaces only its parameter component by expectation. Picard’s theorem constructs the integral solution with a continuous additive input. Projection gives a deterministic parameter equation coupled to the law of the latent component when the initial parameter is deterministic and the input is latent-only.

steps.title: Expectation as a bounded linear map
steps.body:
Under a probability measure, \(\|X\|_{L^1}\le\|X\|_{L^2}\). The norm-of-integral inequality therefore gives \(\|\mathbb E_Q X\|\le\|X\|_2\). Bochner integration is linear on these integrable variables, defining continuous linear map \(\mathcal E:H\to E\) with operator norm at most one.

Continuity makes expectation commute with continuous time integrals. This fact will identify the deterministic parameter equation after projecting the joint Hilbert-space solution.

Formal correspondence: norm_lp_expectation_le : On a probability space, the actual expectation is bounded by the \(L^2\) norm. lpExpectationCLM : Actual Bochner expectation as a bounded linear map out of \(L^2\).

steps.title: Coordinate projections and parameter inclusion
steps.body:
Define latent projection \(P_x(\theta,x)=x\) and parameter inclusion \(I_\theta(\theta)=(\theta,0)\). Coordinate expansion gives \(\|(\theta,0)\|^2=\|\theta\|^2\), so \(I_\theta\) is an isometry. The latent projection is a contraction because its squared norm discards the nonnegative parameter coordinates.

Both maps are bounded and linear, and their pointwise actions preserve these properties on square-integrable random vectors. They consequently commute with the Bochner time integrals in the projected equations.

Formal correspondence: jointLatentCLM : The latent component of one parameter/latent joint vector. jointParameterInclusionCLM : Embed only a parameter block into the joint space.

steps.title: The latent projection on random joint states
steps.body:
Set \(M_x=I-I_\theta P_\theta\). The parameter block of this map is zero, while its latent block equals the original latent block. Squared-norm expansion gives \(\|M_xz\|^2\le\|z\|^2\). Thus the mask is a contraction on the joint space and on \(L^2\).

In particular \(M_x\) preserves square integrability and continuity of an \(L^2\)-valued input. Applied to the Brownian input it removes every parameter coordinate at all times.

Formal correspondence: jointLatentMaskCLM : The actual latent-coordinate projection on the joint space.

steps.title: The parameter-averaging operator
steps.body:
Define the bounded linear averaging operator by

\[\mathcal M X=\operatorname{const}(I_\theta P_\theta\mathbb E_QX)+M_xX.\]

The norm of each summand is at most \(\|X\|_2\), so \(\|\mathcal M X\|_2\le2\|X\|_2\). Linearity gives \(\operatorname{Lip}(\mathcal M)\le2\). This sufficient constant is not asserted optimal.

The operator sends a joint state \((\Theta,X)\) to \((\mathbb E\Theta,X)\), where the first component is represented as a constant random vector. Only the parameter component is averaged. The latent force remains a random function of its current latent state, as required for the mean-field system.

Formal correspondence: meanFieldAverageCLM : Average the parameter coordinates and retain the latent coordinates as actual random variables. This is a bounded linear map, not an assumed drift.

steps.title: The mean-field drift and finite-horizon integral solution
steps.body:
Set \(\mathcal A_V(X)=\mathcal M(\nabla V(X))\). Composition with the Lipschitz gradient preserves \(L^2\) and has constant \(L\). The averaging bound gives \(\operatorname{Lip}(\mathcal A_V)\le2L\). For a continuous \(H\)-valued input \(B\) satisfying \(B_0=0\) and any \(T\ge0\), Picard’s theorem gives continuous \(Y\) with \(Y_0=Y^{\rm in}\) and

\[Y_t-Y^{\rm in}=-\int_0^t\mathcal A_V(Y_s)ds+B_t,\qquad0\le t\le T.\]

The complete space is \(H\). Writing \(E=\mathbb R^{d_\theta+d_x}\), expectation is a bounded linear map \(L^2(Q;E)\to E\). Constant inclusion maps \(E\) back into \(H=L^2(Q;E)\). Composing these maps with the parameter projection averages the parameter component; the latent component is left unchanged. The coordinate maps are bounded. Linear growth makes gradient composition everywhere defined on \(L^2\), so the averaged drift has constant at most \(2L\). Subtracting the continuous additive input reduces the equation to a nonautonomous globally Lipschitz integral equation. This proves finite-horizon existence and the displayed identity from the stated input and potential assumptions.

Formal correspondence: lpMeanFieldDrift : The actual mean-field drift: expected parameter force and pointwise latent force. lpMeanFieldDrift_lipschitz : A conservative global Lipschitz constant for the constructed drift. exists_lp_meanField_integral : Picard constructs the continuous mean-field \(L^2\) integral solution from its actual gradient and a continuous \(L^2\) additive input on every finite horizon.

steps.title: The averaging operator in coordinates
steps.body:
On representatives the averaging operator has formula

\[(\mathcal M X)(\omega)=(\mathbb E_Q P_\theta X,\,P_xX(\omega)).\]

Its parameter projection is \(\operatorname{const}(P_\theta\mathbb E_QX)\), and its latent projection is \(P_xX\). The constant inclusion contributes only the first block and the latent mask only the second. These almost-sure identities give equalities in \(L^2\). Hence the averaging operator gives exactly the expected parameter component and leaves latent randomness unchanged.

Formal correspondence: meanFieldAverageCLM_coe : The averaging map has exactly its intended pointwise block action. meanFieldAverageCLM_parameter : Averaging makes the parameter block a constant random variable. meanFieldAverageCLM_latent : Averaging leaves the actual latent random variable unchanged.

steps.title: The integrated parameter-gradient formula
steps.body:
Define the continuous map \(a_V(X)=P_ heta\mathbb E_Q abla V(X)\) on \(H\). The averaged drift has blocks \(\operatorname{const}(a_V(X))\) and \(P_x abla V(X)\). If \(P_ heta X=\operatorname{const}( heta)\), the state satisfies \(X=( heta,P_xX)\) almost surely. Commuting parameter projection through expectation and applying the pushforward integral formula gives

\[a_V(X)=\int abla_ heta V( heta,x)\,\mathcal L_Q(P_xX)(dx).\]

Indeed a deterministic parameter block identifies the state as \(( heta,P_xX)\). Evaluating and projecting the joint gradient then gives the marginal integral defining \(b_V\). The latent law is the pushforward of the constructed state, rather than an independently specified measure curve.

Formal correspondence: lpMeanFieldParameterForce : The actual expected parameter force of a square-integrable joint vector. lpMeanFieldDrift_parameter : The parameter projection of the actual drift is its expected force. lpMeanFieldDrift_latent : The latent projection of the actual drift is pointwise latent gradient. lpMeanFieldParameterForce_eq_meanFieldDrift : The expected force equals the actual mean-field drift integral whenever the input parameter is deterministic. The latent marginal is its actual law.

steps.title: The deterministic parameter and latent integral equations
steps.body:
Assume initial parameter \(\theta_0\) is constant and \(P_\theta B_t=0\). Projection commutes with the time integral, giving \(P_\theta Y_t=\operatorname{const}(\theta_t)\) where \(\theta_t=\theta_0-\int_0^t a_V(Y_s)ds\). Continuity of the primitive proves continuity of \(\theta\). Define \(\mu_t=\mathcal L_Q(P_xY_t)\) and substitute the force identity:

\[\theta_t-\theta_0=-\int_0^t b_V(\theta_s,\mu_s)ds,\qquad P_xY_t-P_xY_0=-\int_0^tP_x\nabla V(Y_s)ds+P_xB_t.\]

The latent equality is in \(L^2\). The parameter input is zero and the parameter drift is constant as a random vector, so its time integral is constant as well. Thus the deterministic path \(\theta_t\) is derived from the joint solution. In terms of its latent law \(\mu_t\), the equation is

\[\theta_t-\theta_0=-\int_0^t\left[\int\nabla_\theta V(\theta_s,x)\,d\mu_s(x)\right]ds.\]

Latent projection gives the drift-plus-noise equation in the display. Both equations use the same constructed process and its latent distribution.

Formal correspondence: lp_meanField_parameter_equation : Projection of the constructed equation preserves a deterministic parameter and gives its genuine integral equation. lp_meanField_latent_equation : The latent component satisfies the actual projected gradient equation. exists_lp_meanField_equations : The constructed solution has a continuous deterministic parameter, its actual latent marginal, and both mean-field integral equations. No solution trajectory or law evolution is assumed in this existence statement.

steps.title: The continuous latent-only Brownian input
steps.body:
Apply the latent mask to the coordinate Brownian \(L^2\) input. Gaussian second moments show continuity in \(L^2\) and a zero initial value. Its parameter projection vanishes identically.

Indeed the \(L^2\) norm of a Brownian increment is proportional to the square root of its time length, proving \(L^2\) continuity. A bounded linear mask preserves continuity and the zero initial value. These facts establish the continuous additive-input hypotheses of the integral equation by construction.

Formal correspondence: meanFieldBrownianNoise : Actual Brownian-coordinate inputs, with only their latent coordinates retained, give a concrete continuous \(L^2\) input. Noise continuity and its zero initial value are conclusions of the Brownian laws.

steps.title: Brownian input and split-envelope specialization
steps.body:
The latent Brownian input satisfies the preceding input conditions, so the finite-horizon theorem gives the Brownian-driven \(L^2\) solution. For \(V=g_1+g_2^\eta\), proximal calculus supplies gradient constant \(L_1+\eta^{-1}\). This proves continuous \(L^2\) integral equations with the deterministic parameter equation.

Specifically the potential \(g_1+g_2^\eta\) has constant \(L_1+1/\eta\), and substitution yields an \(L^2\)-valued continuous solution. These statements concern mean-square integral equations. They do not assert a pathwise strong stochastic differential equation or a Fokker–Planck theorem, which require further arguments.

Formal correspondence: exists_lp_meanField_integral_of_brownian : Genuine finite-horizon mean-field \(L^2\) existence with a Brownian input. All stochastic input continuity is derived from the coordinate Brownian laws; no pathwise strong-SDE, independence or adaptedness assertion is made. exists_lp_moreau_meanField_integral : Split Moreau smoothing supplies the actual globally Lipschitz gradient needed by the mean-field construction. Its coefficient is \(L_1+1/\eta\).

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldSmoothing.lean.title: Finite smoothing comparison for mean-field integral equations
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldSmoothing.lean.summary:
Assume additionally that the convex penalty is differentiable with Lipschitz gradient. Its proximal residual then equals the original gradient evaluated at the proximal point. The finite proximal displacement bounds the difference between original and envelope gradients by a constant times the smoothing scale. Construct both mean-field integral solutions with identical initial state and additive input. The input cancels on subtraction, and Grönwall bounds the supremum over time of their mean-square norms.

For this module the convex bounded-below \(g_2\) is additionally differentiable, with \(L_2\)-Lipschitz gradient and global value Lipschitz constant \(K\). The finite-horizon comparison uses the same initialization and additive input for the original and split-smoothed systems.

steps.title: Equality of the subgradient and gradient at a differentiability point
steps.body:
If \(s\) is a supporting subgradient, then \(x\mapsto f(x)-\langle s,x angle\) has a global minimum at \(p\). Differentiability makes its derivative zero, giving \(s= abla f(p)\). Applied to the proximal residual and envelope-gradient formula, this gives \( abla f^\eta(x)= abla f(P_\eta(x))\).

Equivalently, a support \(s\) at \(p\) minimizes \(f(x)-\langle s,x angle\) at \(p\), so \(s= abla f(p)\). The conclusion is an equality at the minimizing point, not an asymptotic approximation.

Formal correspondence: IsSubgradient.eq_gradient : A supporting subgradient of a differentiable function is its actual gradient. gradient_moreau_eq_gradient_prox : The actual Moreau score is the original smooth score at the true proximal point.

steps.title: The finite gradient difference under smoothing
steps.body:
The gradient \( abla f\) is \(L_2\)-Lipschitz, and \(P_\eta\) is nonexpansive. Their composition therefore has constant \(L_2\) independently of \(\eta\). The displacement bound \(\|x-P_\eta(x)\|\le\eta K\) then gives

\[\| abla f(x)- abla f^\eta(x)\|\le L_2\|x-P_\eta(x)\|\le\eta L_2K.\]

Optimality and differentiability identify \( abla f^\eta(x)= abla f(P_\eta x)\). When \( abla f\) is \(L_2\)-Lipschitz and \(f\) is \(K\)-Lipschitz, the same argument gives

\[\| abla f^\eta(x)- abla f(x)\|\le L_2\|P_\eta x-x\|\le\eta L_2K.\]

The envelope gradient is \( abla f\circ P_\eta\). Its gradient constant is bounded by \(L_2\), which can be smaller than the generic \(1/\eta\) bound. Comparison with \( abla f(x)\) costs at most \(L_2\|P_\eta x-x\|\le\eta L_2K\). This finite uniform defect supplies the forcing in the integral-equation comparison.

Formal correspondence: smooth_moreau_gradient_lipschitz : Smoothness of the original score is preserved by the actual Moreau envelope. gradient_moreau_defect_le : The uniform score defect is derived from proximal optimality and displacement. Its coefficient is independent of the smoothing parameter.

steps.title: Component regularity from the sum and the smooth term
steps.body:
If \(U=f+g\) and \(f\) are differentiable, then \(g=U-f\) is differentiable. Gradient linearity gives \( abla g= abla U- abla f\). Taking differences at two points and the triangle inequality yields \(\operatorname{Lip}( abla g)\le L_U+L_f\).

Thus the constant \(L_2\) may be supplied from regularity of the original sum and the known smooth component. This gives a justified \(L_2\) without adding an unstated differentiability assumption on the remaining component.

Formal correspondence: component_differentiable_of_sum : Original-model differentiability and smoothness derive the missing component regularity, rather than requiring a separate inverse-scale estimate. component_gradient_lipschitz_of_sum : If the full original score and first component are Lipschitz, the second component's score has their summed Lipschitz constant.

steps.title: Comparison with common additive input
steps.body:
Let integral solutions with drifts \(g,k\) share additive input \(B\) and have initial states \(x,y\). Assume one drift is globally Lipschitz and \(\sup_z\|g(z)-k(z)\|\le\varepsilon\). Subtraction cancels the input. Adding and subtracting one drift at the other state bounds the integrand by \(L\|Y-Z\|+\varepsilon\). Integral Grönwall gives

\[\|Y_t-Z_t\|\le e^{Lt}\|x-y\|+\varepsilon\Psi(L,t),\qquad\Psi(L,t)=\begin{cases}(e^{Lt}-1)/L,&L\ne0,\\t,&L=0.\end{cases}\]

No differentiation of \(B\) is needed. The bounded defect is integrated with factor \(\Psi\). The definition of \(\Psi\) includes zero Lipschitz constant, so the formula requires no division by zero.

Formal correspondence: integral_drift_perturbation : Two actual integral equations driven by common additive input differ by the Grönwall response to a uniform drift defect. No derivative of the input is used, and no error recurrence is assumed.

steps.title: The finite smoothing estimate for the two integral systems
steps.body:
Assume \(g_2\) is differentiable with \(L_2\)-Lipschitz gradient, and retain convexity, a lower bound, and value Lipschitz constant \(K\). The supporting residual equals the gradient at the proximal minimizer:

\[ \nabla g_2^\eta(v)=\nabla g_2(P_\eta(v)). \]

Nonexpansiveness of \(P_\eta\) preserves constant \(L_2\), and \(\|v-P_\eta(v)\|\le\eta K\) gives

\[ \|\nabla g_2(v)-\nabla g_2^\eta(v)\|\le\eta L_2K. \]

If instead regularity is stated for \(U=g_1+g_2\) with constant \(L_U\) and for \(g_1\) with constant \(L_1\), the difference argument supplies \(L_2=L_U+L_1\).

Construct both Hilbert-space solutions with common initial state and continuous additive input. The averaged drifts differ uniformly by at most \(2\eta L_2K\). Their pair-gradient constant is at most \(L_1+L_2\), independent of \(\eta\). The averaging operator gives the corresponding factor two. Grönwall yields

\[ \sup_{0\le t\le T}\|Y_t-Z_t\|_{L^2} \le 2\eta L_2K\,\Psi(2(L_1+L_2),T), \qquad \Psi(a,T)=\begin{cases}(e^{aT}-1)/a,&a>0,\\T,&a=0.\end{cases} \]

For deterministic initial parameter and latent-only Brownian input these are the mean-field systems described above. The finite bound is linear in \(\eta\). More explicitly the averaged drift constant is \(2(L_1+L_2)\) and its uniform difference is \(2\eta L_2K\). The supremum is outside the \(L^2\) norm. Proposition C.3 instead bounds the expectation of the supremum of squared errors. The square root of that quantity bounds the supremum of the \(L^2\) error norms. A bound on the expectation of the supremum of squared errors is not established here.

Both systems are constructed with the same continuous additive input. Subtracting their equations cancels that input and leaves a differentiable integral error. One drift contributes its global Lipschitz constant times the current difference; the other contributes the uniform Moreau score defect just proved. Grönwall then bounds the actual process difference by a coefficient times \(\eta\) on the finite horizon. The component-regularity declarations justify the smoothness constants of each summand from the stated assumptions on the regular sum before this perturbation argument is applied.

Formal correspondence: meanFieldSmoothingConstant : Explicit finite-horizon coefficient for the mean-field \(L^2\) smoothing error. The Grönwall response is \(T\) at zero smoothness and otherwise \(\frac{\exp(2(L_1+L_2)T)-1}{2(L_1+L_2)}\). exists_meanField_smoothing_comparison : Constructed original and smoothed mean-field processes share their actual initial variable and continuous additive input. Their \(L^2\) distance, uniformly over the finite horizon, is bounded by \(\eta\) times an explicit \(\eta\)-independent constant. This is \(\sup_t\|\operatorname{error}_t\|_{L^2}\), not a pathwise supremum inside an expectation.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldVariance.lean.title: Exact iid variance and the empirical parameter force
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldVariance.lean.summary: For \(N>0\), independent centered square-integrable Hilbert-valued vectors have zero mixed expected inner products. Expanding the finite squared sum and integrating termwise therefore gives an exact \(1/N\) variance factor for their sample mean. The finite product measure supplies the required independence. Applying the identity to the parameter-gradient observable gives the empirical mean-field force fluctuation.

steps.title: The centered off-diagonal expectations
steps.body:
View the supplied \(L^2\) functions as \(L^2\) vectors. Cauchy–Schwarz makes each pairwise inner product integrable, so finite expansion gives

\[\mathbb E\left\|\sum_iX_i ight\|^2=\sum_{i,j}\mathbb E\langle X_i,X_j angle.\]

For \(i e j\), independence and zero means give \(\langle\mathbb E X_i,\mathbb E X_j angle=0\). The diagonal terms are \(\mathbb E\|X_i\|^2\). For distinct indices \(i e j\), centering alone would not remove covariance; independence is required for this factorization. Products of \(L^2\) norms are integrable, which justifies the complete termwise identity.

Expand the Hilbert square as \(\|\sum_iX_i\|^2=\sum_{i,j}\langle X_i,X_j angle\). Each mixed product is integrable by the \(L^2\) inner-product bound, which justifies moving the finite double sum through the integral. For \(i e j\), independence factors \(\mathbb E\langle X_i,X_j angle\) into \(\langle\mathbb EX_i,\mathbb EX_j angle=0\). For \(i=j\), it is \(\mathbb E\|X_i\|^2\). The local facts hint, hcross and hexpand establish these prerequisites and identities separately. Centering without independence would leave the off-diagonal covariances.

Formal correspondence: integrable_inner_of_memLp : Every inner product of two \(L^2\) random variables is integrable. integral_norm_sum_sq_centered_independent : Centered independent Hilbert-valued samples have exactly additive second moments. Independence is used for each mixed term.

steps.title: The variance of an independent sample mean
steps.body:
Let \(N>0\) and let \(\phi\) be square-integrable under probability \(\mu\). On \(\mu^{\otimes N}\) the coordinate samples are independent. Center \(\phi\) by its expectation, expand the squared sample mean, and cancel its off-diagonal pairings. This gives

\[ \mathbb E_{\mu^{\otimes N}} \left\|\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\phi(X_i)-\mathbb E_\mu\phi\right\|^2 =\frac1N\mathbb E_\mu\|\phi-\mathbb E_\mu\phi\|^2. \]

The root mean square sampling factor is \(N^{-1/2}\). This variance identity is an ingredient in particle comparison, not by itself a propagation-of-chaos theorem. Exchangeability alone would not cancel covariances.

Indeed let \(C_i=\phi(X_i)-\mathbb E\phi\). Its average is \(N^{-1}\sum_iC_i\), the expected squared sum is \(N\mathbb E\|C_1\|^2\), and the averaging prefactor is \(N^{-2}\). Their product is \(N^{-1}\mathbb E\|C_1\|^2\). Taking square roots gives \(1/\sqrt N\). Independence here comes from the finite product construction, rather than an assumption about interacting particle states.

On the explicit product probability \(P=\mu^{\otimes N}\), set \(C(a)=\varphi(a)-\mathbb E_\mu\varphi\) and \(X_i(\omega)=C(\omega_i)\). Measure-preserving coordinate evaluation proves that each \(X_i\) has the same finite second moment, zero mean and law, and the product construction proves their joint independence. The exact centered-mean identity is \[\frac1N\sum_i\varphi(\omega_i)-\mathbb E\varphi=\frac1N\sum_iX_i(\omega).\] Thus the previous variance identity gives \[\mathbb E_P\left\|\frac1N\sum_i\varphi(\omega_i)-\mathbb E\varphi\right\|^2=\frac{\mathbb E_\mu\|\varphi-\mathbb E\varphi\|^2}{N}.\] In the code, hXi, hind, hmean, hvar and hid verify each of these assertions. Taking the nonnegative square root gives the RMS version.

Formal correspondence: empiricalAverage : The empirical mean on the explicitly specified finite sample space. iid_empirical_variance : The actual iid finite product gives the exact centered empirical variance. All moments are Bochner integrals, including the mean used for centering. iid_empirical_rms : The same exact identity written as an RMS sampling error.

steps.title: The empirical parameter-gradient variance
steps.body:
Assume \(N>0\), fix \( heta\), and put \(\phi(x)= abla_ heta U( heta,x)\). Joint-gradient Lipschitzness gives affine growth of this observable in its latent input, so it is square-integrable under every finite-second-moment law \(\mu\). Its expectation is \(b_U( heta,\mu)\). The independent-sample identity therefore gives

\[\mathbb E\left\| rac1N\sum_i abla_ heta U( heta,X_i)-b_U( heta,\mu) ight\|^2= rac1N\mathbb E\| abla_ heta U( heta,X)-b_U( heta,\mu)\|^2.\]

This is the exact variance of the empirical parameter force. Its finite variance is derived from the gradient and latent-moment assumptions rather than postulated as an additional sampling-error bound.

For \(\varphi(x)= abla_ heta U( heta,x)\), the parameter projection is nonexpansive and the full score is \(L\)-Lipschitz, so \(\varphi\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz in the latent variable. A latent law with finite second moment therefore makes this observable square integrable. Its Bochner mean is exactly meanFieldDrift, so the general iid identity applies without assuming a separate variance bound for this particular gradient observable.

Formal correspondence: iid_parameterGradient_variance : Exact iid empirical parameter-gradient variance for the actual joint potential. The copies are independent under the displayed finite product.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldParticleDrift..title: The particle drift on a product of square-integrable coordinate spaces
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldParticleDrift..summary: Use a finite product of coordinate \(L^2\) spaces to describe the physical particle system. Specifically let \(H_N=L^2(P;\Theta)\times\prod_{i

steps.title: Coordinate inclusions and square-integrable contractions
steps.body:
Define the latent inclusion \(I_x(x)=(0,x)\). Adding zero parameter coordinates gives \(\|I_xx\|=\|x\|\), and latent projection has norm at most one. For a pointwise linear contraction \(C\), integration of \(\|C(X)\|^2\le\|X\|^2\) gives \(\|C\circ X\|_2\le\|X\|_2\).

Thus coordinate inclusion and projection are contractions also in \(L^2\). They introduce no dimension factor in reconstruction of the random pair. The maximum product norm consequently controls every parameter and tagged latent-coordinate difference.

Formal correspondence: MeanFieldParticleState : Coordinate \(L^2\) space, with the usual product/finite-function maximum norm. jointLatentInclusionCLM : Embed a latent vector into the joint space. lp_linear_norm_le : A pointwise nonexpansive linear map remains nonexpansive on \(L^2\).

steps.title: Reconstruction of a random joint pair
steps.body:
Set \(J(\Theta,X)=I_\theta\Theta+I_xX\). Its representative is \((\Theta(\omega),X(\omega))\) almost surely. The bounded linear inclusions and triangle inequality give

\[\|J(\Theta,X)-J(\Theta',X')\|_2\le\|\Theta-\Theta'\|_2+\|X-X'\|_2.\]

The coordinate \(L^2\) differences bound the reconstructed pair difference. Its representative is exactly \((\Theta(\omega),X(\omega))\), so evaluation of a joint potential or gradient on this Hilbert-space pair agrees with evaluation at the intended parameter and latent vectors.

Formal correspondence: lpJointPair : Pair the common parameter random variable with one latent variable.

steps.title: The empirical particle drift
steps.body:
Apply \( abla V\) to the reconstructed pair \(J(\Theta,X_i)\) for each particle. Define the empirical parameter drift and the individual latent drifts by

\[\mathcal A_N(z)=\left( rac1N\sum_i abla_ heta V(\Theta,X_i),\ ( abla_xV(\Theta,X_i))_i ight).\]

The representative formulas follow from composition and the finite-sum identity. Only the parameter components are averaged, with division justified by \(N>0\). This is the interacting physical-particle drift, retaining the common random parameter; no mean-field expectation is substituted in this definition.

Formal correspondence: lpParticleGradient : The actual joint gradient at the common parameter and the selected particle. lpParticleDrift : The actual particle drift: averaged parameter force and individual latent forces. lpParticleGradient_coe : The gradient random variable has the actual parameter/particle coordinates. lpParticleDrift_parameter_coe : The displayed common-parameter force is precisely the empirical mean. lpParticleDrift_latent_coe : Each latent force is the latent block of its own actual joint gradient.

steps.title: Particle-count-independent Lipschitzness and the integral solution
steps.body:
Every coordinate difference is bounded by the maximum product distance, so pair reconstruction and gradient regularity give \(\|\nabla V(J_i z)-\nabla V(J_i w)\|_2\le2L\|z-w\|\). Averaging the \(N\) parameter terms and dividing by \(N>0\) preserves this bound. The maximum latent-coordinate norm preserves it as well. Hence \(\operatorname{Lip}(\mathcal A_N)\le2L\) independently of \(N\). Picard gives continuous \(Z\) satisfying \(Z_t-Z_0=-\int_0^t\mathcal A_N(Z_s)ds+B_t\) for continuous input with \(B_0=0\).

The state consists of one parameter \(L^2\) vector and finitely many latent \(L^2\) vectors. For particle \(i\), reconstruction gives \(\|\operatorname{pair}(\theta,x_i)-\operatorname{pair}(\vartheta,y_i)\|_2\le\|\theta-\vartheta\|_2+\|x_i-y_i\|_2\le2\|z-w\|\). The \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient therefore bounds its force difference by \(2L\|z-w\|\). Averaging cancels factor \(N\) and gives constant \(2L\). Equivalently the reconstruction factor two is multiplied by \(L\); averaging \(N\) parameter bounds and taking the maximum of latent bounds leaves \(2L\). The finite-horizon integral equation follows from completeness and global drift Lipschitzness.

Formal correspondence: lpParticleDrift_lipschitz : A global dimension-free Lipschitz bound in the coordinate-maximum \(L^2\) norm. exists_lp_particle_integral : Picard constructs the actual finite-particle coordinate integral equations from continuous additive inputs, without a stochastic convergence premise.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldCopies.lean.title: Independent copies and the empirical parameter-force residual
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldCopies.lean.summary: Independent copies of the mean-field state give an empirical drift residual with exact \(N^{-1/2}\) norm factor. Starting with a joint random state on \(Q\), use the finite product \(P=Q^{\otimes N}\) and its coordinate pullbacks. When the reference parameter is deterministic, all copies have the same parameter while their latent components are independent. The copy maps are bounded and linear, so they commute with the reference integral equation. All latent drift residuals cancel; only the centered empirical parameter force remains.

steps.title: The measure-preserving coordinate copy map
steps.body:
For product coordinate \(\omega_i\) define \(C_iX=X\circ\omega_i\). Evaluation preserves the reference measure, so pullback is an \(L^2\) isometry and a bounded linear map. Its representative equals \(X(\omega_i)\) almost surely. Coordinate substitution gives \(C_i(CX)=C(C_iX)\) for bounded linear \(C\), and constants satisfy \(C_i(\operatorname{const}x)=\operatorname{const}x\).

The evaluation \(\omega\mapsto\omega_i\) has pushforward \(Q\); hence integration of \(\|X(\omega_i)\|^2\) gives the original second moment. Pullback is consequently an isometry on \(L^2\). These pointwise and integral identities justify copying the projected reference equations.

Formal correspondence: iidCopyCLM : A genuine iid copy of a random variable on the finite product space.

steps.title: The centered empirical fluctuation norm
steps.body:
For \(N>0\) define \(\mathcal C X=X-\operatorname{const}(\mathbb EX)\) and \(\Delta_N(X)=N^{-1}\sum_iC_iX-\operatorname{const}(\mathbb EX)\). Finite-sum representative identities identify the latter with the centered sample mean. Independence on the product space gives

\[\|\Delta_N(X)\|_{L^2(P)}^2=\frac1N\|\mathcal C X\|_{L^2(Q)}^2,\qquad\|\Delta_N(X)\|_2=\frac{\|\mathcal C X\|_2}{\sqrt N}.\]

The pullback \(X\mapsto X(\omega_i)\) preserves \(Q\) and is a linear isometry. Thus the centered copy sum is an \(L^2\) vector represented by that sample mean. The exact variance statement is

\[\|\text{empirical fluctuation}\|_2^2=\frac{\|X-\mathbb EX\|_2^2}{N},\]

Taking nonnegative square roots gives factor \(N^{-1/2}\). The centered force norm is divided by \(\sqrt N\). This uses independence of reference copies; the later interacting particle states are not assumed independent.

Formal correspondence: lpCenterCLM : Center an actual square-integrable random variable by its expectation. iidEmpiricalFluctuation : The actual finite-product centered empirical mean as an \(L^2\) random variable.

steps.title: The reference particle state with deterministic parameter
steps.body:
Define the reference particle state by

\[\mathcal R_N(X)=\left(\operatorname{const}(\mathbb E P_\theta X),\ (P_xC_iX)_i\right).\]

Bounded linear maps commute with expectation, and a constant has its original value as expectation under a probability measure. Thus if \(P_\theta X=\operatorname{const}\theta\), the parameter component of \(\mathcal R_N(X)\) is \(\operatorname{const}\theta\).

The latent coordinates are independent coordinate copies, while the deterministic parameter is unchanged. The construction is a bounded linear map, which permits passage through the reference time integral.

Formal correspondence: lpExpectationCLM_compLp : Actual expectation commutes with any bounded linear map. iidMeanFieldCopiesCLM : Mean-field parameter expectation and genuine iid latent copies.

steps.title: Reconstruction and drift composition for copied pairs
steps.body:
Recombining the parameter and latent projections recovers the original \(L^2\) vector. For deterministic parameter this gives \(J_i\mathcal R_N(X)=C_iX\). Composition of the copied state with a Lipschitz pointwise drift is the same as copying the composition, since both representatives equal \(b(X(\omega_i))\) almost surely.

For the gradient, this common representative is \(\nabla V(X(\omega_i))\). Hence each reconstructed reference pair has precisely the copied joint drift. This equality causes the latent components to cancel in the particle-minus-reference drift.

Formal correspondence: lpJointPair_projections : Reconstructing one pair from a joint random variable loses no coordinates. iidMeanFieldCopies_joint : Each reference pair is the selected genuine joint copy when its parameter is deterministic. This is an equality of actual \(L^2\) random variables. iidCopyCLM_lpDrift : Actual pointwise Lipschitz drift commutes with an iid pullback.

steps.title: The empirical parameter-force drift residual
steps.body:
Apply the particle drift to \(\mathcal R_N(X)\) and compare it with \(\mathcal R_N(\mathcal A_V(X))\). Reconstruction and gradient commutation identify all latent components, leaving

\[\mathcal A_N(\mathcal R_NX)-\mathcal R_N(\mathcal A_VX)=\left(\Delta_N(P_ heta abla V(X)),0 ight).\]

The maximum product norm and sample-mean variance identity give residual norm \(\|\mathcal C(P_ heta abla V(X))\|_2/\sqrt N\). In detail, latent coordinate \(i\) combines with the deterministic parameter to recover joint copy \(i\). The parameter discrepancy is

\[ rac1N\sum_i abla_ heta V( heta,X_i)-\mathbb E abla_ heta V( heta,X).\]

It is the empirical parameter force minus its expectation. Its norm is the centered single-copy force norm divided by \(\sqrt N\), equivalently \(\|\mathcal C(P_ heta abla V(X))\|_2/\sqrt N\). This exact residual supplies the sampling forcing used in the comparison theorem.

Formal correspondence: iidMeanFieldCopies_drift_residual : The finite-particle drift defect at the constructed iid reference is exactly its centered empirical parameter-gradient error. The latent defect is zero. iidMeanFieldCopies_drift_residual_norm : The actual drift defect has its exact independent-sampling norm.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldForcing.lean.title: Grönwall comparison with an extra continuous noise input
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldForcing.lean.summary: A common sampling factor gives an \(N^{-1/2}\) comparison for an integral drift defect and an additional continuous input. In a Banach space let \(F\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz. Compare two integral equations with common input \(B\), additional input \(A\) in one equation, and reference drift \(G\). Subtracting the additional input before applying Grönwall yields a differentiable remainder without differentiating either noise path.

steps.title: The difference after subtraction of the additional input
steps.body:
Let \(L\ge0\) and \(T\ge0\), and define \(\Psi(L,T)=\int_0^T e^{L(T-s)}ds\). Thus \(\Psi(0,T)=T\), and \(\Psi(L,T)=(e^{LT}-1)/L\) for \(L>0\). Assume \(\|A_t\|\le a\), \(\|F(Y_t)-G_t\|\le C\), and

\[X_t-x=-\int_0^tF(X_s)ds+B_t+A_t,\qquad Y_t-x=-\int_0^tG_sds+B_t.\]

Put \(D_t=X_t-Y_t-A_t\). Subtraction cancels the common input, and the Lipschitz and defect bounds give \(\|D_t\|\le\int_0^t[L\|D_s\|+La+C]ds\). Grönwall then yields \(\|X_t-Y_t\|\le(C+La)\Psi(L,T)+a\) on \([0,T]\).

The continuous inputs \(B,A\) may be Brownian inputs in \(L^2\). Defining \(D_t=X_t-Y_t-A_t\) cancels \(B\) and \(A\) algebraically and leaves

\[D_t=-\int_0^t[F(X_s)-G_s]ds,\quad D_0=0.\]

Continuity of the integrand makes this remainder differentiable with derivative \(-F(X_t)+G_t\). Equivalently, for \(D=X-Y-A\), the remainder \(D\) is differentiable although \(A\) need not be. Since \(X-Y=D+A\), its derivative is bounded by \(L\|D\|+La+C\). Grönwall bounds \(D\), and restoring \(A\) adds \(a\). This proves the estimate using only continuous integral equations.

If \(F\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, \(\|A_t\|\le a\) and \(\|F(Y_t)-G_t\|\le C\), then \[\|D'_t\|\le L\|D_t\|+C+La.\] The right-derivative Grönwall theorem gives \(\|D_t\|\le\operatorname{gronwallBound}(0,L,C+La,T)\) uniformly on \([0,T]\). Adding back \(A_t\) produces the final \(+a\). In Lean, hDI identifies the differentiable integral remainder, hderiv proves its derivative, and hb establishes this exact scalar forcing.

Formal correspondence: integral_forcing_perturbation : Actual integral equations with common input, an additional continuous input, and a uniformly controlled reference-force defect satisfy this finite-horizon bound. Neither a derivative of the input nor an error recurrence is assumed.

steps.title: The comparison with a common inverse sampling factor
steps.body:
The zero-initial-error Grönwall bound is \(C\Psi(L,T)\), where \(\Psi\) is defined above. It is linear in \(C\), including when \(L=0\). Let \(r>0\) and suppose that \(\|A_t\|\le a/r\) and \(\|F(Y_t)-G_t\|\le C/r\) throughout the interval. Substitution in the preceding bound gives

\[\|X_t-Y_t\|\le\frac{(C+La)\Psi(L,T)+a}{r}.\]

Indeed, the differential inequality for the remainder has forcing \(C/r+La/r=(C+La)/r\). Grönwall multiplies this forcing by \(\Psi(L,T)\), and restoring the additional input contributes \(a/r\). For \(r=\sqrt N\), with \(N>0\), the resulting coefficient is independent of \(N\) whenever \(C,L,a,T\) are independent of \(N\).

Formal correspondence: gronwallBound_zero_div : The zero-initial-error Grönwall response is homogeneous in its forcing. integral_forcing_perturbation_scaled : The uniform forcing and input bounds of order \(1/r\) give the same scale for the actual solution error, with an explicit coefficient independent of \(r\).

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldNoise.lean.title: The parameter Brownian input at finite particle count
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldNoise.lean.summary: The common parameter Brownian input has amplitude \(\sqrt{2/N}\). A coordinate pullback on the reference product space gives its exact \(L^2\) norm, bounded on a finite horizon by a coefficient times \(N^{-1/2}\). On \(Q^{\otimes N}\) with \(N>0\), use copy zero of the supplied \(d_\theta\)-dimensional Brownian block. Its amplitude is \(\sqrt{2/N}\), matching the empirical-force fluctuation scale.

steps.title: The pulled-back and scaled parameter Brownian vector
steps.body:
Product coordinate evaluation preserves the reference measure, so each pulled-back scalar path retains its Brownian law. Define \(A_t=N^{-1/2}\sqrt2(B_t^\theta-B_0^\theta)\) as an \(L^2\) vector. The Brownian second-moment construction gives \(L^2\) continuity and zero value at time zero.

The coordinate numbered zero exists under \(N>0\). Its Langevin-scaled noise \(\sqrt2W_t\), multiplied by \(N^{-1/2}\), gives the parameter input. Fixed scaling preserves the \(L^2\) continuity and zero initial value. Equivalently the finite-dimensional Brownian vector is multiplied by \(\sqrt{2/N}\); its inherited \(L^2\) continuity verifies the additive-input hypotheses rather than assuming them for an unspecified process.

Formal correspondence: empiricalParameter_preBrownian : Each coordinate of the common parameter source has the actual Brownian law after pullback to the finite iid product. empiricalParameterNoise : The actual parameter Brownian input, with the particle scaling.

steps.title: Its exact second moment and horizon bound
steps.body:
The sum of parameter-coordinate second moments is \(d_\theta t\). Taking square roots gives

\[\|A_t\|_2=\frac{\sqrt{2d_\theta}\sqrt t}{\sqrt N}\le\frac{\sqrt{2d_\theta}\sqrt T}{\sqrt N},\qquad0\le t\le T.\]

Each scalar increment has variance \(t\). Thus its Langevin vector has squared \(L^2\) norm \(2d_\theta t\). Scaling by \(N^{-1/2}\) yields

\[\|A_N(t)\|_2=\frac{\sqrt{2d_\theta}\sqrt t}{\sqrt N}.\]

Monotonicity bounds the time factor by \(\sqrt T\). In coordinate form the squared norm is \((2/N)\sum_{j=1}^{d_\theta}\mathbb E|B_t^j-B_0^j|^2=2d_\theta t/N\). For \(t\le T\) its root gives horizon coefficient \(\sqrt{2d_\theta T}\), independent of \(N\). Substitution of the constructed Brownian probability space gives an explicit example with these distributions and moments.

Formal correspondence: empiricalParameterNoise_norm : The exact Brownian second-moment scale of the actual parameter input. empiricalParameterNoise_bound : A finite-horizon bound with an explicit coefficient independent of \(N\). canonical_empiricalParameterNoise_bound : A concrete source exists: the Brownian coordinates are the already constructed independent Gaussian time-indicator processes.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldBrownianFamily.title: Independent Brownian coordinates for the particle input
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldBrownianFamily.summary: On \(Q^{\otimes N}\), select the common parameter Brownian coordinates from copy zero and latent coordinate \((i,j)\) from copy \(i\). Independence of source rows and scalar paths gives independence of all selected full paths. Parameter and latent coordinate tags are disjoint, so the first source row may provide both parameter noise and the first particle’s latent noise without repeating any scalar coordinate.

steps.title: An injective selection of source coordinates
steps.body:
Send parameter index \(j\) to \((0,\mathrm{parameter}\ j)\) and latent index \((i,j)\) to \((i,\mathrm{latent}\ j)\). Different coordinate tags separate the two kinds. Within either kind equality of selected indices implies equality of original indices, so the selection is injective.

In coordinate notation parameter index \(j\) selects \((0,\theta_j)\), while \((i,j)\) selects \((i,x_j)\). Evaluate the corresponding source Brownian path in the selected copy. A latent coordinate for particle \(i\) comes from copy \(i\). Even when that copy is zero, its latent tag differs from every parameter tag. Thus no scalar Brownian path is reused.

Formal correspondence: particleBrownianIndex : Select a distinct base-copy/coordinate pair for every particle-noise coordinate. particleBrownianIndex_injective : The common parameter uses copy zero; latent blocks use their respective copies. particleBrownianFamily : The actual joint Brownian source for the interacting particle coordinates.

steps.title: The Brownian law of each selected coordinate
steps.body:
For each selected coordinate, product evaluation preserves the source measure. Composition with its supplied scalar path therefore preserves the standard pre-Brownian law. Every time evaluation remains measurable by composition.

These facts establish the individual process distributions and measurability. Independence of their full paths follows separately from the joint source-family argument.

Formal correspondence: particleBrownianFamily_preBrownian : Every selected coordinate is an actual standard pre-Brownian motion. particleBrownianFamily_measurable : Measurable source evaluations remain measurable after selecting a copy.

steps.title: Independence of the selected full paths
steps.body:
