The product measure makes the full source rows independent, and within each row the scalar coordinate paths are jointly independent. Flattening the two indices gives a jointly independent family indexed by \((i,j)\). The injective selection therefore retains independence.

This is independence of complete selected paths, including the common parameter block and the first latent block from row zero. It is stronger than independence at a single time. The constructed Brownian source supplies the row laws and the coordinate-path independence required for this construction.

First pull each whole Brownian row from the source to one coordinate of the finite product; distinct rows are independent by the product measure. Within a row the supplied coordinate paths are independent, and measure-preserving evaluation retains their joint law. The helper iIndepFun_uncurry' flattens these two levels into a jointly independent family indexed by all copy/coordinate pairs. Finally, precomposition with the injective index map selects the intended subfamily and preserves independence. This proves independence of full coordinate paths, including the parameter path and the first particle's latent path; it does not assert independence of interacting particle states.

Formal correspondence: particleBrownianFamily_paths_independent : Full coordinate-path independence is derived on the actual finite product. There is no assumption of independent particles after interaction. canonical_particleBrownianFamily : The concrete canonical Gaussian time-indicator construction supplies all selected scalar Brownian laws and their full-path independence.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldInitialSource..title: Initialization independent of the Brownian family
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldInitialSource..summary: Let \(\mu\) be a latent probability law with finite second moment and let \(\theta_0\) be a deterministic parameter. Use \(Q=\mu\otimes Q_B\), where \(Q_B\) carries the constructed joint Brownian coordinates. The first coordinate gives the latent initialization and the second gives independent full Brownian paths. The pair initialization is square-integrable and retains the prescribed parameter and latent law. Thus the input assumptions for the mean-field and particle equations follow from these initial data.

steps.title: The product measure and Brownian evaluations
steps.body:
The probability space has measure \(\mu\otimes Q_B\). Every Brownian path depends only on the second coordinate, whose projection preserves its source measure. Its scalar Brownian laws, full-coordinate independence, and measurable evaluations are therefore unchanged. The mass identity is \(Q(\Omega)=\mu(X)Q_B(\Omega_B)=1\cdot1=1\).

Coordinate evaluation measurability also gives measurability of the grouped full paths. Adding the independent latent factor does not change their joint pushforward distribution.

Formal correspondence: meanFieldInitialSource : The supplied latent initialization law times the explicit Gaussian Brownian source. meanFieldInitialBrownian : Brownian coordinates use the independent second factor of the source. meanFieldInitialBrownian_preBrownian : Each coordinate has the actual standard Brownian law on the product source. meanFieldInitialBrownian_paths_independent : The entire coordinate paths remain independent after adding initialization.

steps.title: The square-integrable pair initialization
steps.body:
The map \(x\mapsto(\theta_0,x)\) is measurable and nonexpansive as a function of its latent input. The first product coordinate has the supplied finite second moment. Hence \((\theta_0,X_0)\) is square-integrable and defines an \(L^2\) initialization.

The initialized pair \((\theta_0,X_0)\) has squared norm \(\|\theta_0\|^2+\|X_0\|^2\). Its parameter term is a finite constant and its latent term has finite expectation. Thus it is an element of the joint \(L^2\) space with the prescribed coordinates.

Formal correspondence: meanFieldInitialPair_lipschitz : Holding the parameter fixed embeds latent vectors isometrically into pairs. meanFieldInitial_memLp : A fixed parameter and the actual latent initialization form an \(L^2\) joint vector. meanFieldInitialLp : The actual square-integrable initialization used by the integral constructors.

steps.title: The prescribed marginals and full-noise independence
steps.body:
The pair representative equals \((\theta_0,\omega_1)\) almost surely. Its parameter projection is \(\operatorname{const}\theta_0\), and its latent law is \(\mu\). Initialization is a function of the first product coordinate, whereas every Brownian path is a function of the second. Their full families are therefore independent.

For the pointwise pair \((\theta_0,x)\) this factorization is immediate from the product measure. It retains parameter \(\theta_0\) and latent law \(\mu\). The first coordinate still has that law and parameter \(\theta_0\) is deterministic. Replacing the initialization by an almost-surely equal square-integrable representative preserves both its law and independence from the complete Brownian family.

Formal correspondence: meanFieldInitialLp_parameter : The parameter block is exactly the constant initial parameter in \(L^2\). meanFieldInitialLp_latent_law : Its latent marginal is exactly the supplied finite-second-moment law. meanFieldInitialLp_independent_paths : Initialization is independent of every Brownian coordinate at every time.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldParticles.lean.title: A finite-horizon comparison with independent mean-field copies
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldParticles.lean.summary: Construct one continuous mean-field solution and, on each finite product source, its independent copies. Their particle-drift discrepancy is the centered empirical parameter force. A compact-horizon bound on the single-copy force and the parameter Brownian moment both have the inverse-square-root particle factor. Grönwall therefore bounds every tagged \(L^2\) error. For a globally \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, the coefficient is fixed before particle count is chosen, and the conclusion is uniform over time after taking \(L^2\) norms.

steps.title: A finite horizon bound on the centered reference force
steps.body:
Define \(\mathcal C_V(X)=P_\theta\nabla V(X)-\operatorname{const}\mathbb E[P_\theta\nabla V(X)]\). Gradient composition is Lipschitz, projection is bounded linear, and expectation is continuous, so this centered-force map is continuous. For continuous path \(Y_t\) on compact interval \([0,T]\), its norm has finite bound \(C\ge0\). The constant \(C\) depends on the reference and horizon and not on \(N\).

Indeed the reference is continuous in \(L^2\). Its centered force is continuous on \([0,T]\) and bounded there before any \(N\)-particle product space is constructed. This quantifier order gives a single coefficient for all particle counts.

Formal correspondence: centeredMeanFieldForce : The centered actual parameter force of one mean-field copy. exists_centeredMeanFieldForce_bound : Continuity of the constructed reference supplies a finite force coefficient on a compact horizon. This coefficient is independent of particle count.

steps.title: The copied integral equation and comparison coefficient
steps.body:
The reference-copy operator \(\mathcal R_N\) is bounded and linear, so it commutes with the Bochner time integral. Its application to the mean-field equation gives an exact copied equation. Define

\[C_T=2\big[(C+2Lb)\Psi(2L,T)+b\big].\]

Here \(C\) bounds the single-reference centered force, and \(b/\sqrt N\) bounds the extra parameter input. The empirical-residual identity controls the difference between copied mean-field drift and particle drift. The factor two bounds the sum of the parameter and one latent-coordinate error by twice the maximum product norm.

Formal correspondence: iidMeanFieldCopies_integral_equation : The actual iid reference inherits its integral equation by a bounded linear map, so its forcing is constructed from the mean-field solution. meanFieldParticleConstant : Finite-horizon coefficient in the tagged-coordinate \(L^2\) comparison. \(C\) bounds the actual centered reference force, and \(b\) bounds the parameter Brownian input after multiplication by \(\sqrt N\).

steps.title: The particle integral solution and independent-sample residual
steps.body:
For each \(N>0\), global Lipschitzness gives particle solution \(Z\) with copied latent input and continuous additional parameter input \(A\) bounded by \(b/\sqrt N\). The copied reference residual has norm \(\|\mathcal C_V(Y_t)\|_2/\sqrt N\le C/\sqrt N\). Apply the forcing comparison with drift constant \(2L\). Each coordinate error is bounded by the maximum product error, so

\[\|\Theta_t^N-\theta_t\|_2+\|X_t^{i,N}-X_t^i\|_2\le C_T/\sqrt N,\qquad0\le t\le T.\]

The reference centered force has bound \(C\) on \([0,T]\). For input \(A_N\) the residual bound is \(C/\sqrt N\) and the added-input bound is \(\|A_N\|\le b/\sqrt N\). Equivalently these are \(C/\sqrt N\) and \(b/\sqrt N\) for a \(2L\)-Lipschitz particle equation. The common initial states make the initial discrepancy zero. The coefficient is independent of \(N\) and the conclusion retains the constructed integral equation and independent copied initialization.

The scaled integral-forcing theorem, with particle Lipschitz constant \(2L\), yields \[\|Z_t-R_t\|\le\frac{\operatorname{gronwallBound}(0,2L,C+2Lb,T)+b}{\sqrt N}.\] Each parameter or tagged-latent difference is bounded by the maximum product norm; their sum is therefore at most twice this expression. This accounts for the factor two in meanFieldParticleConstant. The reference and \(C\) are chosen before \(N\), making the coefficient independent of particle count.

Formal correspondence: exists_particle_comparison_of_meanField_solution : The constructed particle solution is uniformly close, in each coordinate \(L^2\) norm, to the genuine iid copies of an actual mean-field integral solution. The reference force coefficient is finite and independent of \(N\).

steps.title: The comparison with the specified Brownian inputs
steps.body:
Continuity of the centered reference force on \([0,T]\) gives a finite \(C\ge0\) such that

\[ \sup_{0\le t\le T}\| \nabla_\theta V(Y_t)-\mathbb E_Q\nabla_\theta V(Y_t)\|_2\le C. \]

This \(C\) is chosen independently of \(N\). The common latent noise cancels on subtraction; subtract the extra parameter input as well before applying Grönwall to the remaining drift integral. Define

\[ \Psi(a,T)=\begin{cases}(e^{aT}-1)/a,&a>0,\\T,&a=0,\end{cases} \qquad C_T=2\big[(C+2Lb)\Psi(2L,T)+b\big]. \]

For each \(N>0\) the construction gives a particle solution with the prescribed independent initialization, and for every tag \(i\),

\[ \sup_{0\le t\le T}\left( \|\Theta_t^N-\theta_t\|_2+\|X_t^{i,N}-X_t^i\|_2\right) \le\frac{C_T}{\sqrt N}. \]

For \(V=g_1+g_2^\eta\) use gradient constant \(L=L_1+1/\eta\). The coefficient may depend on \(\eta\), so uniformity in smoothing is not asserted. The Brownian construction gives \(b=\sqrt{2d_\theta T}\) and jointly independent parameter and latent paths, which supply the intended noise amplitudes in the retained integral equations.

The supremum is taken after the \(L^2\) norm. Proposition C.2, equation (45), instead bounds the expectation of the supremum of the unsquared parameter and latent errors. That quantity and the supremum of the \(L^2\) error norms are not generally ordered. The proved result here is the displayed supremum of the \(L^2\) norms.

Formal correspondence: exists_brownian_meanField_particle_comparison : Both the mean-field reference and finite-particle coordinate processes are constructed from actual Brownian-coordinate inputs. The parameter-noise \(N^{-1/2}\) bound is proved from those laws by empiricalParameterNoise_bound . The conclusion controls each time's \(L^2\) norm uniformly over the horizon.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldCanonical.lean.title: Particle comparison from a prescribed initial latent law
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldCanonical.lean.summary: Let \(\mu\) have finite second moment, let \(\theta_0\) be deterministic, assume \(\nabla V\) is globally Lipschitz, and fix \(T\ge0\). The product with the constructed Brownian source supplies independent initialization and all required noise coordinates. One mean-field reference is then constructed, followed by a particle integral solution for every \(N>0\). Their retained equations and the common finite-horizon bound give the timewise mean-square comparison.

steps.title: Brownian coordinate laws and full-path independence
steps.body:
The initialized Brownian probability space has measurable standard scalar Brownian coordinates, independent as complete paths and independent of initialization. A finite product gives independent copies of the full source. Injective selection of coordinate tags gives the common parameter block and each particle’s latent block without repeating a scalar path.

Therefore all individual Brownian distributions, full-family independence, and initialization independence required in the comparison follow from the product construction, including the case where row zero supplies both parameter and first-particle latent coordinates with different tags.

Formal correspondence: initialized_particleBrownianFamily : Actual interacting-particle Brownian coordinates on the iid initialized canonical source: every coordinate is standard Brownian and all full paths are independent, including common-parameter and first-particle coordinates.

steps.title: A common reference and the particle-count-uniform comparison
steps.body:
Use initial pair \((\theta_0,X_0)\) on \(\mu\otimes Q_B\). Its finite second moment and deterministic parameter were established above. The Brownian integral construction gives continuous \(Y,\theta\) and finite centered-force bound \(C\ge0\). For every \(N>0\) it then gives continuous particle solution \(Z^N\) with independent copied initialization. The inputs are \(\sqrt2 B^{x,i}\) in latent coordinates and \(\sqrt{2/N}B^\theta\) in the parameter, and

\[\sup_{0\le t\le T}\big(\|\Theta_t^N-\theta_t\|_2+\|X_t^{i,N}-X_t^i\|_2\big)\le\frac{C_T}{\sqrt N}.\]

The coefficient is fixed before \(N\) is chosen. This is a supremum of \(L^2\) norms. For every positive \(N\)-the integral equations and deterministic reference-parameter equation remain part of the conclusion, and the uniform quantity is \(\sup_{t\le T}\|Z_t-R_t\|_{L^2}\).

For each \(N>0\) copy the already constructed reference, add parameter noise with amplitude \(\sqrt{2/N}\), and solve the empirical drift equation. The residual and forcing comparison gives \(C_T/\sqrt N\). The same reference-dependent \(C_T\) works for all counts. The construction does not assert an expectation of a samplewise time supremum.

Formal correspondence: exists_canonical_meanField_particle_comparison : From a latent probability law with finite second moment, construct the mean-field reference and actual interacting-particle processes for every positive particle count. The displayed constant is independent of that count; its existence follows from proved finite-horizon moments of the reference.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldParticleLaw.le.title: One-time Wasserstein convergence for tagged particles
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldParticleLaw.le.summary:
At each fixed time the tagged particle pair and its reference copy are defined on the same probability space. Both have finite second moments, and the measure-preserving copy has exactly the original mean-field law. Their joint distribution is consequently an admissible finite-cost coupling. The coordinate \(L^2\) estimate bounds its cost and yields the one-time quadratic Wasserstein rate for the constructed particle process.

The constructed particle/reference pair supplies an actual finite-cost coupling of tagged one-time laws. This module transfers the proved timewise \(L^2\) rate to \(W_2\), keeping the original integral equations and initialization.

steps.title: The unchanged law of a measure-preserving copy
steps.body:
The copy representative is \(X(\omega_i)\) almost surely. Product evaluation pushes \(Q^{\otimes N}\) to \(Q\). Composition of pushforwards therefore gives \(\mathcal L_{Q^{\otimes N}}(C_iX)=\mathcal L_Q(X)\).

Almost-sure replacement of representatives preserves this law. Thus the reference coordinate in the tagged coupling has precisely the original mean-field distribution.

Formal correspondence: iidCopyCLM_law : An actual iid \(L^2\) copy has exactly the original law.

steps.title: The coupling of the tagged pair and its reference copy
steps.body:
On the product space couple particle pair \((\Theta^N,X_i^N)\) with the corresponding copy of \((\theta,X)\). Both belong to \(L^2\), so their quadratic coupling cost is finite. Pair reconstruction and Minkowski give

\[W_2(\mathcal L(\Theta^N,X_i^N),\mathcal L(\theta,X))\le\|\Theta^N-\theta\|_2+\|X_i^N-X_i\|_2.\]

The particle pair \((\Theta_t^N,X_t^{i,N})\) and copied reference have the required marginal laws. Their \(L^2\) moments justify the quadratic cost, whose root is bounded by the sum of coordinate \(L^2\) differences. For latent coordinate \(i\), the same reconstruction estimate in \(L^2\) gives the displayed inequality. Transport, as the infimum over couplings, is no larger. Its finiteness is thus proved before real conversion.

Formal correspondence: tagged_particle_wasserstein_le : The actual tagged-particle pair and the genuine iid copy provide a finite transport coupling. This helper only translates coordinate \(L^2\) distances.

steps.title: The one-time law estimate for the specified particle equation
steps.body:
The pair \((\Theta_t^N,X_t^{i,N})\) has finite second moment, and its reference copy has the law of \(Y_t=(\theta_t,X_t)\). The explicit coupling and coordinate comparison give

\[ W_2\!\left(\mathcal L(\Theta_t^N,X_t^{i,N}),\mathcal L(\theta_t,X_t)\right) \le\frac{C_T}{\sqrt N},\qquad 0\le t\le T. \]

For every positive \(N\), tag, and time, the conclusion retains the empirical-gradient integral equation, independent copied initialization, and copied latent Brownian input plus scaled parameter Brownian input. Thus the law estimate refers to those specified processes.

At each fixed time the coupling proves finite \(W_2\) and bound \(C_T/\sqrt N\), uniformly over the stated interval. This is convergence of tagged one-time laws. A pathwise strong stochastic equation, expected path-supremum bound, or gradient-flow partial differential equation is not asserted by this result.

Formal correspondence: particleBrownianInput : The actual Brownian input in the particle coordinate equations. The parameter noise is scaled by \(1/\sqrt N\); every latent copy keeps its noise. exists_canonical_meanField_particle_law_comparison : From an arbitrary finite-second-moment latent law and independent canonical Brownian source, construct both integral solutions and prove the actual tagged-particle one-time Wasserstein bound, uniformly over the horizon. This uses a different process norm from the source's expected path supremum and does not establish that printed bound.

ProximalLangevin/Check.lean.title: Assumptions and conclusions of the proximal arguments
ProximalLangevin/Check.lean.summary:
The results use convex proximal minimization, the exact particle updates, finite Gaussian-law moments, stationary splitting comparisons, and mean-field integral constructions. The assumption check records where these hypotheses are stated and where they are derived before numerical inequalities are applied. It introduces no further convergence estimate.

This module imports the proximal development and asks Lean to print the axioms used by its principal analytic, algorithmic and stochastic declarations. It is an audit entry point rather than a new mathematical assumption.

steps.title: Hypotheses and scope of the convergence results
steps.body:
A scalar inequality deduced from an assumed recurrence differs from a recurrence proved for a transition law. The splitting convergence theorem uses a recurrence derived from its stationary coupling. The mean-field results retain the constructed integral equations, independent copied initialization, and Brownian input. Checking these dependencies preserves those scopes; the algebraic examples and conditional scalar estimates do not by themselves assert broader stochastic convergence results.

Run lake build ProximalLangevin +ProximalLangevin.Check from the repository root. Each #print axioms command reports the dependency closure of an already checked declaration, including proximal optimality, the three actual algorithm bounds, Brownian coupling and mean-field constructions. The file introduces no new theorem or definition. The audit complements compilation; it does not strengthen any theorem’s stated assumptions or turn conditional scalar statements into algorithm convergence results.

Each #check command asks Lean to elaborate the complete theorem type, retaining every displayed assumption. Each #print axioms command reports the transitive foundational dependencies of that theorem. Compile this module after the library build to inspect that report; these commands check the existing proofs and do not supply new mathematical hypotheses or conclusions.

ProximalLangevin.lean.title: Proximal particle algorithms and mean-field comparisons
ProximalLangevin.lean.summary:
Proximal optimality identifies the Moreau gradient and the particle update formulas. MYIPLA is a smooth Gaussian Euler scheme, PIPULA uses the full envelope’s reduced curvature, and PIPGLA is controlled by its pairwise energy inequality and stationary comparison. Mean-field equations and particle comparisons follow from Lipschitz integral equations and independent-sample variance. Finite potential gaps give the original marginal-center comparisons under their stated assumptions.

The root module gathers proximal calculus, actual particle algorithms, corrected original-center bounds and constructed mean-field comparisons into one importable Lean library. Its imported theorems retain their exact assumptions and scope.

steps.title: Proximal calculus and the different particle estimates
steps.body:
The proximal minimizer and its residual are the common definitions used throughout. The three algorithms then require different analyses: the smoothed Euler identity for MYIPLA, the full-envelope curvature for PIPULA, and the averaged pairwise energy estimate for PIPGLA. The mean-field comparison instead subtracts the empirical particle integral equation from independently copied reference equations. Each result retains its own target distribution, scale-dependent constants, finite-moment conditions, and additional regularity assumptions.

Importing ProximalLangevin makes the checked public development available. The mathematical chain is true proximal minimization, residual/Moreau calculus, exact algorithm identities, genuine finite-moment Gaussian laws, concentration and transport, then the original-center comparison. The splitting chain additionally constructs Brownian stationarity and orthogonality; the mean-field branch constructs continuous \(L^2\) integral equations and actual iid comparisons. Run lake build ProximalLangevin +ProximalLangevin.Check. This umbrella has no local declarations; its proof content is in the linked imported modules.
